title: English, Class 5
subject: English
description: NCERT Grade 5 English, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Unit 1: Let’s Have Fun
chapters.summary: In this chapter: papa searches for his spectacles; papa finds the spectacles; thinking about the poem; ordering words and pair phrases.

lessons.title: Papa Searches for His Spectacles

activities.prompt: Where might Papa’s spectacles be hiding?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Papa Has Lost Something!
activities.body: Today our papa is searching everywhere. He has lost his spectacles. They were his only pair. Without them, Papa cannot read the newspaper, watch TV or cut the vegetables. He wonders where they can be. He checked his pockets, glanced under his chair and searched near the window.
keyPoints: Papa has lost his spectacles.
They were his only pair.
He cannot read, watch TV or cut vegetables without them.
He looked in his pockets, under his chair and near the window.
activities.explanation: When we lose something we use every day, we miss it at once!

activities.prompt: Why does Papa keep searching after looking everywhere?
steps: His spectacles were his only pair, so he needs to find them.
He needs them to read the newspaper, watch TV, and cut vegetables.
He checked pockets, chair, and window because they may hold them.
He looked everywhere without finding them, so he must keep searching.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What has Papa lost today?
options: His spectacles
His umbrella
His school bag
His water bottle
activities.explanation: Papa has lost his spectacles, his only pair.

activities.prompt: The lost spectacles were Papa's only pair.
activities.explanation: Yes, they were his only pair, so Papa misses them a lot.

activities.prompt: Which of these can Papa NOT do without his spectacles?
options: Sing a song
Cut the vegetables
Water the plants
Comb his hair
activities.explanation: Papa cannot cut the vegetables without his spectacles. Singing and combing do not need them.

activities.prompt: Match each thing Papa lost or searched to the right word.
activities.explanation: Papa searched in his pockets, under his chair and near the window.

activities.prompt: Papa can watch TV happily without his spectacles.
activities.explanation: Papa cannot watch TV without his spectacles. Keep looking, Papa!

activities.prompt: Put Papa's search in the order of the story.
activities.explanation: Papa checked his pockets first, then under his chair, then near the window, and at last looked everywhere.

activities.prompt: Why is Papa searching everywhere so carefully?
options: The spectacles were his only pair
He wants to tidy the room
The spectacles were a gift
He wants to find his keys
activities.explanation: They were his only pair, so he wonders where they can be and keeps searching.

activities.prompt: Papa checks his pockets, then his chair, then near the window. Why does he keep looking?
options: He lost his only pair of spectacles.
His spectacles are too small for his face.
His chair is hiding another pair of spectacles.
He wants to find the newspaper first.

why.His spectacles are too small for his fac: This mistake thinks lost spectacles are only a size problem.
why.His chair is hiding another pair of spec: This mistake thinks another pair is hidden under the chair.
This mistake thinks the newspaper matters more than his spectacles.

activities.explanation: This is right because his lost spectacles stop him seeing.

activities.prompt: Papa cannot read today's newspaper. Why can he not read it?
options: His lost spectacles stop him from seeing.
His empty pockets stop him from seeing.
His moved chair stops him from seeing.
His closed window stops him from seeing.

This mistake links empty pockets to poor eyesight.
This mistake links a moved chair to poor eyesight.
This mistake links a closed window to poor eyesight.

activities.explanation: This is right because his lost spectacles stop him seeing the words.

lessons.title: Papa Finds the Spectacles

activities.prompt: What did the child notice that helped Papa find his spectacles?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Papa's Spectacles
activities.body: In the poem Papa's Spectacles, Papa cannot find his spectacles. He cannot read the newspaper, watch TV or cut the vegetables. He looks in his pockets, under his chair and near the window. But the funny thing is this: the spectacles are right there on his head! The child sees them and helps Papa.
keyPoints: The poem is called Papa's Spectacles and it is in Unit 1: Let's Have Fun.
Papa cannot read, watch TV or cut vegetables without his spectacles.
The spectacles are on Papa's head all the time.
activities.explanation: Sometimes we search hard for a thing that is right in front of us!

activities.prompt: Papa cannot read the newspaper. Why does the child go close and speak?
steps: Papa cannot read the newspaper, so he may need his spectacles.
The spectacles are on his head, so the child has a clue.
The child goes close and speaks because Papa may not notice his spectacles.
Therefore, the child tells Papa to stop and says where they are.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the name of the poem you will read?
options: Papa's Spectacles
Papa's Umbrella
Papa's Slippers
activities.explanation: The poem is named Papa's Spectacles. It is in Unit 1: Let's Have Fun.

activities.prompt: Without his spectacles, what could Papa NOT do?
options: Read the newspaper
Ride his bicycle
Water the plants
activities.explanation: The poem says Papa cannot read the newspaper without his spectacles.

activities.prompt: Papa glanced under his ______ while looking for the spectacles.
activities.hint: You sit on it at the table.
activities.explanation: The poem says Papa glanced under his chair. Glanced means he took a quick look.

activities.prompt: Match each place to what Papa did there.
activities.explanation: Papa checked his pockets, glanced under the chair and searched near the window.

activities.prompt: Why does the child go up close and speak to Papa?
options: To tell him his spectacles are on his head
To ask him for a story
To give him a glass of water
activities.explanation: The child goes up close and says that Papa's spectacles are on his head. What a helpful child!

activities.prompt: Put the places Papa looked at in the order of the poem.
activities.explanation: First Papa checked his pockets, then he glanced under his chair, and last he searched near the window.

activities.prompt: Papa searched his pockets, chair, and window. What might he feel?
options: Happy and excited
Calm and relaxed
Confused and worried
Sleepy and bored

why.Happy and excited: Happiness is a mistake; the search shows a problem.
why.Calm and relaxed: Relaxation is a mistake; the repeated search shows concern.
why.Sleepy and bored: Sleepiness is a mistake; active searching does not show tiredness.

activities.explanation: He cannot find the spectacles that are on his head.

activities.prompt: Papa cannot read, watch TV, or cut vegetables. What may he need?
options: His newspaper
His television
His vegetables
His spectacles

why.His newspaper: Newspaper is a mistake; it is what he tries to read.
why.His television: Television is a mistake; it is what he tries to watch.
why.His vegetables: Vegetables are a mistake; they are what he tries to cut.

activities.explanation: The poem links these problems with the spectacles on his head.

activities.prompt: Papa cannot read, watch TV, or cut vegetables. What does this suggest?
options: Papa may enjoy doing all these tasks.
Each task may have a different fault.
One problem may stop all his tasks.
The newspaper, TV, and vegetables may be broken.

Enjoyment is a mistake; inability does not mean he likes a task.
Separate faults are a mistake; the poem gives one clear clue.
why.The newspaper, TV, and vegetables may be: Broken objects are a mistake; the clue points to his spectacles.

activities.explanation: The missing spectacles may explain every problem.

activities.prompt: Papa checked his pockets and looked under his chair. He searched near the window too. What does this show?
options: He cannot find what he is looking for.
He is only waiting for the newspaper.
He is getting ready to take a nap.
He is playing a fun hiding game.

Waiting is a mistake; searching shows active effort.
A nap is a mistake; active searching does not show tiredness.
A game is a mistake; Papa has a real reading problem.

activities.explanation: His repeated searches show that he has not found it.

lessons.title: Thinking About the Poem

activities.prompt: What could Papa be searching for, and where might he find it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What This Lesson Asks You
activities.body: This lesson makes you think about the poem. Papa has lost something, and the poem asks what he is searching for. It asks where he can look and where he finds it at last. It also asks what makes your papa happy. Then you make lists of things people often misplace at home and at school, and think about who helps find them.
keyPoints: Papa is searching for something he has lost.
The poem asks where he can look and where he finds it at last.
You make lists of things misplaced at home and at school.
You think about who helps and how to thank them.
activities.explanation: Good readers think about the poem, not just read it.

activities.prompt: How can a child help Papa search for a lost item and thank the person who helps?
steps: Think of possible places because Papa may have left the item there.
Ask who can help because another person may notice the item.
Express gratitude because it shows that the helper's help mattered.
Therefore, help with the search and thank the helper when the item is found.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is Papa searching for in the poem?
options: His lost item
His school bag
His tiffin box
His favourite toy
activities.explanation: The poem asks what Papa is searching for, and it is something he has lost. Well done!

activities.prompt: The poem asks what makes your ______ happy.
activities.hint: Think about who lost the item in the poem.
activities.explanation: The poem asks you to think about what makes your papa happy. Lovely thinking!

activities.prompt: Match each part of the poem's questions to what it asks about.
activities.explanation: Each question in the poem helps you think about Papa and his lost item.

activities.prompt: About things misplaced at school, what does the list ask you?
options: Who helps find them
Who bought them
Who drew on them
Who packed them
activities.explanation: The list asks who helps in finding misplaced things at school. Good spotting!

activities.prompt: The poem asks you to guess other ______ Papa cannot do without spectacles.
activities.hint: These are small jobs people do every day at home.
activities.explanation: The poem asks you to guess other chores Papa cannot do without his spectacles.

activities.prompt: Put the poem's questions about Papa in the order they come.
items: Where does Papa find it at last?
What other chores can Papa not do without spectacles?
activities.explanation: First we wonder what is lost, then where to look, then where it is found, then what else Papa cannot do.

activities.prompt: Papa searches in several possible places each day. Why does he keep looking?
options: He needs to find his lost item.
He wants to finish all his chores.
He hopes to make someone happy.
He thinks each room is very large.

This mistakes his search for a wish to finish chores.
This mistakes his search for a wish to make someone happy.
This mistakes his search for an opinion about room sizes.

activities.explanation: This is right because Papa is searching for his lost item.

activities.prompt: The story says Papa cannot do a chore without his spectacles. What does this imply?
options: Spectacles help him with the chore.
Spectacles make the chore much longer.
Spectacles hide the chore from him.
Spectacles make Papa forget the chore.

This wrongly treats spectacles as something that adds time.
This wrongly treats spectacles as something that hides the chore.
This wrongly treats spectacles as something that causes forgetfulness.

activities.explanation: This is right because the chore needs his spectacles.

activities.prompt: A child finds a lost item at home and follows the chapter's list. What should the child do next?
options: Name who helped and thank that helper.
Name who helped and ask for some money.
Name who helped and keep the helper's secret.
Name who helped and tell the helper to leave.

This wrongly replaces gratitude with a request for money.
why.Name who helped and keep the helper's se: This wrongly replaces gratitude with keeping a secret.
why.Name who helped and tell the helper to l: This wrongly replaces gratitude with telling the helper to leave.

activities.explanation: This is right because the list asks for gratitude to the helper.

activities.prompt: A child thanks a helper after finding a lost school item. How does the child probably feel?
options: The child feels grateful to the helper.
The child feels angry at the helper.
The child feels afraid of the helper.
The child feels bored by the helper.

This wrongly treats gratitude as anger toward the helper.
This wrongly treats gratitude as fear of the helper.
This wrongly treats gratitude as boredom toward the helper.

activities.explanation: This is right because thanking the helper shows gratitude.

lessons.title: Ordering Words and Pair Phrases

activities.prompt: Can you help words and phrases find their perfect place?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sorting from Small to Big
activities.body: Ascending order means putting things from smallest or lightest to biggest or heaviest. The smallest one comes first. The biggest or heaviest one comes last. You will also meet the word 'pair', as in 'a pair of shoes'. A pair means two things that go together.
keyPoints: Ascending order means smallest or lightest first.
The biggest or heaviest object comes last.
The word 'pair' is used in phrases like 'a pair of shoes'.
activities.explanation: Sort from small to big, and remember that a pair means two things that go together.

activities.prompt: How can a child finish the ordering and pair phrase work?
steps: The smallest or lightest words go first because that is ascending order.
The biggest or heaviest words go last because ascending order ends there.
The child fills each blank because the pair phrases must be complete.
Two more examples finish the task because the chapter asks for them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does ascending order mean?
options: Smallest or lightest first
Biggest or heaviest first
Words in A to Z order
Any order you like
activities.explanation: Ascending order starts with the smallest or lightest. Well done if you picked it!

activities.prompt: In ascending order, the biggest or heaviest object comes last.
activities.explanation: Yes! You save the biggest for the end when you sort in ascending order.

activities.prompt: Complete the phrase: a pair of ______.
activities.hint: You wear them on your feet.
activities.explanation: 'A pair of shoes' is a phrase from your book. A pair means two that go together.

activities.prompt: Put these number words in ascending order. Smallest first!
activities.explanation: Fourteen is smallest, then Twenty-nine, then Forty-seven, and Ninety-one is the biggest.

activities.prompt: Hen, Crow, Sparrow and Eagle are sorted by size in ascending order. Which bird comes last?
options: Sparrow
Crow
Hen
Eagle
activities.explanation: The Eagle is the biggest bird, so it comes last in ascending order.

activities.prompt: In ascending order, the heaviest object comes first.
activities.explanation: Not quite! The heaviest comes last. The lightest one leads the line.

activities.prompt: Match each half to make the idea complete.
pairs: The word used in all the phrases
activities.explanation: Small first, big last, and 'pair' teams up with 'shoes'. Great matching!

activities.prompt: You have arranged a group in ascending order. What does your book ask you to do next?
options: Write two more examples
Draw the biggest object
Count all the objects
Erase the smallest one
activities.explanation: After arranging, your book asks you to write two more examples of your own.

activities.prompt: The numbers are Twenty-nine, Fourteen, Ninety-one, and Forty-seven. Which number comes last in ascending order?
options: the number Fourteen
the number Twenty-nine
the number Forty-seven
the number Ninety-one

why.the number Fourteen: This is the smallest number, so it belongs first.
why.the number Twenty-nine: This number is second, so it cannot be last.
why.the number Forty-seven: This number is third, so it cannot be last.

activities.explanation: This is the biggest number, so it belongs last.

lessons.title: Spelling and Prepositions

activities.prompt: Can you choose the correct spellings and discover where Dad’s spectacles hide?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Check the Spelling and Choose Prepositions
activities.body: The chapter asks you to encircle each word spelt correctly. One example is already done. You can check spellings such as water, vegetables, balloon, house, elephant and spectacles. The chapter calls around, after, before, in, above, on and among the prepositions for the story. The story is about a father who keeps his spectacles at random places.
keyPoints: Choose the correctly spelt word.
Use the listed prepositions to complete the story.
The father keeps his spectacles at random places.
activities.explanation: Read each choice carefully, then check the spelling and the preposition.

activities.prompt: My father cannot find his spectacles. Where should I look?
steps: His spectacles stay at random places, so one usual spot may not work.
He could not find them last week, so a wider search is needed.
The prepositions around, in, above, on, and among help describe places.
Looking around these places gives the best chance of finding them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Spelling
activities.prompt: Which is the correctly spelt word?
options: watter
water
weter
activities.explanation: Good try! The correct spelling is water.

activities.title: Complete the Correct Spelling
activities.prompt: The correctly spelt word in the first choice is ______.
activities.hint: It is the middle spelling in the first choice.
activities.explanation: Great! Water is the correct spelling.

activities.title: Check the First Choice
activities.prompt: The first spelling choice is watter.
activities.explanation: Yes! Watter is the first spelling choice.

activities.title: Find a Preposition
activities.prompt: Which preposition is included in the chapter's list?
options: among
water
elephant
spectacles
activities.explanation: Yes! Among is one of the listed prepositions.

activities.title: Order the Spelling Choices
activities.prompt: Put the spelling choices in the order shown in the chapter.
activities.explanation: Excellent! The choices run from the first to the fifth.

activities.title: Answer from the Story
activities.prompt: When could the father not find his spectacles?
options: last week
at random places
among the prepositions
before the story
activities.explanation: You found it! He could not find his spectacles last week.

activities.prompt: A thirsty child asks for a drink. Which spelling fits?
options: watter
water
weter
whater

why.watter: This spelling has the correct vowel sound in the word.
why.weter: This changes the vowel sound and misspells the word.
why.whater: This adds an extra letter and misspells the word.

activities.explanation: This spells the drink correctly.

activities.prompt: Mum needs green vegetables for dinner. Which spelling fits?
options: vegatables
veggetables
vegetables
vegatabeles

why.vegatables: This changes the middle vowel sound and misspells the word.
why.veggetables: This changes the middle consonant sound and misspells the word.
why.vegatabeles: This changes the ending and misspells the word.

activities.explanation: This spells the word correctly.

activities.prompt: Dad keeps his spectacles at random places. Which spelling fits?
options: spactacles
spektacles
spectacles
spectakles

why.spactacles: This changes the middle vowel sound and misspells the word.
why.spektacles: This changes the middle consonant sound and misspells the word.
why.spectakles: This changes the middle vowel sound and misspells the word.

activities.explanation: This spells the word correctly.

activities.prompt: Dad keeps his spectacles in random places. Last week, he could not find them. What should you do?
options: Look around the room.
Look in one exact place.
Look after the room.
Look above the room.

One exact place may not be where he keeps them.
After means later than something, not around it.
Above means higher than something, not around it.

activities.explanation: Random places are all around, so a wide search helps.

activities.prompt: A balloon is above the house. Which preposition shows the higher place?
options: on the house
in the house
above the house
around the house

why.on the house: On means touching the top or surface of something.
why.around the house: Around means on every side of something.

activities.explanation: Above means higher than something.

activities.prompt: The spectacles are among the books. Which word means with the books?
options: around the books
after the books
before the books
among the books

why.around the books: Around means on every side of the books.
why.after the books: After means later than the books.
why.before the books: Before means earlier than the books.

activities.explanation: Among means together with other things in a group.

lessons.title: Crossword, Speaking, Listening, Writing and Fun

activities.prompt: What secret words will you discover, and can you solve the tricky challenges?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Lesson Full of Fun Tasks
activities.body: This lesson is full of fun tasks. You will solve a crossword using across and down clues. You will say the word for father in your language. You will listen to word pairs and spot the ones that sound different. You will write a poem as a story. Then come puzzles, a star game and a riddle.
keyPoints: A crossword is solved by using across and down clues.
Papa is a common English word for father.
In the listening task, you encircle pairs in which words sound different.
The fun pages have a matchstick puzzle, a red star game and a riddle.
activities.explanation: This lesson mixes word play, speaking, listening and writing with puzzles and a riddle.

activities.prompt: A child hears word pairs and must encircle the pair with different sounds.
steps: The teacher reads the pairs aloud because the task tests careful listening.
Pair-peer, ate-eight, and knot-not sound alike, so they do not meet the rule.
Bed-bad sounds different, so it is the only pair that meets the rule.
The child should encircle bed-bad because the rule asks for different sounds.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: One across clue says: Not far, it's ............ . Which word fits?
options: far
near
under
high
activities.explanation: The clue says not far, so near is the word that fits. Well done if you spotted it!

activities.prompt: One down clue says: I said no but he said ______.
activities.hint: Think of the opposite of no.
activities.explanation: If one person says no and the other agrees to do it, the other says yes. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Papa is a common English word for father.
activities.explanation: Yes, papa is a common English word for father. Many children use it every day.

activities.prompt: The chapter asks you to say one word aloud. Which one?
options: The days of the week
The names of your friends
The word for father in your language
The letters of the alphabet
activities.explanation: You say aloud the word for father in your own language. Every language has its own lovely word for it.

activities.prompt: Match each word with the word it is paired with.
activities.explanation: These word pairs come from the listening task. Listen carefully to hear which pairs sound different.

activities.prompt: While listening, you encircle the pairs in which the words sound the same.
activities.explanation: You encircle the pairs in which the words sound different. Listen carefully to catch them!

activities.prompt: Match each task with what you do in it.
pairs: Use the clues to fill it
Write the poem as a story
Touch the star with the tip of your nose
activities.explanation: Each task has its own instruction. Remember them and the fun pages become easy.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the listening task in the right order.
items: Your teacher reads a few word pairs aloud
You listen carefully to each pair
You encircle the pairs in which words sound different
activities.explanation: First the teacher reads the pairs, then you listen, then you encircle. You followed the steps perfectly!

activities.prompt: A child finds an across clue in the crossword. It says, “Not far, it’s ……” Which word fits?
options: near
far
yes
papa

why.far: Far has the opposite meaning of the clue, so it cannot fit.
why.yes: Yes answers a question but does not fit this clue.
why.papa: Papa means father, but the clue gives no father clue.

activities.explanation: “Not far” means near, so near fits the across clue.

activities.prompt: A child writes, “My ___ is my father.” The class learned a common English word. Which word fits?
options: papa
pair
peer
ate

why.pair: This mistakes a listening word for the word that means father.
why.peer: This mistakes a listening word for the word that means father.
why.ate: This mistakes a listening word for the word that means father.

activities.explanation: Papa is the common English word for father, so it fits the blank.

activities.context: Today, Papa is searching everywhere because he has lost his spectacles. They were his only pair. Without them, he cannot read the newspaper or watch TV, and he cannot cut the vegetables. He wonders where they might be. He has checked inside his pockets, glanced under his chair, and searched near the window. Although he has looked everywhere, he still needs to find them.
activities.prompt: Papa only glanced under his chair. What is the most useful next step?
options: Check beneath the chair more carefully.
Search near the window once more.
Look inside his pockets again.
Check every place he has already searched again.

He has already searched near the window.
He has already checked inside his pockets.
why.Check every place he has already searche: Repeating old searches may not be as useful as checking the chair carefully.

activities.explanation: A careful check may find what the quick glance missed.

activities.context: Today, Papa is searching everywhere because he has lost his spectacles. They were his only pair. Without them, he cannot read the newspaper or watch TV, and he cannot cut the vegetables. He wonders where they might be. He has checked inside his pockets, glanced under his chair, and searched near the window. Although he has looked everywhere, he still needs to find them.
activities.prompt: Why should Papa keep searching instead of stopping now?
options: His missing spectacles are still needed for the tasks he cannot do.
He has already checked every possible place.
The tasks can safely wait until the search is over.
The spectacles will probably appear without another search.

why.He has already checked every possible pl: Looking everywhere does not prove every place was checked.
why.The tasks can safely wait until the sear: He cannot complete the tasks while his spectacles are missing.
why.The spectacles will probably appear with: Nothing suggests that the spectacles will appear by themselves.

activities.explanation: His only pair is needed for several activities.

activities.prompt: Explain why Papa’s search matters so much.
activities.answer: His spectacles are his only pair, so losing them causes several difficulties at once. He cannot read the newspaper or watch TV, and he cannot cut the vegetables. The search matters because finding this pair would remove the problem in all three activities.
points: The spectacles are his only pair.
He cannot read the newspaper without them.
He cannot watch TV or cut the vegetables.
Finding them would solve these difficulties.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child noticed Papa was having trouble. Papa checked inside his pockets, glanced under his chair, and searched near the window. The child told Papa to stop and went up close to speak. The child said Papa’s spectacles were on his head. They were right there on his head. The poem, named Papa’s Spectacles, is in Unit 1: Let’s Have Fun. It says Papa cannot read the newspaper, watch TV, or cut the vegetables.
activities.prompt: Why did Papa check his pockets, glance under his chair, and search near the window?
options: He was trying to find the spectacles that were already on his head.
He was getting ready to cut the vegetables.
He was looking for a newspaper he could read.
He was looking for something to watch on TV.

why.He was getting ready to cut the vegetabl: Cutting vegetables is a task the poem says Papa cannot do.
why.He was looking for a newspaper he could: The poem says Papa cannot read the newspaper.
why.He was looking for something to watch on: The poem says Papa cannot watch TV.

activities.explanation: The searches were meant to locate the spectacles, which were on his head.

activities.prompt: How does the poem’s title and unit information help a reader identify it?
activities.answer: The title, Papa’s Spectacles, tells the reader that the poem is about Papa’s spectacles. The Unit 1: Let’s Have Fun information shows which unit contains the poem. Together, these details help a reader identify the poem and understand what it is about.
points: The poem is named Papa’s Spectacles.
The title identifies Papa’s spectacles as the subject.
The poem is in Unit 1.
The unit is called Let’s Have Fun.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child watches Papa search for something and wonders what he is looking for, which places he should check, and where he will find the lost item at last. The child also thinks about chores Papa cannot do without spectacles and what makes Papa happy. The child makes lists for things often misplaced at home and at school, then thinks about who can help and how to thank them.
activities.prompt: Papa cannot find his missing item, and the child wants to help. What should the child do first?
options: Think about possible places where the item might be, and ask who can help find it.
Ask what makes Papa happy and stop looking for the item.
Wait for Papa to find it and do nothing to help.
Begin with the school list and leave the home list for later.

why.Ask what makes Papa happy and stop looki: Discussing happiness does not help locate the missing item.
why.Wait for Papa to find it and do nothing: Waiting wastes a chance to help with the search.
why.Begin with the school list and leave the: Both home and school lists are part of the task.

activities.explanation: This follows the lesson's questions about possible places and helpers.

activities.context: A child watches Papa search for something and wonders what he is looking for, which places he should check, and where he will find the lost item at last. The child also thinks about chores Papa cannot do without spectacles and what makes Papa happy. The child makes lists for things often misplaced at home and at school, then thinks about who can help and how to thank them.
activities.prompt: A child remembers that something is missing at school. What is the best way to use the lesson's lists?
options: Make a list but do not think about anyone who can help.
Identify the missing school item, think about who can help, and thank the helper after it is found.
Make a list of Papa's chores instead of listing misplaced school things.
Search alone and leave the helper's help out of the plan.

why.Make a list but do not think about anyon: The list should include the missing school item.
why.Make a list of Papa's chores instead of: Papa's chores belong to a different question.
why.Search alone and leave the helper's help: The plan should include both helpers and thanks.

activities.explanation: The lesson also asks about helpers and gratitude.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the home list and the school list?
activities.answer: The home list focuses on things generally misplaced at home and asks who helps find them. The school list does the same for things generally misplaced at school. In both lists, the reader should think about helpers and show gratitude. The main difference is the place connected with the missing things.
points: Home list concerns things misplaced at home
School list concerns things misplaced at school
Both lists ask who helps
Both lists ask how to show gratitude
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is preparing examples for the lesson. The student must arrange each group in ascending order, putting the smallest or lightest first and the biggest or heaviest object last. The groups are Towel, Sari, Handkerchief, Bedsheet; Apple, Strawberry, Cherry, Watermelon; Twenty-nine, Fourteen, Ninety-one, Forty-seven; Hen, Crow, Sparrow, Eagle; and Ox, Rabbit, Elephant, Squirrel. The student must also write two more examples, fill blanks, complete phrases, and note "a pair of shoes."
activities.prompt: The student starts with the number group. Which line places it in ascending order?
options: Fourteen, Twenty-nine, Forty-seven, Ninety-one
Twenty-nine, Fourteen, Ninety-one, Forty-seven
Fourteen, Forty-seven, Twenty-nine, Ninety-one
Ninety-one, Forty-seven, Twenty-nine, Fourteen

why.Twenty-nine, Fourteen, Ninety-one, Forty: This swaps the first two words and breaks ascending order.
why.Fourteen, Forty-seven, Twenty-nine, Nine: This places Forty-seven before the smaller Twenty-nine.
why.Ninety-one, Forty-seven, Twenty-nine, Fo: This starts with the biggest word instead of the smallest.

activities.explanation: Correct: each word is larger than the word before it.

activities.context: A student is preparing examples for the lesson. The student must arrange each group in ascending order, putting the smallest or lightest first and the biggest or heaviest object last. The groups are Towel, Sari, Handkerchief, Bedsheet; Apple, Strawberry, Cherry, Watermelon; Twenty-nine, Fourteen, Ninety-one, Forty-seven; Hen, Crow, Sparrow, Eagle; and Ox, Rabbit, Elephant, Squirrel. The student must also write two more examples, fill blanks, complete phrases, and note "a pair of shoes."
activities.prompt: The student has arranged the groups and completed the phrases. What should the student do to finish the chapter's work?
options: Create two additional examples.
Repeat one of the same groups.
Leave out the extra examples.
Write only the completed shoes phrase.

Repeating a group does not provide two more examples.
This leaves out work that the chapter asks for.
This does not provide the two extra examples.

activities.explanation: Correct: the chapter asks for two more examples.

activities.prompt: Explain how ascending order and putting the biggest or heaviest object last are connected.
activities.answer: Ascending order means placing the words from smallest or lightest first toward biggest or heaviest. Putting the biggest or heaviest object last is therefore the final part of the same order. The student can use both rules together: begin with the smallest or lightest word and end with the biggest or heaviest one.
points: Defines ascending order correctly.
Places the smallest or lightest word first.
Places the biggest or heaviest object last.
Shows that the two rules work together.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A pupil is helping the father find his spectacles because he could not find them last week. He keeps them at random places, so the pupil turns to the spelling and prepositions lesson. The pupil completes the story with the correct prepositions, then returns to the spelling choices and encircles each word that is written correctly. The search then follows the chapter's guidance.
activities.prompt: The father keeps his spectacles at random places. Which preposition should the pupil use for a general search of the possible places?
options: around
among
above
after

why.among: Among would describe a place inside a group.
why.after: After describes something later in sequence.

activities.explanation: Around fits a general search of possible places.

activities.context: A pupil is helping the father find his spectacles because he could not find them last week. He keeps them at random places, so the pupil turns to the spelling and prepositions lesson. The pupil completes the story with the correct prepositions, then returns to the spelling choices and encircles each word that is written correctly. The search then follows the chapter's guidance.
activities.prompt: If the possible places are grouped together and the spectacles are within that group, which preposition should the pupil use?
options: among
around
before
in

why.around: Around describes something surrounding a place.
why.before: Before describes something earlier in sequence.
why.in: In describes something inside one place.

activities.explanation: Among shows that something is within a group.

activities.prompt: How does the spelling task differ from the preposition task in the chapter?
activities.answer: The spelling activity asks the pupil to encircle the word spelt correctly from each choice. The preposition activity asks the pupil to complete the story using the correct prepositions. The first checks the form of words, while the second checks which words fit the places and sequence in the story.
points: The spelling task asks the pupil to encircle the correct word.
The preposition task asks the pupil to complete the story.
Spelling checks word form, while prepositions show position or sequence.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student began the English lesson “Crossword, Speaking, Listening, Writing and Fun” with the crossword activity. The page asked for clues to be used to complete two blanks: across, “Not far, it’s .............,” and down, “I said no but he said .............” For the speaking part, Papa was written beside a prompt. The teacher then prepared to read the word pairs pair-peer, ate-eight, bed-bad, and knot-not while the class listened.
activities.prompt: The student is looking at the across blank and cannot decide what to write. What should the student do next?
options: Read the across clue closely and select a word that fits the blank.
Use the down clue to fill the across blank without checking the across wording.
Put the same word in both blanks because they are on the same page.
Leave the across blank empty until another student gives a word.

why.Use the down clue to fill the across bla: The down clue is meant to guide a different answer.
why.Put the same word in both blanks because: Using one word for both blanks ignores the different clues.
why.Leave the across blank empty until anoth: Leaving the blank empty does not complete the crossword.

activities.explanation: The across clue gives information about the missing word.

activities.context: A student began the English lesson “Crossword, Speaking, Listening, Writing and Fun” with the crossword activity. The page asked for clues to be used to complete two blanks: across, “Not far, it’s .............,” and down, “I said no but he said .............” For the speaking part, Papa was written beside a prompt. The teacher then prepared to read the word pairs pair-peer, ate-eight, bed-bad, and knot-not while the class listened.
activities.prompt: It is the student’s turn for the speaking part of the lesson. What should the student say aloud?
options: Say the word for father in their own language.
Say only the English word Papa.
Say the word silently while pointing to it.
Read one of the word pairs aloud.

Papa is the English word, so saying only Papa misses the language requirement.
why.Say the word silently while pointing to: The speaking task requires saying the word aloud.
The word pairs belong to the listening part of the lesson.

activities.explanation: The chapter asks for the word for father in the student’s own language.

activities.prompt: Explain why listening carefully matters during the word-pair activity.
activities.answer: Listening carefully matters because the task depends on how the pairs sound. The student must hear both words in each pair and decide whether they sound different. After the reading, the student can encircle only the pairs that meet the sound rule instead of marking every pair.
points: Explains that the task depends on sound.
Says that both words in each pair must be heard.
Explains that only pairs with different-sounding words should be encircled.
Says that every pair should not be marked.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Unit 1: Let's Have Fun

activities.prompt: Papa is searching everywhere in the poem. What has he lost?
options: His newspaper
His spectacles
His chair
His pockets
activities.explanation: Papa has lost his spectacles, and they were his only pair. Well done if you remembered!

activities.prompt: Papa cannot cut the vegetables without his spectacles.
activities.explanation: The poem tells us Papa cannot cut the vegetables, read the newspaper or watch TV. His spectacles are very important!

activities.prompt: Papa glanced ______ his chair while searching.
activities.hint: Think of where Papa looked, below the seat.
activities.explanation: Papa glanced under his chair. He also checked his pockets and searched near the window.

activities.prompt: The child goes up close and tells Papa where his spectacles are. Where are they?
options: Under the chair
Near the window
On his head
In his pocket
activities.explanation: The spectacles were right there on Papa's head all along! What a funny surprise.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its correct spelling.
activities.explanation: These are the correct spellings from your book. Practise them and you will always pick the right one.

activities.prompt: Put these fruits in ascending order, from smallest to biggest.
activities.explanation: Ascending order means smallest or lightest first, and the biggest comes last.

activities.prompt: In ascending order, the biggest or heaviest object comes first.
activities.explanation: It is the other way round! Ascending order starts with the smallest or lightest, and the biggest comes last.

activities.prompt: The poem in Unit 1: Let's Have Fun is named Papa's ______.
activities.hint: It is the thing Papa lost and found on his head.
activities.explanation: The poem is called Papa's Spectacles, and it is in Unit 1: Let's Have Fun.

activities.prompt: Put the places Papa searched in the order the poem tells us.
activities.explanation: First Papa checked his pockets, then he glanced under his chair, and then he searched near the window.

chapters.title: Gone with the Scooter
chapters.summary: In this chapter: a summer afternoon; the white ball; gopi asks his friends; claims and the game begins.

lessons.title: A summer afternoon

activities.prompt: What did Gopi hope had fallen from the tree?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A summer afternoon
activities.body: It was a summer afternoon. Gopi was sitting in the veranda, reading a book. Suddenly, he heard something rustling past. Then something fell with a thud in the garden. Gopi wondered what it could be. He thought perhaps a mango had fallen from the tree. He put his book aside, ran into the garden, and searched near the fence and among the bushes.
keyPoints: Gopi was reading a book in the veranda.
He heard a rustle, then something fell with a thud in the garden.
He searched the garden but found nothing.
activities.explanation: A quiet afternoon changes when Gopi hears a strange sound and goes to look.

activities.prompt: Gopi hears a rustle and thud. How can he find the cause?
steps: A rustle and a thud make him wonder about the cause.
He thinks a mango may have fallen because the sounds fit.
He puts his book aside to search for the cause.
The search gives no answer, so the cause stays unknown.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where was Gopi sitting at the start of the story?
options: In the garden
In the veranda
Under a tree
Near the fence
activities.explanation: The lesson says Gopi was sitting in the veranda and reading a book.

activities.prompt: Gopi was sitting in the veranda and reading a ______.
activities.hint: It is something you read.
activities.explanation: Yes! Gopi was enjoying a book in the veranda.

activities.prompt: What did Gopi think had fallen from the tree?
options: A mango
A leaf
A stick
A bird
activities.explanation: Gopi thought that perhaps a mango fell from the tree.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what happened to it.
pairs: fell with a thud in the garden
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each part of the story fits with what Gopi did or heard.

activities.prompt: Put the events of the story in the right order.
items: Something fell with a thud in the garden
He searched between the thick grass
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First the sounds, then Gopi gets up and searches.

activities.prompt: Why did Gopi run into the garden?
options: He wanted to finish his book outside
He wanted to find out what had fallen
He wanted to pick mangoes from the tree
He wanted to play near the fence
activities.explanation: Gopi wondered what had fallen with a thud, so he ran to look for it.

activities.prompt: Gopi hears rustling and a thud. How does he feel?
options: He feels angry because the sounds spoiled his reading.
He feels curious because he wants to know the cause.
He feels excited because he already knows the cause.
He feels worried because he cannot explain the sound.

why.He feels angry because the sounds spoile: This mistakes Gopi's curiosity for anger.
why.He feels excited because he already know: This is wrong because he does not know the cause yet.
why.He feels worried because he cannot expla: This mistakes his curiosity for worry.

activities.explanation: This fits because he wonders what caused the sounds.

activities.prompt: Rustling passes, then a thud follows. What does this imply?
options: A person ran past and then entered the garden.
A mango tree bent and then broke apart.
A moving thing fell and made the thud.
Gopi dropped his book and then stood up.

why.A person ran past and then entered the g: This assumes the sound came from a person.
This turns the sounds into a broken tree.
This mixes Gopi's later actions with the earlier sounds.

activities.explanation: The sounds suggest that something moved and then fell.

activities.prompt: Gopi wonders about a sound. Why does he put his book aside?
options: So he can search for what made the sound.
So he can finish his reading more quickly.
So he can take the book into the garden.
So he can show the book to a visitor.

why.So he can finish his reading more quickl: This assumes reading matters more to him than the sound.
This mistakes putting aside for carrying into the garden.
This mistakes searching for showing the book.

activities.explanation: He wants to find the cause before searching the garden.

activities.prompt: Gopi searches thick grass and then bushes. What does this show?
options: He found the mango and wanted to eat it.
He stopped looking because nothing was there.
He checked places where the fallen thing might be.
He knew the mango stayed in the tree.

This mistakes his guess for something he actually found.
why.He stopped looking because nothing was t: This mistakes finding nothing for deciding to stop.
This mistakes his possibility for something he knows.

activities.explanation: The search shows that he checked likely places.

activities.prompt: Gopi says, “Perhaps a mango fell.” What does “perhaps” show?
options: The mango definitely fell from the tree.
A mango is one possible explanation.
Gopi already saw a mango falling.
Gopi wanted to eat a fallen mango.

This wrongly treats a guess as a certain fact.
This adds a sight that the story does not give.
This mistakes the cause of his thought for his wish.

activities.explanation: It shows that the mango is only one possible answer.

lessons.title: The white ball

activities.prompt: What happens when Gopi finds something unexpected?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Gopi finds a ball
activities.body: Gopi's eyes fell on a heap of dry leaves. On the heap lay a white ball. He reached out and took it in his hands. It was a hockey ball. Gopi wondered whose ball it could be. He looked around and peeped outside the gate, but he could see no one. Just then, he heard his mother calling.
keyPoints: Gopi found a white ball on a heap of dry leaves.
The ball was a hockey ball.
Gopi could see no one outside the gate.
activities.explanation: A small find in the garden starts a big question: whose ball is it?

activities.prompt: Why did Gopi look outside after taking the white ball?
steps: Gopi took the ball because he had noticed it on the dry leaves.
He wondered whose ball it was because he did not know the owner.
He looked around and peeped outside the gate to find the owner.
No one was outside, so Gopi did not find the owner there.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did Gopi find the white ball?
options: On a heap of dry leaves
Under his bed
In the kitchen sink
On the garden wall
activities.explanation: Well done! Gopi's eyes fell on a heap of dry leaves, and the ball was on it.

activities.prompt: The ball on the heap of dry leaves was ______ in colour.
activities.hint: Think of the colour of milk or snow.
activities.explanation: Yes! The lesson calls it a white ball.

activities.prompt: What did Gopi wonder when he held the ball?
options: Whose ball it could be
How much the ball cost
Whether the ball was clean
How to play hockey
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Gopi wondered whose ball it could be.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to what happened with it.
pairs: Gopi found the ball on it
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each part of the story fits neatly with what happened next.

activities.prompt: Put these things in the order they happened in the lesson.
items: Gopi saw a white ball on a heap of dry leaves
Gopi took the ball in his hands
Gopi's mother told him to come inside
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First the find, then the search, then Mother's call.

activities.prompt: Why did Gopi's mother tell him to come inside?
options: Because it was very hot
Because it was getting dark
Because his friends were waiting
Because the ball was broken
activities.explanation: Right! His mother said it was very hot, so she told him to come inside.

activities.prompt: Gopi's eyes fell on a white ball among dry leaves. What did he most likely feel?
options: Curious about the ball and its owner.
Angry that the ball was among dry leaves.
Afraid to leave the ball among dry leaves.
Happy that the white ball was his own.

why.Angry that the ball was among dry leaves: This mistakes his curiosity for anger.
why.Afraid to leave the ball among dry leave: Nothing says that he feared the leaves or ball.
He wondered whose ball it was, so it was not known as his.

activities.explanation: He wanted to know whose ball it was.

activities.prompt: Gopi saw no one outside the gate. What had he hoped to find there?
options: The unknown owner of the white hockey ball.
A different ball for his hockey game.
His own mother waiting near the gate.
A safe place to leave the ball.

This wrongly assumes that he wanted a different ball.
His mother called after he had already seen no one.
He wanted to find the owner, not a place for the ball.

activities.explanation: He wondered whose ball it was before looking outside.

activities.prompt: “He peeped outside the gate.” What does “peeped” mean here?
options: He looked outside without showing himself.
He opened the gate and walked outside.
He shouted loudly for someone to come.
He closed the gate and went inside.

This wrongly treats peeping as opening the gate.
This wrongly treats peeping as calling loudly for someone.
This wrongly treats peeping as closing the gate and leaving.

activities.explanation: Peeping means looking outside carefully without being seen.

activities.prompt: Gopi peeped outside and saw no one. His mother then called him. What can we say?
options: He had not found the ball's owner outside.
He had found the owner waiting outside.
His mother had seen the ball outside.
The ball belonged to nobody at all.

This directly disagrees with the fact that he saw no one.
His mother called him, but she had not seen the ball.
No owner outside did not mean that the ball had no owner.

activities.explanation: Since he saw no one, he did not find the owner outside.

lessons.title: Gopi asks his friends

activities.prompt: What would you do if you found a ball that might belong to someone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Gopi makes a good choice
activities.body: Gopi found a ball that afternoon. He went inside, drank a glass of water and lay down on the mat. He thought he cannot keep the ball for himself. He said he will ask around. In the evening, he went to the nearby playground where his friends gathered to play hockey. He told them about the ball and asked if anyone lost one recently.
keyPoints: Gopi found a ball and decided not to keep it.
He went to the playground in the evening to ask his friends.
His friends gathered there regularly to play hockey.
activities.explanation: Gopi is honest. He wants to find the real owner of the ball.

activities.prompt: Gopi found a ball. How can he find the person who lost it?
steps: He cannot keep it because someone may have lost it.
He will ask around because he wants to find the owner.
The playground is useful because his friends gather there regularly.
Ramani may be the owner because she says the ball is hers.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did Gopi go in the evening?
options: To the market
To the nearby playground
To his school
To a friend's house
activities.explanation: In the evening, Gopi went to the nearby playground to meet his friends.

activities.prompt: All his friends regularly gathered at the playground to play ______.
activities.hint: It is a game played with sticks and a ball.
activities.explanation: The friends met at the playground to play hockey together.

activities.prompt: Match each person to what they said or did.
pairs: Lost a ball four months ago
activities.explanation: Each friend said something different about the ball Gopi found.

activities.prompt: How long ago did Manoj lose his ball?
options: Four months ago
Four days ago
One week ago
One year ago
activities.explanation: Manoj said he lost a ball four months ago. That was a long time before Gopi found his ball.

activities.prompt: Put the things Gopi did in the correct order.
items: He drank a glass of water.
He lay down on the mat.
In the evening, he went to the playground.
He told his friends about the ball.
activities.explanation: First Gopi went inside, drank water and rested. Later, in the evening, he asked his friends about the ball.

activities.prompt: Why did Gopi ask his friends if anyone lost a ball recently?
options: He wanted to sell the ball for money
He wanted to find the ball's real owner
He wanted to play hockey with it
He wanted to buy a new ball
activities.explanation: Gopi felt he could not keep the ball for himself. Asking around was his way to find its true owner.

activities.prompt: You find a ball. It may belong to someone. What does Gopi's choice show?
options: He wants to hide it from everyone.
He wants to return it to its owner.
He wants to give it to a stranger.
He wants to keep it for himself.

This mistake thinks Gopi plans to hide the ball.
This mistake assumes he will give it to a stranger.
This mistake ignores his words about keeping the ball.

activities.explanation: This is right because Gopi does not want to keep the ball.

activities.prompt: A friend claims, "The ball is mine." What does this suggest about the ball?
options: The speaker never plays with any ball.
Another friend must be the ball's owner.
The finder may have found two different balls.
The speaker may be the ball's owner.

This mistake assumes claiming ownership means she never plays.
This mistake ignores Ramani's claim about the ball.
why.The finder may have found two different: This mistake confuses one claim about ownership with another ball.

activities.explanation: This is right because Ramani says the ball is hers.

activities.prompt: Gopi says he will ask around. How does he feel about the ball?
options: He feels sure that no one owns it.
He feels angry with all his friends.
He feels responsible for finding its owner.
He feels that he should keep it.

This mistake treats asking around as proof that nobody owns it.
This mistake mistakes his responsibility for anger at his friends.
This mistake ignores his statement that he cannot keep it.

activities.explanation: This is right because asking around shows that he wants to help.

activities.prompt: Your friends regularly play hockey nearby. Why ask there about a lost ball?
options: Your friends may have kept the ball.
Your friends may have lost the ball.
Your friends may have wanted a new ball.
Your friends may have forgotten the playground.

This mistake changes losing the ball into keeping it.
This mistake thinks wanting a new ball explains his question.
why.Your friends may have forgotten the play: This mistake forgets that his friends gather at the playground.

activities.explanation: This is right because Gopi asks if a friend lost a ball.

lessons.title: Claims and the game begins

activities.prompt: How will the friends react when Gopi reveals the surprising ball?

activities.body: Jay hit the ball very hard. It flew past the playground gate and fell into the basket of a passing scooter. The scooterist did not know this and drove on. The children ran to the gate, but the scooter and the ball were both gone. They looked at each other and burst into laughter.

activities.context: On a summer afternoon, Gopi was sitting in the veranda and reading a book. Suddenly, he heard something rustling past. Something fell with a thud in the garden. He wondered what it could be and thought that perhaps a mango had fallen from the tree. Gopi put his book aside, got up, and ran into the garden. He searched between the thick grass near the garden fence but found nothing. He looked among the bushes, but nothing was there again.
activities.prompt: After finding nothing in the grass or bushes, what would Gopi most sensibly do next?
options: Keep looking around the garden for the cause of the sounds.
Go back to the veranda and wait for the sound to happen again.
Search only among the bushes and ignore other parts of the garden.
Decide that the sound came from the veranda and stay there.

why.Go back to the veranda and wait for the: Waiting might be sensible, but he had already searched the grass and bushes.
why.Search only among the bushes and ignore: Looking only among the bushes would limit his search unnecessarily.
why.Decide that the sound came from the vera: The sound came from outside in the garden, so staying in the veranda would not help.

activities.explanation: This is sensible because the cause of the sounds was still unknown.

activities.explanation: He would first check the place where the sound occurred.

points: The unusual sounds made him curious.
A falling mango was only one possible explanation.
He put his book aside before investigating.
He searched the grass and the bushes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

The instructions tell Jay to score.
Jay's task is not to wait for Gopi.
why.Move the ball towards the centre of the: Deepak and Ramani have already played the ball.

activities.explanation: Manoj is waiting at the goalpost.

activities.context: During the game, Manoj went to the goalpost. He liked to be a goalkeeper. Gopi stood at the centre of the field with the hockey stick and passed the ball to Deepak. Deepak drove the ball towards Ramani. Ramani dribbled the ball with the stick, and the ball went to Jay. Manoj told Jay to play the shot and drive it towards the goalpost. Jay tightened his wrist around the stick, and the flat side touched the ball.
activities.prompt: If Manoj had not told Jay where to direct his shot, what would Jay not know?
options: Which direction to send the shot.
When to take the shot.
How firmly to hold the stick.
Whether to use the flat side of the stick.

The instruction also tells Jay to play the shot.
Jay tightens his wrist as he prepares to play.
why.Whether to use the flat side of the stic: The flat side touches the ball when he plays the shot.

activities.explanation: Manoj's direction was towards the goalpost.

activities.prompt: Explain how passing, driving and dribbling are different in this passage.
activities.answer: Passing sends the ball from one player to another, as Gopi does to Deepak. Driving sends the ball towards another player, as Deepak does towards Ramani. Dribbling means moving the ball with the stick, as Ramani does before the ball goes to Jay.
points: Gopi passes the ball to Deepak.
Deepak drives the ball towards Ramani.
Ramani dribbles with the stick.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Gone with the Scooter

activities.prompt: Something fell with a thud in the garden. What did Gopi first think it was?
options: A mango from the tree
A hockey ball
A bird's nest
A dry leaf heap
activities.explanation: Gopi thought perhaps a mango had fallen from the tree. Good remembering!

activities.prompt: Gopi's eyes fell on a heap of dry leaves. On it lay a white ______.
activities.hint: It is round and Gopi picked it up.
activities.explanation: A white ball lay on the heap of dry leaves. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Manoj said he lost a ball four months ago.
activities.explanation: That is why Gopi said the ball he found could not be Manoj's.

activities.prompt: Gopi said he cannot keep the ball for himself. What did he decide to do?
options: Ask around for the owner
Hide it under the leaves
Throw it over the gate
Give it to his mother
activities.explanation: Gopi is honest. He went to the playground to ask who had lost the ball.

activities.prompt: Match each friend to what they did in the game.
pairs: Dribbled the ball with the stick
activities.explanation: The ball travelled from Gopi to Deepak, then Ramani, then Jay. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Put the journey of the ball in the right order.
items: Jay hit the ball very hard
The ball went past the playground gate
The ball fell into the basket of a passing scooter
The children ran to the gate
activities.explanation: The ball flew off, landed in the scooter basket, and was gone before the children reached the gate.

activities.prompt: The scooterist knew that the ball had fallen into his basket.
activities.explanation: The scooterist was unaware of what had happened, so he just drove past.

activities.prompt: Manoj grabbed the ball and tossed it to Deepak. Why did Gopi shout 'Stop'?
options: He wanted to play before dark
He wanted to keep the ball
He wanted to go home
He wanted to give it to Ramani
activities.explanation: Gopi shouted stop and said, 'Let us play before it gets dark.'

activities.prompt: The scooter was gone and the ball was gone too. What did the children do?
options: They burst into laughter
They began to cry
They ran after the scooter
They went home sadly
activities.explanation: They looked at each other and burst into laughter. What a funny ending!

chapters.title: Unit 2: My Colourful World
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the rainbow poem; new words and let us think; let us learn and let us listen; let us speak.

lessons.title: The Rainbow poem

activities.prompt: Why might a rainbow seem to bow over trees and skies?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sailing and the lovely bow
activities.body: In Unit 2, My Colourful World, you will recite a poem in the Let us Recite section. Boats sail on rivers and ships sail on seas. Clouds sail across the sky. The poem says clouds are prettier than boats and ships. It also tells us about bridges on rivers, and a bow that builds a road from earth to sky.
keyPoints: Boats sail on rivers and ships sail on seas.
Clouds sail across the sky and are prettier than boats and ships.
The bow builds a road from earth to sky.
activities.explanation: The poem takes you from rivers and seas right up to the sky.

activities.prompt: A child watches boats and clouds and wonders which the poem calls prettier.
steps: Boats and ships sail on water, so they form the first comparison.
Clouds sail across the sky, so they can be compared with boats and ships.
The poem calls clouds prettier than both, so clouds are the clear favourite.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What sails on the rivers in the poem?
options: Ships
Clouds
Boats
Bridges
activities.explanation: Well done! The poem says boats sail on the rivers.

activities.prompt: Clouds sail across the ______.
activities.hint: It is the high space far above us.
activities.explanation: Great! Clouds sail across the sky.

activities.prompt: The poem says something is prettier than boats and ships. What is it?
options: Clouds
Rivers
Bridges
Seas
activities.explanation: The poem says clouds are prettier than boats and ships.

activities.prompt: Match each thing in the poem to where it sails or what it does.
activities.explanation: Each one has its own place, from the rivers up to heaven.

activities.prompt: Put these lines from the poem in the order you recite them.
activities.explanation: The poem starts on the rivers, moves to the seas, then the sky, and finally heaven.

activities.prompt: The bow rises so high that it overtops something. What does it overtop?
options: The seas
The trees
The boats
The bridges
activities.explanation: Yes! The bow overtops the trees as it builds a road from earth to sky.

activities.prompt: A child hears the clouds are prettier. How might the child feel?
options: excited and happy about the clouds
worried and afraid of the clouds
angry and upset with the boats
lonely and bored by the sky

why.worried and afraid of the clouds: The poem does not make clouds seem frightening.
why.angry and upset with the boats: The praise is for clouds, not anger at boats.
why.lonely and bored by the sky: The poem does not show boredom with the sky.

activities.explanation: This fits the poem's positive view of clouds.

activities.prompt: What might a child do after hearing the poem praise clouds?
options: Look up to watch the clouds.
Watch only the boats and ships.
Go and hide below a bridge.
Look down at the river water.

Choosing only boats and ships ignores the praise of clouds.
Hiding below a bridge is not suggested by the poem.
Looking down moves away from the clouds the poem praises.

activities.explanation: A child wanting to see what the poem praises would look up.

activities.prompt: In "The bow overtops the trees," what does "bow" most likely mean?
options: a shape that rises above the trees
a boat that stays below the trees
a bridge that crosses the rivers
a cloud that moves above the seas

why.a boat that stays below the trees: Boats sail on water and cannot overtake trees.
why.a bridge that crosses the rivers: Bridges stay on rivers, while the bow rises above trees.
why.a cloud that moves above the seas: Clouds sail across the sky, while the bow overtops trees.

activities.explanation: A bow rises over trees and reaches toward the sky.

activities.prompt: Why does the poem make the bow sound prettier than the bridges?
options: It rises over trees and reaches the sky.
It stays on rivers below the trees.
It sails on seas beside the clouds.
It moves across the sky like clouds.

This wrongly places the bow on rivers below the trees.
This wrongly makes the bow another thing sailing on the seas.
This confuses the bow with clouds, which merely sail across the sky.

activities.explanation: The bow overtops trees and reaches from earth to sky, unlike bridges.

activities.prompt: What do bridges and the bow share in the poem?
options: They are both among the prettiest things.
They are both the only things that sail.
They both build roads from earth to sky.
They both travel across rivers and seas.

Only clouds, boats, and ships are described as sailing.
Only the bow builds a road from earth to sky.
Bridges stay on rivers, while the bow rises above trees.

activities.explanation: The poem praises the bridge and makes the bow prettier than it.

lessons.sceneCaption: White clouds float across a bright blue sky.

lessons.title: New Words and Let us Think

activities.prompt: Which bridge does the poet like most, and why?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three New Words from the Poem
activities.body: This lesson teaches three new words: overtops, bridges and bow. A bow here is the lovely arch in the sky. The poem says the bow overtops the trees, so it rises higher than them. It says the bow builds a road from earth to sky, and it is prettier than the bridges. Then you think about what 'these' means in each stanza.
keyPoints: The new words are overtops, bridges and bow.
The bow overtops the trees and builds a road from earth to sky.
The poem says the bow is prettier than the bridges.
The word 'these' means different things in stanza one and stanza two.
activities.explanation: Learn the new words first, then the poem's ideas become easy to think about.

activities.prompt: Why does the poem's bow seem special beside trees and bridges?
steps: The bow overtops the trees, because it rises above them.
The bow is prettier than the bridges, because the poem compares their beauty.
The bow builds a road from earth to sky, so it joins the ground and sky.
Therefore, the bow seems special because it is beautiful and reaches high.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which new word means 'rises higher than'?
options: overtops
bridges
bow
river
activities.explanation: The poem says the bow overtops the trees, so it goes higher than them. Well done!

activities.prompt: The poem says the bow builds a road from earth to ______.
activities.hint: Look up on a rainy day. What do you see far above?
activities.explanation: The bow makes a lovely road that goes from the earth right up to the sky.

activities.prompt: Match each word to what the poem says about it.
pairs: builds a road from earth to sky
activities.explanation: Each word tells us something special about the poem's picture. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: What does the word 'these' do in the poem?
options: It means different things in each stanza
It means the same thing in both stanzas
It means only the bow
It means only the trees
activities.explanation: 'These' points to different things in stanza one and stanza two. That is why the chapter asks what it means each time.

activities.prompt: Which question does the chapter ask you to think about?
options: Which bridge does the poet like more?
Which boat is the fastest?
Which river is the longest?
Which tree is the tallest?
activities.explanation: The chapter asks which bridge the poet likes more. Thinking about it helps you understand the poem.

activities.prompt: Put the bow's road in order, from where it starts to where it ends.
items: The road starts on the earth
It goes over the tops of the trees
activities.explanation: The bow overtops the trees and builds a road from earth to sky, so it climbs up and up. Lovely ordering!

activities.prompt: The bow is called prettier than the bridges. What does this show?
options: The bow is valued for its beauty.
The bridges are valued for their beauty.
Both bow and bridges look equally beautiful.
Beauty is not compared in the poem.

This reverses which thing the poem praises.
why.Both bow and bridges look equally beauti: This misses the clear comparison between bow and bridges.
This ignores the poem's direct beauty comparison.

activities.explanation: The poem directly says that the bow is prettier.

activities.prompt: The bow builds a road from earth to sky. What picture does this create?
options: Earth and sky seem joined together.
Earth seems covered with many roads.
Sky seems pushed down onto earth.
The road seems to sink far underground.

This imagines many roads instead of one joining road.
This imagines the sky coming down instead of joining.
This imagines the road going down instead of upward.

activities.explanation: The road links earth and sky in the poem's image.

activities.prompt: In two stanzas, 'these' points at different things. What does this show?
options: It points to whatever things are being shown.
It always points to boats in each stanza.
It always points to bridges in each stanza.
It keeps the same meaning in each stanza.

why.It always points to boats in each stanza: This assumes one fixed object, like boats.
why.It always points to bridges in each stan: This assumes one fixed object, like bridges.
why.It keeps the same meaning in each stanza: This ignores the different things in the two stanzas.

activities.explanation: 'These' takes its meaning from what it points at.

activities.prompt: The chapter asks which bridge the poet likes more. Why?
options: To compare the bridges and explain a choice.
To find one bridge name and copy it.
To count how many bridges are shown.
To choose quickly without any reasons.

This mistakes thinking for copying a name.
This ignores the need to think about meaning.

activities.explanation: It invites readers to compare choices and explain them.

activities.prompt: The chapter asks about ships on rivers and boats on seas. Why?
options: To see whether each boat fits that water.
To show that both boats must stay on land.
To compare both boats with every bridge.
To find what kind of trees make boats.

why.To show that both boats must stay on lan: This mistakes water questions for a claim about land.
This mistakes the subject from sailing to bridges.
This mistakes the subject from sailing to boat materials.

activities.explanation: The questions check ships with rivers and boats with seas.

lessons.title: Let us Learn and Let us Listen

activities.prompt: Can we discover new words by listening, playing, and rearranging letters?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rhyming Words are Sound Friends
activities.body: Rhyming words end with the same sound, like ship, chip and trip. In this lesson you will play with words from a poem. You will rearrange letters to make words, find rhyming pairs, give the poem a new title, and play an action game with a friend.
keyPoints: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
Ship rhymes with chip and trip.
The lesson has word games and a pair action game.
activities.explanation: Words that rhyme are sound friends, and this lesson is full of them.

activities.prompt: A child wants to show understanding of the poem. How can the child complete the chapter's poem tasks?
steps: The child rearranges letters because the chapter asks for words from the poem.
The child finds two pairs of rhymes because the poem's matching sounds should be checked.
The child writes a new title because a fresh title is another required choice.
These steps help the child finish the poem work and show understanding.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Listen Carefully, Play Together
activities.body: Your ears are your best tool here. Listen for the ending sound of each word. Tree, bow and rain are words your book gives for rhyming. For each one, you can think of five rhyming words. Then play the action game in pairs and have fun with a friend.
keyPoints: Listen for the ending sound to find rhymes.
Tree, bow and rain are words for rhyming.
The action game is played in pairs.
activities.explanation: Good listening helps you hear rhymes and enjoy the game.

activities.prompt: Which pair of words rhymes?
options: tree and bow
rain and ship
chip and trip
chip and tree
activities.explanation: Chip and trip both end with the same sound as ship, so they rhyme.

activities.prompt: Chip rhymes with ship.
activities.explanation: Well done! Chip and ship end with the same sound, so they rhyme.

activities.prompt: The lesson gives chip and ______ as rhyming words for ship.
activities.hint: It starts with t and rhymes with ship.
activities.explanation: Trip ends with the same sound as ship and chip.

activities.prompt: Match each task in the lesson to what it means.
pairs: A different name for the poem
activities.explanation: Each task in your book has its own fun job. You know them all now!

activities.prompt: The lesson asks you to write ______ rhyming words for each word.
activities.hint: Count the fingers on one hand.
activities.explanation: Five rhyming words for each word. You can do it!

activities.prompt: Bow and rain rhyme with each other.
activities.explanation: Bow and rain end with different sounds. They are both rhyming words in the lesson, but they do not rhyme with each other.

activities.prompt: Put these tasks from your book in the order they appear in the lesson.
items: Rearrange letters to make words from the poem
Find two pairs of rhyming words from the poem
Give the poem a new title
Play an action game in pairs
activities.explanation: This is the order of the tasks in your book. You remembered it well!

activities.prompt: The poem's letters are mixed up on the page. What should the child do next?
options: Rearrange the letters to form poem words.
Read the letters aloud without changing them.
Give every letter a new title.
Play an action game with a friend.

why.Read the letters aloud without changing: This mistake thinks unchanged letters can still make the words.
This mistake treats a title as something made for each letter.
This mistake chooses the action game instead of solving the letters.

activities.explanation: This is right because rearranging mixed letters forms the poem's words.

activities.prompt: The reader thinks the poem's current title needs a fresh choice. What should the reader make?
options: Make a new title for the poem.
Find two pairs of rhyming words.
Give each word five new rhymes.
Play an action game with a friend.

This mistake thinks a rhyme task can replace a new title.
This mistake follows the five-rhyme task instead of the title task.
This mistake chooses a game when a title is needed.

activities.explanation: This is right because the chapter asks for a new title.
