lessons.sceneCaption: Two children play a lively blindfold game together.

lessons.title: Let us Speak

activities.prompt: How can our voice make a poem feel happy, angry, or surprised?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One Poem, Many Voices
activities.body: Speaking a poem is more than saying words. You can say the same poem in a happy voice, an angry voice or a surprised voice, and it feels different each time. In this lesson you will practise voices with two poems. Colours is about crayons and sharing. Aachoo! is about a mighty elephant with a mighty cold who goes shopping.
keyPoints: The same poem can be said in a happy, angry or surprised voice.
Colours is a poem about crayons and sharing.
Aachoo! is a poem about an elephant with a cold.
activities.explanation: Your voice can paint feelings, just like colours paint pictures.

activities.prompt: Your crayon pack has only a few crayons. What can you do to get a full pack?
steps: Your pack has only a few crayons because it does not yet have everything.
The poem says that sharing crayons gives a full pack.
You should share your crayons because sharing fills the pack.
So, sharing crayons helps you get a full pack.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You recite a poem about a glad, sunny day. Which voice fits best?
options: An angry voice
A surprised voice
A happy voice
activities.explanation: A glad poem sounds best in a happy voice. Your voice shows the feeling.

activities.prompt: The chapter asks you to recite a poem in an angry voice.
activities.explanation: Yes, an angry voice is one of the ways to say the poem. Try it softly first!

activities.prompt: The poem Colours says you have a few ______.
activities.hint: You colour pictures with them.
activities.explanation: The poem says you have a few crayons, in red, yellow and blue.

activities.prompt: Match each voice to the line or scene that fits it best.
pairs: Sharing crayons for a full pack
An elephant in a handkerchief shop
activities.explanation: Sharing crayons is happy news. Needing the red can sound cross. An elephant shopping is a big surprise.

activities.prompt: Put the story of Aachoo! in the right order.
items: A mighty elephant got a mighty cold
The elephant went to buy a handkerchief
The elephant asked for a sheet instead
activities.explanation: First came the cold, then the shopping trip, then the surprise, then the clever ask for a sheet.

activities.prompt: The sales girl was angry when the elephant came to her shop.
activities.explanation: She was not angry. She was surprised to see an elephant buying a handkerchief!

activities.prompt: Why was the sales girl surprised in the poem Aachoo!?
options: A tiny mouse came to buy a crayon
A mighty elephant came to buy a handkerchief
A happy child came to share some crayons
activities.explanation: A mighty elephant asking for a handkerchief is a big surprise for a shop girl.

activities.prompt: The poem says sharing crayons gives a full pack. You have only a few crayons. What should you do?
options: Share the crayons
Hide the crayons
Keep one crayon
Buy more crayons

why.Hide the crayons: This keeps the crayons apart instead of sharing them.
why.Keep one crayon: This keeps only one crayon instead of sharing the crayons.
why.Buy more crayons: This misses the poem’s idea that sharing fills the pack.

activities.explanation: This is right because the poem says sharing gives a full pack.

lessons.sceneCaption: A colorful 24-pack of Crayola crayons includes the colors named in the poem.

lessons.title: Let us Write

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how two words become one brand-new word?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words Make Friends Too
activities.body: A word can join a friend word to make a brand new word. Rain joins bow to make rainbow. Earth joins worm to make earthworm. Table joins cloth, and note joins book. Some words, like bridge, can be a naming word (noun) and also a doing word (verb). Watch how words team up!
keyPoints: Two words can join to make one new word.
Rain + bow makes rainbow; note + book makes notebook.
Bridge can be a noun and also a verb.
activities.explanation: Words are friendly. When they join hands, they make new words.

activities.prompt: Can 'bridge' name a thing and describe an action?
steps: Roots form a bridge, which names a thing. So 'bridge' works as a noun.
Planks bridge a stream, which shows an action. So 'bridge' works as a verb.
Both uses appear, so 'bridge' can be a noun and a verb.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its friend word.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins to make one new word: rainbow, earthworm, tablecloth and notebook.

activities.prompt: The word 'bridge' can be a noun and also a verb.
activities.explanation: Yes! Bridge can name a thing (noun) and also show an action (verb).

activities.prompt: In Meghalaya, the writer saw a special bridge. What was it made of?
options: steel
roots
stones
rope
activities.explanation: The bridge in Meghalaya was made of roots. Nature can build bridges too!

activities.prompt: Some planks of wood were used to ______ the stream.
activities.hint: Here the word shows an action, not a thing.
activities.explanation: Here bridge is a verb. The planks joined across the stream to bridge it.

activities.prompt: Put these in order to build the new word.
activities.explanation: First word, then friend word, then the new word they make together: rainbow!

activities.prompt: In your book, every opposites answer begins with the same letter. Which letter is it?
options: S
M
P
T
activities.explanation: All the opposites answers begin with S. Keep that trick in mind!

activities.prompt: Rain appears in the sky. A bow curves beside it. Together, they make a word. Which word is it?
options: rainbow
raincoat
raindrop
rainboat

why.raincoat: Raincoat uses coat instead of bow.
why.raindrop: Raindrop uses drop instead of bow.
why.rainboat: Rainboat uses boat instead of bow.

activities.explanation: Rain and bow make rainbow, so this is right.

activities.prompt: A worm lies in the earth. The words 'earth' and 'worm' join. Which joined word do they make?
options: earthworm
earthwork
earthware
earthward

why.earthwork: Earthwork uses work instead of worm.
why.earthware: Earthware uses ware instead of worm.
why.earthward: Earthward uses ward instead of worm.

activities.explanation: Earth and worm make earthworm, so this is right.

activities.prompt: A cloth covers a table. The words 'table' and 'cloth' join. Which joined word do they make?
options: tablecloth
tableware
tablebook
notetable

why.tableware: Tableware uses ware instead of cloth.
why.tablebook: Tablebook uses book instead of cloth.
why.notetable: Notetable uses note instead of table.

activities.explanation: Table and cloth make tablecloth, so this is right.

activities.prompt: A child keeps many notes inside a book. The joined word names this book. Which word is it?
options: notebook
notecase
notehouse
notetable

why.notecase: Notecase uses case instead of book.
why.notehouse: Notehouse uses house instead of book.
why.notetable: Notetable uses table instead of book.

activities.explanation: Note and book make notebook, so this is right.

activities.prompt: Roots form a bridge. Planks also bridge a stream. How does 'bridge' work in both sentences?
options: Only a naming word
Only an action word
Both naming and action
Neither naming nor action

why.Only a naming word: The child missed the action use in the plank sentence.
why.Only an action word: The child missed the naming use in the roots sentence.
why.Neither naming nor action: The child treated both clear uses as missing.

activities.explanation: One use names a thing, and the other shows an action.

lessons.title: VIBGYOR, Kitchen Colours, Let us Do, Let us Explore

activities.prompt: Can you discover what secrets colours hold in rainbows and kitchens?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Colours All Around Us
activities.body: VIBGYOR helps you remember the seven rainbow colours in order. Its letters stand for Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red. Sunlight splits into these colours when it passes through rain droplets. Kitchen items add colour and taste to food. A spinning colour disc shows that white light contains many colours.
keyPoints: VIBGYOR shows rainbow colours in order.
Sunlight splits into seven colours through rain droplets.
Kitchen items add colour and taste to food.
activities.explanation: Colours help us understand rainbows, kitchen food and white light.

activities.prompt: After rain, a child sees sunlight split into seven colours. How can the child explore and remember their order?
steps: The child uses VIBGYOR because it gives seven rainbow colours in order.
The child matches seven letters to seven colours, making VIBGYOR a guide.
The child spins the disc because white light contains many colours.
The child concludes that rain droplets split sunlight into VIBGYOR's seven colours.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which colour comes third in VIBGYOR?
options: Blue
Green
Violet
Orange
activities.explanation: Blue comes after Violet and Indigo. Great remembering!

activities.prompt: In VIBGYOR, G stands for ______.
activities.hint: This letter comes after B.
activities.explanation: G stands for Green. You remembered it well!

activities.prompt: Match each letter to its rainbow colour.
activities.explanation: These pairs match V and Violet through Y and Yellow.

activities.prompt: What do kitchen items add to food, according to the lesson?
options: Heat and weight
Colour and taste
Sound and size
Speed and distance
activities.explanation: Kitchen items add both colour and taste to food.

activities.prompt: Put these VIBGYOR colours in order.
activities.explanation: VIBGYOR begins with Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green and Yellow.

activities.prompt: What does the spinning disc show about white light?
options: It has no colours.
It is made of rain.
It has one colour only.
It has many colours.
activities.explanation: The disc shows many colours. When it spins very fast, your eyes see white.

activities.prompt: Sunlight passes through rain droplets. Why might the child look for a rainbow?
options: To watch sunlight split into seven colours.
To find human-made things in the rain.
To make kitchen items taste colourful.
To learn about kitchen items and food.

Ships and bridges do not explain why rainbows appear.
Kitchen items do not make sunlight split into colours.
Learning about food does not explain this rainbow sighting.

activities.explanation: Sunlight and rain droplets can show all seven colours.

activities.prompt: A child must say the seven rainbow colours quickly and in order. Which plan is best?
options: Use VIBGYOR and match each letter.
Sort the colours by kitchen item size.
Read the colours from a spinning disc.
List human-made things before natural things.

Kitchen item sizes do not match the rainbow colour order.
The disc shows many colours, but not their rainbow order.
why.List human-made things before natural th: Human-made and natural groups do not match the rainbow order.

activities.explanation: VIBGYOR keeps all seven colours in order through their letters.

activities.prompt: A child spins the colour disc very fast and sees white. What does this show?
options: White light is made of many colours.
White light is made of no colours.
Many colours together always look black.
Slow spinning makes every colour disappear.

No colours misunderstands what the disc shows.
Black is not what the spinning disc makes the child see.
why.Slow spinning makes every colour disappe: Slowing the disc does not remove the colours.

activities.explanation: Many colours blend into white when the disc spins fast.

activities.prompt: A child adds kitchen items to food. What should the child expect to change?
options: The colour and the taste of food.
The colour and the smell of food.
The taste and the texture of food.
The texture and the smell of food.

Smell is not one of the two changes from kitchen items.
Texture is not one of the two changes from kitchen items.
Texture and smell are not the two changes from kitchen items.

activities.explanation: Kitchen items add both colour and taste to food.

activities.prompt: A poem joins clouds and rainbows in one group. It joins ships and bridges in another group. What does the poem show?
options: Natural things and human-made things form groups.
Kitchen items add colour and taste to food.
Sunlight and rain droplets make seven colours.
VIBGYOR helps us remember seven colours.

why.Kitchen items add colour and taste to fo: The poem groups things, but it does not discuss kitchen food.
why.Sunlight and rain droplets make seven co: The poem does not explain how sunlight splits into colours.
The poem does not use VIBGYOR to remember rainbow colours.

activities.explanation: Clouds and rainbows are natural, but ships and bridges are human-made.

activities.context: A child stands beside a river and looks from the water to the sky. A boat sails on the river, while a ship sails on the sea. Clouds sail across the sky, and the child thinks they are prettier than boats and ships. There are bridges on the river. The child also sees the bow above the trees, where it builds a road from earth to sky, and thinks it is prettier than the bridges.
activities.prompt: If the bow appears above the trees, what change in the scene should the child expect?
options: A road would open from the ground toward the sky.
A boat would begin sailing through the trees.
A bridge would sink below the river.
Clouds would stop moving across the sky.

why.A boat would begin sailing through the t: Boats sail on rivers, not through trees.
Bridges are on rivers, and nothing says they sink.
The clouds sail across the sky, and the bow does not change that.

activities.explanation: The bow builds a road from earth to sky.

activities.context: A child stands beside a river and looks from the water to the sky. A boat sails on the river, while a ship sails on the sea. Clouds sail across the sky, and the child thinks they are prettier than boats and ships. There are bridges on the river. The child also sees the bow above the trees, where it builds a road from earth to sky, and thinks it is prettier than the bridges.
activities.prompt: What would remain above the trees even if the clouds stopped sailing across the sky?
options: An arch rising from earth toward sky
A boat crossing the river
A ship sailing on the sea
A bridge on the river

why.A boat crossing the river: The boat sails on the river.
why.A ship sailing on the sea: The ship sails on the sea.
why.A bridge on the river: The bridges are on the rivers.

activities.explanation: The bow builds a road from earth to sky.

activities.prompt: Explain how the poem compares the things in the sky with the things on the earth.
activities.answer: The poem places boats and ships on water, bridges on rivers, and clouds in the sky. It then places the bow above the trees and gives it a road from earth to sky. This makes the bow special because it connects the ground with the sky and is prettier than the bridges.
points: Boats and ships sail on water.
Bridges are on the rivers.
Clouds sail across the sky.
The bow connects earth and sky and is prettier than the bridges.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the English lesson, a student opens “New Words and Let us Think” and sees overtops, bridges, and bow. The poem uses “bow,” and “these” points to different things in stanzas one and two. The class discusses which bridge the poet likes more, what “these” means in each stanza, and whether ships sail on the river, boats sail on the sea, bridges are built on the river, or a road is built from earth to sky.
activities.prompt: If the poem stopped saying that the bow is prettier than the bridges, which conclusion would be correct?
options: The poem would no longer clearly prefer the bow.
The bridges would then be preferred in the comparison.
The bow would then be shown rising above the trees.
The two meanings of “these” would become identical.

why.The bridges would then be preferred in t: Changing the preference does not automatically reverse the poet’s choice.
why.The bow would then be shown rising above: The detail about the bow being above the trees is separate from the comparison.
why.The two meanings of “these” would become: The meanings of “these” depend on the stanzas, not on which bridge is preferred.

activities.explanation: Without the stated preference, the comparison no longer clearly favors the bow.

activities.context: During the English lesson, a student opens “New Words and Let us Think” and sees overtops, bridges, and bow. The poem uses “bow,” and “these” points to different things in stanzas one and two. The class discusses which bridge the poet likes more, what “these” means in each stanza, and whether ships sail on the river, boats sail on the sea, bridges are built on the river, or a road is built from earth to sky.
activities.prompt: If a reader says that bridges are built on the river and the bow makes a path from earth to sky, which poem details support that reading?
options: The bridge question and the road image.
The sea-sailing question and the meaning of “these.”
The word list and the tree-topping detail.
The ship question and the question about the bow’s prettiness.

why.The sea-sailing question and the meaning: The sea-sailing question and the word’s meaning do not support both claims.
why.The word list and the tree-topping detai: The word list does not support both claims, and the tree detail supports only part of the reading.
why.The ship question and the question about: The ship question and the comparison do not establish the two details.

activities.explanation: The chapter asks about a bridge on the river, and the poem links the bow with a road to the sky.

activities.prompt: Explain why the bow is presented as more attractive than the bridges.
activities.answer: The poem says that the bow is prettier than the bridges. It also shows the bow overtopping the trees and building a road from earth to sky. The direct comparison explains the poet’s choice, while the other descriptions strengthen the bow’s attractive place in the poem.
points: States that the bow is prettier than the bridges.
Explains that the bow overtops the trees.
Mentions the road from earth to sky.
Connects the details to the poet’s preference.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the lesson, a student group works through “Let us Learn and Let us Listen.” They rearrange letters from the poem to make words, find two pairs of rhyming words, and think of a new title. For ship, chip and trip are given as rhymes. Tree, bow, and rain are listed as words for rhyming. The students must find five rhyming words for each word. Finally, they organize themselves in pairs for the action game.
activities.prompt: The group has completed the word-making, rhyme-finding, and title tasks. What should they do next according to the lesson?
options: Begin the action game in pairs.
Find only one more pair of rhyming words.
Rearrange the poem’s letters once more.
Give the poem the title they already wrote.

why.Find only one more pair of rhyming words: They have already found the required two pairs.
The letter-rearranging task is already complete.
why.Give the poem the title they already wro: The new-title task is also complete.

activities.explanation: This is the final task in the case.

activities.context: During the lesson, a student group works through “Let us Learn and Let us Listen.” They rearrange letters from the poem to make words, find two pairs of rhyming words, and think of a new title. For ship, chip and trip are given as rhymes. Tree, bow, and rain are listed as words for rhyming. The students must find five rhyming words for each word. Finally, they organize themselves in pairs for the action game.
activities.prompt: The teacher has written a title on the board. A student thinks this means the title task is finished. What should the student do?
options: Write a different title for the poem.
Copy the title already written by the teacher.
Rearrange the letters in the teacher’s title.
Use the teacher’s title for the action game.

why.Copy the title already written by the te: Copying the teacher’s title does not meet the task.
why.Rearrange the letters in the teacher’s t: Rearranging a title is not the title task.
why.Use the teacher’s title for the action g: The action game does not require using a title.

activities.explanation: Students are asked to provide their own title.

activities.prompt: Why does the lesson include word, rhyme, title, and pair activities?
activities.answer: The poem is used for several kinds of work. Students rearrange its letters, find two pairs of rhyming words, and create a new title. They also find five rhyming words for each word and work in pairs for an action game. This makes the lesson include both written and shared activities.
points: Rearranging letters from the poem
Finding two pairs of rhymes
Providing a new title
Working in pairs for the action game
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the lesson, pupils recited in happy, angry and surprised voices. They first recited “Colours.” It said, “I need the red,” and described red, yellow and blue crayons while also mentioning green, purple and black. Sharing crayons gives a full pack. Then they recited “Aachoo!” A mighty elephant with a mighty cold went to buy a handkerchief. The sales girl was surprised when asked for a sheet instead.
activities.prompt: In the “Colours” part of the lesson, what would the pupils have if they shared their crayons as the poem suggests?
options: They would have a complete collection.
They would have only the red crayons.
Their pack would still be missing crayons.
The green, purple and black crayons would disappear.

Sharing adds crayons instead of leaving only red.
why.Their pack would still be missing crayon: A full pack means that no crayons are missing.
why.The green, purple and black crayons woul: The poem mentions those colours, but sharing does not remove them.

activities.explanation: The poem says that sharing produces a full pack.

activities.context: During the lesson, pupils recited in happy, angry and surprised voices. They first recited “Colours.” It said, “I need the red,” and described red, yellow and blue crayons while also mentioning green, purple and black. Sharing crayons gives a full pack. Then they recited “Aachoo!” A mighty elephant with a mighty cold went to buy a handkerchief. The sales girl was surprised when asked for a sheet instead.
activities.prompt: Which recitation voice should pupils use for the sales girl’s part in “Aachoo!”?
options: The voice that shows an unexpected reaction.
The voice that shows anger.
The voice that shows happiness.
The voice that shows annoyance.

Anger does not match the reaction described in the poem.
Happiness does not match the reaction described in the poem.
Annoyance is not the reaction stated; the girl was surprised.

activities.explanation: The sales girl was surprised by the request for a sheet.

activities.prompt: How does the happy voice differ from the angry and surprised voices when reciting the same poem?
activities.answer: The words of the poem do not change. The speaker changes the manner of reciting them: happy, angry or surprised. Therefore, the same poem can be presented in different ways, and the chosen voice tells the listener which of these feelings the speaker is showing.
points: The poem’s words stay the same
The speaker changes the voice
The voices are happy, angry and surprised
The voice changes how the poem is presented
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a lesson, a learner joins words. Rain and bow make rainbow. Earth joins with a friend word to make earthworm, table joins with cloth to make a new word, and note joins with a friend word to make notebook. Bridge can be a noun and a verb. The learner has seen a bridge made of roots in Meghalaya. Some planks of woods were used to bridge the stream. All opposites answers must begin with S.
activities.prompt: If the learner joins table and cloth, which new word should be written?
options: tablecloth
earthworm
notebook
rainbow

why.earthworm: Earthworm is made by joining earth with a friend word.
why.notebook: Notebook is made by joining note with a friend word.
why.rainbow: Rainbow is made by joining rain and bow.

activities.explanation: Table and cloth join to make tablecloth.

activities.context: During a lesson, a learner joins words. Rain and bow make rainbow. Earth joins with a friend word to make earthworm, table joins with cloth to make a new word, and note joins with a friend word to make notebook. Bridge can be a noun and a verb. The learner has seen a bridge made of roots in Meghalaya. Some planks of woods were used to bridge the stream. All opposites answers must begin with S.
activities.prompt: The learner is writing an answer to an opposites question. What should the learner do?
options: Start with the letter S.
Start with the letter N.
Start with the letter R.
Start with the letter T.

Starting with N would not follow the rule.
Starting with R would not follow the rule.
Starting with T would not follow the rule.

activities.explanation: All opposites answers must begin with S.

activities.prompt: Explain how joining a friend word can make a new word, using examples from the case.
activities.answer: A word can join a friend word to make a new word. Rain and bow make rainbow. Earth with a friend word makes earthworm, table with cloth makes a new word, and note with a friend word makes notebook. In each example, joined words give a new word.
points: Words are joined with friend words.
Rain and bow form rainbow.
Earth, table, and note show different joining examples.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why VIBGYOR is useful for remembering the colours of the rainbow.
activities.answer: VIBGYOR is useful because it is an easy way to remember the seven colours of the rainbow in the correct order. Each letter gives the first letter of a colour: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red. The learner can therefore recall the whole sequence from one word.
points: VIBGYOR is an easy memory method.
It gives the correct order of all seven colours.
Each letter begins the name of a rainbow colour.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Unit 2: My Colourful World

activities.prompt: In the poem, where do boats sail?
options: On the seas
Across the sky
On the rivers
Over the trees
activities.explanation: The poem says boats sail on the rivers. Ships sail on the seas, and clouds sail across the sky.

activities.prompt: The poem says that ships sail on the river.
activities.explanation: Ships sail on the seas. Boats are the ones that sail on the rivers.

activities.prompt: The bow builds a road from earth to ______.
activities.hint: Think of where the rainbow ends, high above the trees.
activities.explanation: The bow builds a road from earth to sky. That is why the poet loves it so much.

activities.prompt: Match each letter of VIBGYOR to its colour.
activities.explanation: VIBGYOR helps you remember the seven colours of the rainbow in order.

activities.prompt: The poet thinks the bow is prettier than which things?
options: The boats and ships
The bridges
The clouds
The trees
activities.explanation: The poem says the bow is prettier than the bridges. Bridges are pretty, but the bow wins!

activities.prompt: Clouds and rainbows are human-made things.
activities.explanation: Clouds and rainbows are natural things. Ships and bridges are the human-made ones.

activities.prompt: Rain and bow are friend words. Together they make a ______.
activities.hint: It is the colourful arch in the sky after rain.
activities.explanation: A word can join a friend word to make a new word. Rain plus bow makes rainbow.

activities.prompt: Put the rainbow colours in VIBGYOR order.
activities.explanation: VIBGYOR runs Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red. You have placed the first five in order!

activities.prompt: In the poem Aachoo!, what did the elephant ask for instead of a handkerchief?
options: A sheet
A blanket
A big towel
A new trunk
activities.explanation: A handkerchief is far too small for a mighty elephant, so he asked for a sheet instead. That surprised the sales girl!

activities.prompt: Match each word to the new word it makes with a friend.
activities.explanation: Words love to join friends. Earth, note, table and rain each make a brand new word this way.

chapters.title: The Wise Parrot
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the parrot in the golden cage; a message in the forest; words, phrases and groups; present perfect and bird sanctuaries.

lessons.title: The Parrot in the Golden Cage

activities.prompt: What might the parrot ask the merchant to bring back from far away?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Golden Cage and a Free Sky
activities.body: A rich merchant lived in a quiet village. He kept a bright, talkative parrot in a cage of gold. The parrot had a sharp mind and entertained the merchant with stories and songs. The merchant looked after its needs very well. Yet the parrot wanted open skies, green trees, and flying. When the merchant went away, he wanted to bring back something from the far-off land.
keyPoints: The merchant cared for the parrot very well.
The parrot wanted open skies, green trees, and flight.
The merchant wanted to bring the parrot a gift.
activities.explanation: The parrot was cared for, but it still wanted to fly.

activities.prompt: The merchant goes far away for business. What should he bring back for the parrot?
steps: The parrot has already tasted tender fruits and chillies, so food is not its main wish.
Stories and songs already entertain the merchant, so they are not its deepest wish.
The parrot wants open skies, green trees, and the joy of flying.
Therefore, the merchant should bring back something that lets the parrot enjoy flying.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did the merchant keep his parrot?
options: A cage of gold
A box of wood
A room of stone
A nest of leaves
activities.explanation: The merchant kept the bright parrot in a cage of gold.

activities.prompt: The merchant lived in a busy city.
activities.explanation: Good effort. The merchant lived in a quiet village.

activities.prompt: The parrot had tasted tender ______ and chillies.
activities.hint: It is the food listed before chillies.
activities.explanation: The parrot had already tasted tender fruits and chillies.

activities.prompt: Match each beginning with its matching ending.
pairs: looked after its needs very well
activities.explanation: The parrot entertained the merchant with stories and songs. The merchant cared for the parrot's needs.

activities.prompt: Why did the merchant go far away?
options: For business
For pleasure
For shopping
For hunting
activities.explanation: The merchant went far away for business.

activities.prompt: What did the merchant find very hard to accept?
options: Letting the parrot go
Buying a golden cage
Keeping the parrot fed
Waiting for more songs
activities.explanation: The merchant could not bear to let the parrot go away.

activities.prompt: The parrot wants open skies and green trees. How does it feel inside the golden cage?
options: It wants to be free outside.
It wants a new golden cage.
It wants more stories and songs.
It wants the merchant to leave.

This mistake confuses a comfortable home with what the parrot truly wants.
This ignores the parrot's wish to fly in the sky.
This confuses wanting open space with wanting the merchant to leave.

activities.explanation: This is right because the parrot wants the open skies and green trees.

activities.prompt: The merchant looks after the parrot’s needs well. Why can he not let it go?
options: He cares deeply and wants it close.
He dislikes caring for the parrot.
He wants the parrot to leave.
He thinks the cage is too small.

This mistake ignores how well the merchant looks after the parrot.
This says the opposite of what his feelings show.
This mistake gives the parrot's wish to the merchant instead.

activities.explanation: This is right because he cannot bear to let the parrot go away.

activities.prompt: The merchant wants to bring back something special. What does the parrot most hope for?
options: To fly freely in the open sky.
To hear more stories and songs.
To eat tender fruits and chillies.
To live in another golden cage.

This mistake chooses entertainment instead of the parrot's greatest wish.
The parrot has already tasted these foods, so they are not its main wish.
This mistake thinks a rich cage can replace the open sky.

activities.explanation: This is right because the parrot wants to taste the joy of flying.

lessons.title: A Message in the Forest

activities.prompt: Could a message hidden in the forest surprise someone far away?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Parrot's Message
activities.body: The merchant travelled through a forest and saw a flight of parrots. He gave them his pet's greetings. One parrot fell like a stone from a tree to the ground. The merchant hurried home, worried about his message. At home, his own parrot fell from its perch. He thought it had died. Then it stretched its green wings and flew into the sky. It said its friend had shown it how to escape.
keyPoints: The merchant sent his pet's greetings to forest parrots.
One parrot fell from a tree, and the merchant hurried home.
The merchant's pet flew away after its friend taught it how to escape.
activities.explanation: The pet flies away after the merchant shares the message.

activities.prompt: A pet bird falls from its perch. Why might its owner think it has died?
steps: The pet fell from the perch, so the merchant thought it had died suddenly.
He placed it on the windowsill so it could reach the open sky.
The parrot stretched its wings and flew, so it was alive.
Its friend taught it to escape, so the merchant's fear was wrong.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Merchant's Gift
activities.prompt: What did the merchant give the parrots?
options: his pet's greetings
a closed basket
a broken branch
a shiny coin
activities.explanation: He passed on his pet's greetings, as the lesson describes.

activities.title: A Flight of Birds
activities.prompt: The merchant saw a flight of ______ in a forest.
activities.hint: They were a group of birds.
activities.explanation: The lesson says he saw a flight of parrots in the forest.

activities.title: Story Details
activities.prompt: Match each part of the story with its matching detail.
pairs: described his journey's wonders and beauty
showed the pet how to escape
activities.explanation: Each detail helps you remember what happened in the story.

activities.title: At Home
activities.prompt: What did the merchant think had happened to his pet?
options: It had gone outside.
It was singing loudly.
It had died suddenly.
It was sleeping deeply.
activities.explanation: The sudden fall made him think his beloved pet had died.

activities.title: The Parrot's Escape
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: The merchant's parrot fell from the perch to the cage floor.
The merchant placed the bird on the windowsill.
The parrot stretched its green wings and flew into the open sky.
The parrot said its friend had shown it how to escape.
activities.explanation: The order follows the events from falling to escape.

activities.title: How Did It Escape?
activities.prompt: Why could the parrot escape from the cage?
options: Its friend had shown it how.
The wind had carried it outside.
The merchant had opened the door.
A hunter had freed it.
activities.explanation: The parrot said that its friend had shown it how to escape.

activities.prompt: A parrot falls like a stone. The merchant suddenly hurries away. Why does he act this way?
options: He is distressed by what he has seen.
He is excited to chase the other parrots.
He wants to sell the fallen bird.
He is bored that the forest has birds.

why.He is excited to chase the other parrots: This mistakes fear for excitement, which would not cause him to leave.
This wrongly assumes that he wanted to catch and sell the bird.
This mistakes urgency for boredom, but the fall made him distressed.

activities.explanation: The fall causes distress, so the merchant hurries away.

activities.prompt: The merchant's pet falls from its perch. He puts the bird on the windowsill. Why might he do this?
options: He may want a cleaner place for the cage floor.
He may give the bird a way to fly away.
He may expect the bird to call its friends.
He may want to show the bird to his friends.

why.He may want a cleaner place for the cage: This thinks he cared about tidiness rather than the bird's flight.
why.He may expect the bird to call its frien: This mistakes a possible greeting for the real reason for moving it.
why.He may want to show the bird to his frie: This assumes visitors mattered more than helping the bird fly.

activities.explanation: The windowsill gives the bird a route toward the open sky.

activities.prompt: The merchant tells his pet about the other bird's shock. Soon the pet falls from its perch. What does this suggest?
options: The pet was pleased to hear about the forest.
The pet wanted to hide the merchant's keys.
The pet had forgotten the forest completely.
The pet was strongly affected by the news.

why.The pet was pleased to hear about the fo: This mistakes a fall for happiness, but the pet seemed deeply affected.
why.The pet wanted to hide the merchant's ke: This invents a wish for keys, with no support from the story.
why.The pet had forgotten the forest complet: This claims forgetfulness, but the pet reacted strongly to the news.

activities.explanation: The pet's fall soon after the news suggests a strong reaction.

activities.prompt: At home, the merchant describes the wonders and beauty of his journey. What does this show about the trip?
options: He found the forest journey amazing and lovely.
He thought the journey was dull and empty.
He wanted to forget every sight he saw.
He only cared about leaving the forest.

why.He thought the journey was dull and empt: This mistakes admiration for boredom, which the merchant did not show.
This assumes he wanted to forget the journey he proudly described.
This suggests that leaving mattered more than the beauty he described.

activities.explanation: He calls the journey amazing and lovely, so he enjoyed it.

activities.prompt: The pet says its friend showed it how to escape, then flies into the open sky. What does this reveal?
options: The pet will never try to leave its cage.
The pet has lost the power to fly away.
The pet can use the escape lesson from its friend.
The friend wanted the merchant to leave home.

why.The pet will never try to leave its cage: This mistakes freedom for endless captivity, which the ending denies.
This claims the pet cannot fly, but it flew into the sky.
why.The friend wanted the merchant to leave: This mistakes the friend's help as a wish to remove the merchant.

activities.explanation: The pet says its friend taught the escape, and it flies away.

lessons.title: Words, Phrases and Groups

activities.prompt: What can a winter walk inspire, and how do groups get special names?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Phrases, Story Details and Groups
activities.body: This lesson looks at phrases, story details and collective nouns. The phrase box contains seven phrases for a fill-in exercise. The story begins on a winter morning. The writer sees snow around his home and notices an injured puppy while walking uphill. The puppy is in pain and may collapse. The writer takes it home, expecting good care to remove its pain. The collective-noun list includes pack, bouquet, army and flock.
keyPoints: The phrase box contains seven phrases.
The writer takes the puppy home.
Good care would remove all the puppy's pain.
The collective-noun list includes pack, bouquet, army and flock.
activities.explanation: These details help you understand phrases, groups and the example story.

activities.prompt: What should the writer do when a hurt puppy cannot keep walking?
steps: Because the puppy's leg is injured, walking is hard for him.
Because the puppy is in pain and may collapse, he needs help.
So the writer takes the puppy home, where good care can remove all the pain.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the writer see around his home?
options: Snow
Leaves
Rain
Smoke
activities.explanation: The writer saw snow around his home.

activities.prompt: The phrase box contains ______ phrases.
activities.hint: Count the phrases mentioned in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The phrase box contains seven phrases for a fill-in exercise.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its detail from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The phrase box contains seven phrases. The example uses flight for parrots and shows sheep and wolves.

activities.prompt: Why did the writer take the puppy home?
options: It was in pain and about to collapse.
It was barking near the writer's shop.
It was walking beside the writer.
It was hiding under the snow.
activities.explanation: The puppy was in pain and about to collapse. The writer decided to take it home.

activities.prompt: The writer decided to take the puppy ______.
activities.hint: Choose a place mentioned in the story.
activities.explanation: The writer decided to take the puppy home.

activities.prompt: Which collective noun does the completed example use for parrots?
options: flight
pack
army
bouquet
activities.explanation: The completed example uses the word flight for parrots.

activities.prompt: A hurt puppy may collapse. What should the writer do?
options: Take the puppy home and care for him.
Leave the puppy beside the uphill path.
Walk to the shop while the puppy rests.
Ask the hurt puppy to walk faster.

Leaving him alone ignores his pain and the danger of collapse.
This chooses the writer's trip over the puppy's need for help.
The puppy is hurt, so asking him to walk faster is wrong.

activities.explanation: Taking him home gives the puppy the care that can stop his pain.

activities.prompt: A hurt puppy appears during his walk. Why does the writer stop?
options: Take the puppy home for good care.
Run uphill and leave the puppy alone.
Wait for the puppy to stand up.
Carry the puppy towards his shop.

This leaves a puppy who may collapse without help.
This risks waiting while the puppy stays in pain.
This sends the puppy towards the shop instead of home.

activities.explanation: This is the writer's choice, and good care can end the pain.

activities.prompt: Sheep stand together in the fields. Which collective noun fits?
options: pack
bouquet
army
flock

why.pack: This confuses pack with the word shown for sheep.
why.bouquet: This confuses bouquet with the word shown for sheep.
why.army: This confuses army with the word shown for sheep.

activities.explanation: Flock is the collective noun used for sheep.

activities.prompt: Wolves are howling loudly together. Which collective noun fits?
options: army
bouquet
flock
pack

why.army: This confuses army with the word shown for wolves.
why.bouquet: This confuses bouquet with the word shown for wolves.
why.flock: This confuses flock with the word shown for wolves.

activities.explanation: Pack is the collective noun used for wolves.

lessons.title: Present Perfect and Bird Sanctuaries

activities.prompt: What do birds and the present perfect have to do with each other?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is present perfect?
activities.body: Present perfect shows a recent past action. It can also show a past experience that still matters now. The usual pattern is Subject + has/have + Verb + Object. For example, “I have come from Jalandhar” tells about a recent arrival. Birds have feathers and wings, and many bird species have become endangered.
keyPoints: Recent past actions can use present perfect.
Past experiences can still affect the present.
The pattern is Subject + has/have + Verb + Object.
Many bird species have become endangered.
activities.explanation: Present perfect connects a past action or experience with the present.

activities.prompt: How can Rita say that her past reading still matters now?
steps: Rita’s reading happened in the past, because it is already finished.
It still matters in the present, because its importance remains today.
Present perfect fits because it links past actions with the present.
So Rita should use Subject + has/have + Verb + Object.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the meaning
activities.prompt: Which meaning belongs to present perfect?
options: Actions completed in the recent past
Actions happening only at this moment
Plans for the future
Commands for another person
activities.explanation: Present perfect describes actions completed in the recent past.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: They ______ written letters to their friends.
activities.hint: Choose the helping word.
activities.explanation: “They” takes “have” in this example, making the sentence complete.

activities.title: Rita’s reading
activities.prompt: Rita’s reading happened in the past but still matters now.
activities.explanation: Yes. Rita’s reading is linked to the present, so present perfect fits.

activities.title: What do birds have?
activities.prompt: What are birds described as having?
options: Feathers and wings
Roots and leaves
Flippers and fins
Claws and shells
activities.explanation: The lesson describes birds as beautiful creatures with feathers and wings.

activities.title: Complete the sentences
activities.prompt: Match each beginning with its ending.
activities.explanation: Each ending completes the matching present perfect sentence.

activities.title: Build the sentence pattern
activities.prompt: Put the parts of the present perfect rule in order.
activities.explanation: The rule places the subject first, then the helping word, verb and object.

activities.prompt: Rita’s reading happened in the past and still matters now. Why use present perfect?
options: It shows a past action linked to the present.
It shows an action happening at this moment.
It shows a future action linked to tomorrow.
It shows an action that never happened at all.

why.It shows an action happening at this mom: This treats the past reading as happening now.
why.It shows a future action linked to tomor: This treats the past reading as a future event.
why.It shows an action that never happened a: This treats the reading as something that never happened.

activities.explanation: This shows a past action that still matters now.

activities.prompt: They have written letters to their friends. What does this sentence show?
options: The writing is past, but the messages can still matter.
The writing is happening now, so nothing is finished.
The writing is future, so the messages are not ready.
The writing never happened, so no messages exist.

why.The writing is happening now, so nothing: This mistakes the completed writing for an action now.
why.The writing is future, so the messages a: This mistakes the past writing for a future action.
why.The writing never happened, so no messag: This denies the action stated in the sentence.

activities.explanation: Present perfect can connect a past action with now.

activities.prompt: The speaker has visited Delhi many times. What can we infer about him?
options: He has past experiences of a city with historical sites.
He has one future visit waiting for him soon.
He has never travelled anywhere before this moment.
He knows Delhi only from a future plan.

why.He has one future visit waiting for him: This treats a past visit as a future one.
why.He has never travelled anywhere before t: This denies the many visits he has already had.
This ignores his past visits and replaces them with a plan.

activities.explanation: This uses his past visits and Delhi’s historical sites.

activities.prompt: Mr Joon has bought a new car. What does this sentence show?
options: A finished past action connected with the present.
An action still happening at this exact moment.
A future action that has not started yet.
An action from before Mr Joon was born.

why.An action still happening at this exact: This mistakes a completed purchase for one happening now.
why.A future action that has not started yet: This mistakes the past purchase for a future event.
This invents a time before Mr Joon’s birth.

activities.explanation: This shows the buying is complete and still matters now.

activities.prompt: Birds have feathers and wings, and many species are endangered. Why protect them?
options: Their beauty makes them worth protecting from danger.
Their feathers mean no bird needs protection.
Their wings mean every bird species is safe.
Their beauty means all species are already safe.

why.Their feathers mean no bird needs protec: This ignores that many bird species are endangered.
why.Their wings mean every bird species is s: This assumes beautiful birds never need protection.
why.Their beauty means all species are alrea: This confuses feathers and wings with complete safety.

activities.explanation: Beautiful birds deserve care when some species face danger.

activities.prompt: The guide says, “Many species of birds have become endangered.” What does this word mean here?
options: Some bird kinds now face danger.
All bird kinds have vanished forever.
Every bird is safe from danger.
New bird kinds will appear next year.

This mistakes some kinds for every kind disappearing.
This mistakes danger for complete safety.
This guesses a future change instead of present danger.

activities.explanation: This means some bird kinds now face danger.

lessons.title: Sounds, Ideas and the Parrot’s Next Adventure

activities.prompt: Which bird would you choose, and what adventure would you imagine next?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sounds, Ideas and the Parrot
activities.body: You will listen and repeat words, then look at two birds. You will decide which bird you would want to be and share your views with the class. You will also distinguish the ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds. In the story, a parrot tricks a merchant into releasing it. The parrot’s story continues after its escape, and you will use your imagination to complete it.
keyPoints: Listen and repeat words.
Distinguish the ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds.
Choose a bird and explain why.
Use imagination to complete the parrot’s story.
activities.explanation: This lesson combines sounds, speaking, and an imaginative story.

activities.prompt: What should happen next after the parrot escapes?
steps: The parrot’s story continues after its escape, so the ending is not finished.
The class should use imagination to create a clear next problem.
Imagine that the parrot meets another bird and asks for help.
This adds a new event and gives the story a clear next step.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the speaking task show?
options: One bird
Two birds
Three birds
A parrot alone
activities.explanation: The speaking task shows two birds. You will choose which bird you would want to be.

activities.prompt: Match each task to its learning goal.
pairs: Choose a bird and say why
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a task with the learning goal it practises.

activities.prompt: Which two sounds must you distinguish?
options: ‘ai’ and ‘oi’
‘ai’ and ‘ee’
‘oi’ and ‘ou’
‘ai’ and ‘oo’
activities.explanation: The lesson asks you to distinguish the ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds. Listen carefully and practise them.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: The story continues after the escape.
activities.explanation: The parrot tricks the merchant, is released, and escapes. Its story continues after that escape.

activities.prompt: What happens after the parrot escapes?
options: The story ends there.
The class repeats words.
The story continues.
The merchant returns.
activities.explanation: The parrot’s story does not end after its escape. The adventure continues.

activities.prompt: Learners must use their ______ to complete the parrot’s story.
activities.hint: Think about the power of your ideas.
activities.explanation: You must use your imagination to complete the parrot’s story. What could happen next?

activities.prompt: The teacher says a word with the ‘ai’ sound. What should the learner do?
options: Listen for ‘ai’, then repeat the word correctly.
Listen for ‘oi’, then repeat the word correctly.
Change ‘ai’ to ‘oi’ before repeating.
Ignore the sound and repeat another word.

This changes the sound instead of practising it.
why.Ignore the sound and repeat another word: This avoids listening to the word that was said.

activities.explanation: This follows the task of listening and repeating carefully.

activities.prompt: The speaking task shows two birds. What does a good answer need?
options: The chosen bird and a reason for choosing it.
The names of both birds and their colour.
A repeated sound from the first bird only.
A decision without explaining the reason.

why.The names of both birds and their colour: This adds details that the task does not ask for.
why.A repeated sound from the first bird onl: This focuses on a sound instead of the learner’s choice.
why.A decision without explaining the reason: This leaves out the reason that the task requires.

activities.explanation: This gives a choice and answers why the learner chose it.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks learners to distinguish the ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds. The sentence says, ‘The bird can see the coin.’ Which word has the ‘oi’ sound?
options: ‘coin’ has the ‘oi’ sound.
‘see’ has the ‘oi’ sound.
‘the’ has the ‘oi’ sound.
‘bird’ has the ‘oi’ sound.

This mistakes the long ‘ee’ sound in ‘see’ for ‘oi’.
This mistakes the short sound in ‘the’ for ‘oi’.
This mistakes the word’s final sound for ‘oi’.

activities.explanation: The word ‘coin’ contains the ‘oi’ sound.

activities.prompt: The parrot tricks the merchant into releasing it. Why does the parrot act this way?
options: To become free from the merchant.
To make the class repeat new words.
To show two birds to the learners.
To finish the parrot’s story at once.

This connects the trick to a speaking activity instead of its purpose.
This connects the trick to the birds instead of its purpose.
This connects the trick to the ending instead of its purpose.

activities.explanation: The trick leads to the parrot’s release, so it brings freedom.

activities.prompt: The parrot’s story does not end after its escape. What should the class do next?
options: Imagine a problem and a clear next event.
Stop telling the story after the escape.
Repeat the escape with exactly the same words.
Choose another bird instead of continuing.

This ends the story even though it should continue.
why.Repeat the escape with exactly the same: This repeats an event instead of adding a new one.
why.Choose another bird instead of continuin: This leaves the parrot’s story without its next event.

activities.explanation: This uses imagination to continue the unfinished story.

lessons.title: Bird Feeders and Bird Facts

activities.prompt: What could we build to help our feathered friends find something tasty?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making a Bird Feeder
activities.body: A bird feeder keeps food for birds. Place it in a balcony, garden or park. Fill it with seeds, grains or nuts. Put it somewhere safe so birds can easily find food. Materials are easy to find at home. Make one, then fill it with water, seeds and grains like millets. Ask a parent to place it outside. Choose two birds and find facts. Your self-assessment includes understanding new words.
keyPoints: Bird feeders keep food for birds.
Use seeds, grains or nuts.
Ask a parent to place the feeder outside.
activities.explanation: This card explains how to make, fill and place a bird feeder.

activities.prompt: How can a learner make and place a useful bird feeder?
steps: The learner chooses a home material because it is easy to get.
They fill it with water, seeds, and grains because birds need food.
A parent places it outside because birds should easily find the food.
So the learner makes and fills it; a parent places it safely.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is a bird feeder?
options: An object for keeping bird food
A tool for digging soil
A shelter for sleeping birds
A pot for growing plants
activities.explanation: A bird feeder is an object used to keep food for birds.

activities.prompt: Bird feeders are filled with ______, grains or nuts.
activities.hint: This food comes from plants.
activities.explanation: Bird feeders can be filled with seeds, grains or nuts.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct word.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important part of making and placing a bird feeder.

activities.prompt: Why are bird feeders placed in safe places?
options: So people can find birds
So birds can build nests
So birds can find food
So birds can avoid food
activities.explanation: Safe places help birds find the food easily.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to make and place a bird feeder.
items: Fill it with water, seeds and grains
Ask parents to place it outside
activities.explanation: First make the feeder, fill it and then place it outside.

activities.prompt: What should you do for the bird facts activity?
options: Make a feeder and find bird facts
Fill a feeder and find bird facts
Place a feeder and find bird facts
Choose two birds and find facts
activities.explanation: You choose two birds and find out some interesting facts.

activities.prompt: A learner fills a container with seeds and grains. The container stays outside. What is it for?
options: Keeping bird food for later.
Keeping garden soil for later.
Keeping parent tools for later.
Keeping seed water for later.

This confuses the feeder with a container for garden soil.
Parents help place the feeder, not store tools in it.
Water goes inside the feeder, but it is not kept for seeds.

activities.explanation: Seeds and grains are bird food kept in the feeder.

activities.prompt: A learner makes a feeder, and a parent puts it outside. What does this show?
options: Making and placing have different helpers.
Parents make and place every feeder.
Learners make and place every feeder.
Only parents fill feeders with food.

This wrongly says parents make the feeders too.
This wrongly leaves out the parent's help with placement.
The learner fills the feeder, while the parent helps place it.

activities.explanation: The learner makes it, while the parent helps place it.

activities.prompt: A poem says, “Seeds and grains go in the feeder.” The bird food stays there. What does the poem imply?
options: The feeder is for keeping bird food.
The feeder is for keeping garden soil.
The feeder is for keeping water alone.
The feeder is for keeping young birds.

This confuses a bird feeder with a garden container.
Water is one filling, but it does not replace the seeds and grains.
The feeder keeps food, not birds themselves.

activities.explanation: The poem links the feeder with food that stays inside it.

lessons.sceneCaption: Indian house sparrows flutter toward a bird feeder at home, showing how feeders attract birds.

lessons.sceneCaption: A rose-ringed parakeet hangs from a tree in Rabindra Sarobar.
