activities.context: A rich merchant lived in a quiet village and kept a bright, talkative parrot in a cage of gold. The parrot had a sharp mind and entertained the merchant with stories and songs. Inside the cage, it wanted the open skies and green trees. When the merchant went far away for business, he planned to give his pet something from the far-off land. Before leaving, he asked the parrot what it would like him to bring back.
activities.prompt: After hearing the parrot’s wish, what is the best thing for the merchant to do?
options: Take the wish for flying seriously and think of a way to help the parrot experience it.
Give more tender fruits and chillies, because food meets every wish the parrot has.
Keep offering gifts from far-off lands, because a gift alone can satisfy every longing.
Keep the parrot inside the golden cage and ignore its wish, because the merchant cannot bear to let it go.

why.Give more tender fruits and chillies, be: Treating food as its only wish ignores its longing to fly.
why.Keep offering gifts from far-off lands,: Giving repeated gifts may not satisfy the parrot’s wish to experience the sky.
why.Keep the parrot inside the golden cage a: Avoiding the wish may protect the merchant’s feelings but does not help the parrot.

activities.explanation: Taking the wish seriously respects what the parrot actually wants.

activities.context: A rich merchant lived in a quiet village and kept a bright, talkative parrot in a cage of gold. The parrot had a sharp mind and entertained the merchant with stories and songs. Inside the cage, it wanted the open skies and green trees. When the merchant went far away for business, he planned to give his pet something from the far-off land. Before leaving, he asked the parrot what it would like him to bring back.
activities.prompt: Why can the parrot still feel unhappy even though the merchant looked after its needs very well?
options: The parrot’s wish for flying can remain even when food and other needs are cared for.
Once food and other needs are cared for, the parrot has no reason to want anything more.
The merchant’s business trip is the only cause of the parrot’s wish for open skies and green trees.
The bird’s sharp mind and habit of talking must remove any wish to leave its cage.

why.Once food and other needs are cared for,: This choice wrongly assumes that meeting needs removes all wishes.
why.The merchant’s business trip is the only: The trip explains the parrot’s loneliness, but not its wish to fly.
why.The bird’s sharp mind and habit of talki: A sharp mind and talkative nature do not remove the bird’s longing.

activities.explanation: Good physical care does not necessarily satisfy every wish.

activities.prompt: How does asking the parrot what to bring back show that the merchant cares for his pet?
activities.answer: Before leaving, the merchant asked the parrot what it would like him to bring from the far-off land. By asking, he showed that the parrot’s wishes mattered to him. He wanted to bring back something chosen by the parrot, not merely something that suited the merchant.
points: The merchant asked the parrot before choosing what to bring.
He included the parrot’s wishes in his plan.
He wanted his pet to receive something it had requested.
The question shows that the parrot’s happiness mattered to him.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A merchant saw parrots in a forest and gave them his pet’s greetings. One parrot fell like a stone to the ground, so he hurried away distressed. At home, he told his pet about the message and the other bird’s shock. His parrot fell to the cage floor. He thought it had died suddenly and placed it on the windowsill. It stretched its green wings and flew into the open sky, saying its friend had shown it how to escape.
activities.prompt: If the forest parrot had not fallen from the tree, how might the merchant’s reaction have changed?
options: He might have continued through the forest without feeling that sudden distress.
He might have stayed beside the tree until the other parrots left.
He might have believed that every parrot around him had fallen.
He might have forgotten that he had greeted the parrots.

why.He might have stayed beside the tree unt: Waiting is not supported because no need to wait is described.
why.He might have believed that every parrot: One falling parrot does not mean that all the parrots fell.
why.He might have forgotten that he had gree: He later reported the greetings, so forgetting them is unlikely.

activities.explanation: Correct: the fall was the cause of his distress.

activities.context: A merchant saw parrots in a forest and gave them his pet’s greetings. One parrot fell like a stone to the ground, so he hurried away distressed. At home, he told his pet about the message and the other bird’s shock. His parrot fell to the cage floor. He thought it had died suddenly and placed it on the windowsill. It stretched its green wings and flew into the open sky, saying its friend had shown it how to escape.
activities.prompt: If the merchant noticed that his pet had fallen but seemed alive, what should he do?
options: Give it room by the window so it can move freely.
Keep it under the perch where its wings cannot spread.
Hold it close so that it cannot move.
Keep it in the corner farthest from the window.

why.Keep it under the perch where its wings: Keeping it under the perch would restrict its wings.
Holding it close would prevent free movement.
why.Keep it in the corner farthest from the: Keeping it away from the window would prevent escape.

activities.explanation: Correct: this allows the bird to recover and use its wings.

activities.prompt: How was the merchant’s first belief about his pet different from what happened after he placed it on the windowsill?
activities.answer: He first thought that his beloved pet had died suddenly when it fell from the perch. However, after he placed the bird on the windowsill, it stretched its green wings and flew into the open sky. It then said that its friend had shown it how to escape.
points: The pet fell from the perch to the cage floor.
The merchant thought it had died suddenly.
He placed the bird on the windowsill.
It spread its wings, flew away, and explained its escape.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On a winter morning, the writer saw snow around his home. While walking uphill towards his shop, he noticed a small puppy. Its leg was injured. The puppy was in pain and was about to collapse, so he decided to take it home. Good care would make all its pain go away. The lesson’s group words included pack, bouquet, army and flock. Its completed example used flight for parrots, while sentences showed sheep in fields and wolves howling loudly.
activities.prompt: Why was the puppy’s situation urgent?
options: The snow around the home made the morning difficult
The uphill walk made the puppy tired
Because it was a winter morning
The hurt leg was causing pain and collapse seemed close

why.The snow around the home made the mornin: Snow explains the weather, but not the puppy’s danger.
why.The uphill walk made the puppy tired: The walk explains the journey, not the puppy’s pain.
why.Because it was a winter morning: The season gives context but does not show an emergency.

activities.explanation: Its injury, pain and possible collapse required quick help.

activities.context: On a winter morning, the writer saw snow around his home. While walking uphill towards his shop, he noticed a small puppy. Its leg was injured. The puppy was in pain and was about to collapse, so he decided to take it home. Good care would make all its pain go away. The lesson’s group words included pack, bouquet, army and flock. Its completed example used flight for parrots, while sentences showed sheep in fields and wolves howling loudly.
activities.prompt: If the writer wanted to name the group of wolves shown in the example, which collective noun should he choose?
options: pack
bouquet
army
flock

why.bouquet: Bouquet is in the lesson’s list, but it does not fit the wolves.
why.army: Army is in the list, but it does not fit the wolves.
why.flock: Flock fits the sheep example rather than the wolves.

activities.explanation: Pack is the collective noun used for the group of wolves.

activities.prompt: Why did the writer decide to take the puppy home, and how would good care help it?
activities.answer: The writer decided to take the puppy home because its leg was injured, it was in pain, and it was about to collapse. Good care would make all the puppy’s pain go away. Taking it home would therefore give it the care needed to recover from its injury.
points: The leg was injured
The puppy was in pain
It was about to collapse
Good care would remove all the pain
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Rita has come from Jalandhar, so she is describing a recent past action. Her reading happened in the past, but it still matters in the present. Many bird species have become endangered, and birds are beautiful creatures with feathers and wings. Onshangla, an artist, has visited Delhi many times; Delhi is a city with many historical sites. Mr Joon has bought a new car. They have written letters to their friends about birds and Delhi.
activities.prompt: Onshangla has visited Delhi many times. What can she tell others about her experience?
options: She can share what she knows from repeated visits.
She can describe only a first-time journey.
She can explain why Delhi has no historical places.
She can report that she has never experienced the city.

why.She can describe only a first-time journ: A first-time journey does not match many visits.
why.She can explain why Delhi has no histori: The passage says that Delhi has many historical sites.
why.She can report that she has never experi: Her visits to Delhi are part of her experience.

activities.explanation: Her repeated visits have given her experience to share.

activities.context: Rita has come from Jalandhar, so she is describing a recent past action. Her reading happened in the past, but it still matters in the present. Many bird species have become endangered, and birds are beautiful creatures with feathers and wings. Onshangla, an artist, has visited Delhi many times; Delhi is a city with many historical sites. Mr Joon has bought a new car. They have written letters to their friends about birds and Delhi.
activities.prompt: Many bird species have become endangered. What should people do?
options: Act to protect the endangered birds.
Wait and do nothing because the problem is already over.
Treat every bird as safe because birds are beautiful.
Ignore the birds because they have feathers and wings.

why.Wait and do nothing because the problem: The situation still matters in the present, so doing nothing is not sensible.
why.Treat every bird as safe because birds a: Being beautiful does not mean that every bird is safe.
why.Ignore the birds because they have feath: Feathers and wings are features of birds, not reasons to ignore their danger.

activities.explanation: The continuing danger calls for action to protect them.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the two meanings of the present perfect used in this lesson.
activities.answer: The sentence “I have come from Jalandhar” presents an action finished in the recent past. Rita’s reading also happened in the past, but it still matters now. The difference is the reason for using present perfect: one stresses recent completion, while the other connects a past event with the present.
points: Identifies the recent-past action
Explains the present connection
Uses both examples correctly
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an English lesson, the teacher shows two birds and asks pupils to choose one and give reasons. The class also hears word examples and says them back, focusing on ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds. The story tells how a parrot tricked a merchant into releasing it, but the escape is not the ending. The teacher asks pupils to use imagination to continue the parrot’s next adventure.
activities.prompt: After seeing the two birds, one pupil chooses one but does not explain why. What should the pupil do next to complete the speaking task?
options: Give a reason for the choice and share it with the class.
Give a reason for choosing, but keep it to themselves.
Share a view about the birds without saying which bird they chose.
Choose the other bird without saying why.

why.Give a reason for choosing, but keep it: Keeping the explanation private leaves the sharing task unfinished.
why.Share a view about the birds without say: The pupil must identify the chosen bird as well as explain it.
why.Choose the other bird without saying why: Changing the choice still fails to provide a reason.

activities.explanation: It adds the missing reason and includes class sharing.

activities.context: During an English lesson, the teacher shows two birds and asks pupils to choose one and give reasons. The class also hears word examples and says them back, focusing on ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds. The story tells how a parrot tricked a merchant into releasing it, but the escape is not the ending. The teacher asks pupils to use imagination to continue the parrot’s next adventure.
activities.prompt: The class reaches the point where the parrot has escaped, and the teacher asks for the story to be completed. What should pupils produce?
options: An imagined continuation showing what happens after the escape.
A retelling that stops as soon as the parrot is released.
A summary of the parrot’s trick without imagining any later events.
A continuation in which the parrot stays with the merchant after escaping.

why.A retelling that stops as soon as the pa: Stopping at the release makes the escape the ending.
why.A summary of the parrot’s trick without: A summary does not add the imaginative events the task requires.
why.A continuation in which the parrot stays: The parrot has already been released, so remaining with the merchant misunderstands the story.

activities.explanation: It uses imagination to continue the story beyond the escape.

activities.prompt: How does repeating the words help learners distinguish the ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds?
activities.answer: During the speaking activity, learners listen to examples and repeat the words. As they repeat, they can focus on whether each word contains the ‘ai’ or ‘oi’ sound. This gives them practice in noticing the exact difference the teacher asks them to distinguish.
points: Learners listen to the spoken examples.
They repeat the words rather than only reading them.
They focus specifically on the ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds.
They practise noticing the difference between them.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner makes a bird feeder from a material chosen from things available at home. The learner fills it with water, seeds and grains such as millets. The feeder is then placed outside the house with a parent's help, in a safe place where birds can easily find the food. The learner also chooses two birds and reads about some interesting facts about them.
activities.prompt: The learner keeps the bird feeder inside the house, so birds cannot easily find the food. What should happen next?
options: Ask a parent to help move the feeder outdoors.
Fill the feeder again with the same seeds.
Place the feeder in a room where birds cannot enter.
Move the food into a different container and leave the feeder empty.

why.Fill the feeder again with the same seed: Refilling it does not solve the problem of its location.
why.Place the feeder in a room where birds c: Birds still cannot enter the room to find the food.
why.Move the food into a different container: An empty container does not place the feeder where birds can find it.

activities.explanation: This moves the feeder outdoors with parental help.

activities.context: A learner makes a bird feeder from a material chosen from things available at home. The learner fills it with water, seeds and grains such as millets. The feeder is then placed outside the house with a parent's help, in a safe place where birds can easily find the food. The learner also chooses two birds and reads about some interesting facts about them.
activities.prompt: If the learner fills the feeder with only seeds, what should be added to match the activity in the case?
options: Add water and a grain such as millet.
Add nuts and a grain such as millet.
Add more seeds and a grain such as millet.
Leave it with only the seeds.

Nuts do not provide the missing water and grains.
why.Add more seeds and a grain such as mille: More seeds do not provide the missing water and grains.
Leaving it unchanged does not add the missing contents.

activities.explanation: The case includes water and grains such as millets in the feeder.

activities.prompt: How should a learner make, fill and place a bird feeder?
activities.answer: The learner should make a bird feeder from a material of their choice, using materials available at home. They should fill it with water, seeds and grains such as millets. A parent should help place it outside the house in a safe place where birds can easily find the food.
points: Makes the feeder from a chosen material.
Uses materials available at home.
Fills it with water, seeds and grains.
Gets parental help to place it safely outside.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Wise Parrot

activities.prompt: What did the parrot want while inside its cage?
options: The open skies and trees
More stories and songs
A larger golden cage
Fresh food and water
activities.explanation: The parrot wanted to enjoy the open skies and green trees.

activities.prompt: The parrot entertained the merchant with stories and songs.
activities.explanation: The talkative parrot shared both stories and songs with the merchant.

activities.prompt: The merchant placed his pet on the ______.
activities.hint: It is found beside a window.
activities.explanation: The windowsill gave the parrot a place near the open sky.

activities.prompt: Match each character or moment with what happened.
pairs: gave the parrots the pet’s greetings
fell from the perch to the cage floor
activities.explanation: These pairings show the parrot’s wish for freedom and the merchant’s journey.

activities.prompt: Put these events from The Wise Parrot in the correct order.
items: The merchant sees a parrot fall
The merchant describes his journey at home
The merchant tells his pet about the message
The pet parrot falls from its perch
activities.explanation: The order follows the events from the forest to the parrot’s escape.

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the present perfect tense?
options: The speaker has visited Delhi many times.
The speaker had visit Delhi many times.
The speaker has visit Delhi many times.
The speaker visiting Delhi many times.
activities.explanation: Present perfect follows Subject + has/have + Verb + Object.

activities.prompt: The example story uses the word flight for a group of parrots.
activities.explanation: The completed example uses flight when it describes parrots together.

activities.prompt: Learners fill their bird feeders with water, ______ and grains like millets.
activities.hint: Birds eat these small food items.
activities.explanation: The bird feeder is filled with water, seeds and grains like millets.

activities.prompt: Match each speaking task with its instruction.
pairs: which bird they would want to be
share their views with the class
activities.explanation: The speaking activity includes bird choices, class sharing and sound practice.

activities.prompt: Put the bird-feeder project steps in the correct order.
items: Learners fill it with water, seeds and grains
The feeder is kept in a safe place
activities.explanation: First you make and fill the feeder. Then it is placed outside safely.

chapters.title: Unit 3: Water
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the frog’s poem; think, discuss and learn; sentences and tongue twisters; my frog's world and writing.

lessons.title: The Frog’s Poem

activities.prompt: How does a frog swim, hide, and stay safe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Frog’s World
activities.body: Frogs can sit in ponds and in the rain. They can hop about in a muddy drain. A frog may live on land and in water. It may live in damp places with drops of dew. A tadpole swims cheerfully in water and looks like a tiny fish. Webbed feet help a frog swim easily.
keyPoints: A frog can live on land and in water.
A tadpole looks like a tiny fish.
Webbed feet help a frog swim easily.
activities.explanation: These clues help you picture the frog and its tadpole.

activities.prompt: A frog sits in the rain and then in a muddy drain. The child thinks it is stuck. Why should the child think differently?
steps: Frogs sit in ponds and rain, so wet places suit them.
Frogs hop about in muddy drains, so this frog can move.
Webbed feet help them swim easily in water.
The frog is not stuck; it moves on land and in water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does a tadpole look like?
options: A small stone
A tiny fish
A green leaf
A soft cloud
activities.explanation: A tadpole looks like a tiny fish. This gives you a clear picture.

activities.prompt: A frog can sit in ponds and in the ______.
activities.hint: This word names what falls from the sky.
activities.explanation: Rain is the missing word. A frog can sit in ponds and rain.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair links an animal or body part with what it does.

activities.prompt: How does a frog catch food?
options: By using its webbed feet
By croaking loudly
By flicking out its tongue
By sitting in ponds
activities.explanation: The frog catches food with its tongue. Webbed feet help it swim.

activities.prompt: Which animal must a frog beware of nearby?
options: Fish
Birds
Snakes
Tadpoles
activities.explanation: Snakes are the animal named in the lesson. A frog must beware of them.

activities.prompt: A frog may live in damp places with drops of ______.
activities.hint: This word names tiny drops found in damp places.
activities.explanation: Dew is the missing word. It can rest in damp places.

activities.prompt: A frog sits in the rain and hops in a muddy drain. What does this show?
options: It can move between wet places.
It is trapped in the muddy drain.
It is trying to leave the water.
It cannot move on dry land.

This mistakes a place frogs visit for a place that traps them.
This assumes the frog dislikes water, but frogs live in water.
This mistakes frogs for animals that cannot move on land.

activities.explanation: Frogs can sit in rain and hop about in muddy drains.

activities.prompt: A tiny shape that looks like a fish swims in a pond. What should the child think?
options: A tiny fish in the pond.
A frog hiding in the pond.
A tadpole swimming in the pond.
A plant moving in the pond.

This mistakes a fish-like shape for proof that it is a fish.
This mistakes a swimming tadpole for a full frog.
This mistakes a swimming animal for a moving plant.

activities.explanation: A tadpole swims in water and looks like a tiny fish.

activities.prompt: A frog sees a snake near grass and leaves. What may help it stay safe?
options: It may croak loudly at the snake.
It may hide among grass and leaves.
It may use its tongue to escape.
It may show bright colours nearby.

This mistakes loud croaking for protection from a snake.
This mistakes the food-catching tongue for an escape tool.
This mistakes bright colours for colours that match plants.

activities.explanation: Grass and leaves help a frog hide well.

lessons.sceneAlt: Two tadpoles swim in different directions in a pond at Capitol Reef National Park in Utah.
lessons.sceneCaption: Two tadpoles swim in different directions in a pond at Capitol Reef National Park.

sceneCredit.text: Tadpole at Capitol Reef Waterpocket by Wing-Chi Poon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Wing-Chi Poon

lessons.title: Think, Discuss and Learn

activities.prompt: What clever tricks help frogs find food and stay safe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Frog
activities.body: Frogs like to sit in ponds and enjoy the rain. They hop about in muddy drains and catch food with their tongues. Webbed feet help them swim with ease. Grass and leaves help them hide from danger. A tadpole is a young frog that looks fish-like. A frog's colours can match plants and trees.
keyPoints: Frog features help with swimming, catching food, and hiding.
A tadpole is a young frog.
Frogs live around ponds, drains, plants, and trees.
activities.explanation: Different frog features help it swim, hide, and catch food.

activities.prompt: A child sees a frog near a pond after rain. A muddy drain is nearby. How can it move and stay safe?
steps: A frog likes ponds and rain, because it likes wet places.
It hops through a muddy drain, because mud does not stop hops.
Grass and leaves help it hide, because they give cover from danger.
Thus, it can move through mud and hide among leaves from snakes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Compare Animals
activities.body: A frog must watch out for snakes. A tiger hunts silently at night. Elephants live in large groups in forests. These animals show different ways of living. Frogs can hide with grass, leaves, and matching colours. Compare each animal with your book. Give a reason that matches the animal's special feature or behaviour.
keyPoints: Frogs must watch out for snakes.
Tigers hunt silently at night.
Elephants live in large forest groups.
activities.explanation: Each animal has a clear feature or behaviour described in your book.

activities.prompt: What helps a frog swim with ease?
options: Grass and leaves
Webbed feet
A fish-like body
A tiger's claws
activities.explanation: Webbed feet help a frog swim with ease.

activities.prompt: A frog catches its food with its tongue.
activities.explanation: You are right. A frog catches its food with its tongue.

activities.prompt: A frog catches its food with its ______.
activities.hint: This body part helps the frog catch food.
activities.explanation: The answer is tongue. A frog catches its food with it.

activities.prompt: Match each frog feature or animal with its matching clue.
pairs: A young frog that looks fish-like
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a feature or animal with something described in your book.

activities.prompt: When does a tiger hunt?
options: During the day
At night
In forest ponds
Beside a muddy drain
activities.explanation: A tiger hunts silently at night.

activities.prompt: Elephants live alone in small forest groups.
activities.explanation: Elephants live in large groups in forests.

activities.prompt: A frog sits in grass near a pond. A snake is close by. The frog stays among leaves. What do you think it is doing?
options: It is hiding from the snake.
It is looking for muddy water.
It is waiting to catch rain.
It is trying to swim away.

This mistake mixes up liking wet places with hiding from a snake.
This mistake treats rain as food that the tongue can catch.
This mistake confuses swimming with hiding among leaves.

activities.explanation: It is right: grass and leaves help the frog hide from danger.

activities.prompt: It is night. A tiger walks quietly near a large group of elephants. A child hears no sound. What can the child think the tiger is doing?
options: The tiger is hunting silently.
The tiger is hiding from elephants.
The tiger is swimming in a pond.
The tiger is looking for grass.

The facts about large groups belong to elephants, not the tiger.
Night is a clue to the tiger's hunting, not to swimming.
Grass helps frogs hide, but the animal here is a tiger.

activities.explanation: It is right: a tiger hunts silently at night.

activities.prompt: A child sees a fish-like young frog. The child thinks about how it will hide when it grows. What can the grown frog do?
options: Match the colours of plants and trees.
Use webbed feet to swim away.
Hunt silently through the forest.
Stay with a large elephant group.

Webbed feet help swimming, but matching colours helps hiding.
Hunting silently belongs to tigers, not to this hiding question.
This mistake uses the elephant group fact for a frog.

activities.explanation: It is right: a frog's colours can match plants and trees.

activities.prompt: An elephant walks with many other elephants in a forest. What can the child think about how elephants live?
options: They live in large groups in forests.
They hunt silently at night.
They catch food with their tongues.
They hide among grass and leaves.

This mistake mixes up tigers with elephants.
This mistake uses the frog's tongue fact for elephants.
This mistake uses the frog's hiding fact for elephants.

activities.explanation: It is right: elephants live in large groups in forests.

activities.prompt: A frog poem says: 'Its colour looks like the plants around it.' What does this make you think the frog can do?
options: The frog can match plants and trees.
The frog can catch rain with its tongue.
The frog can hop over muddy drains.
The frog can swim with webbed feet.

The tongue catches food, not rain, so this mixes up two facts.
Hopping through mud is true, but the line points to matching colours.
Webbed feet help swimming, but the line points to matching colours.

activities.explanation: It is right: a frog's colours can match plants and trees.

activities.prompt: A poem says: 'The frog waits. Its tongue snaps up the meal.' What does this make you think the frog is doing?
options: The frog is catching its food.
The frog is hopping through mud.
The frog is hiding from snakes.
The frog is resting in the rain.

The poem mentions the tongue and meal, not hopping through mud.
Snakes are a danger, but the poem describes the frog catching food.
The frog likes rain, but the poem describes the frog catching food.

activities.explanation: It is right: a frog catches its food with its tongue.

lessons.title: Sentences and Tongue Twisters

activities.prompt: Which tongue twister will be the trickiest for you to say?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speaking with Tongue Twisters
activities.body: A tongue twister is a speaking challenge. This activity has three tongue twisters. Speak each one slowly first. Then repeat it, becoming faster each time. You can count your correct tries. The examples show a silent crocodile, a slow turtle, and funny frogs.
keyPoints: Speak each tongue twister slowly first.
Become faster with each repetition.
Count your correct tries.
activities.explanation: Each tongue twister starts slowly and becomes faster with each repetition.

activities.prompt: How can I practise three tongue twisters and count my correct tries?
steps: Say each tongue twister slowly because each word becomes clearer.
Repeat it faster because speed should grow with each try.
Count the correct tries because this shows your successful tries.
Keep this order because it gives each twister clear practice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What should you do first with each tongue twister?
options: Speak it slowly
Speak it very fast
Skip the speaking
Count every word
activities.explanation: Each tongue twister should first be spoken slowly.

activities.prompt: A crocodile waits ______ near the riverbank.
activities.hint: How does the crocodile wait?
activities.explanation: The crocodile waits silently near the riverbank.

activities.prompt: Which sentence matches the turtle?
options: A turtle swims quickly in the ocean.
A turtle waits silently near the riverbank.
A turtle swims slowly in the ocean.
A turtle flips across fluffy fields.
activities.explanation: The turtle swims slowly in the ocean.

activities.prompt: Match each animal or frog phrase with its action.
activities.explanation: Each animal and frog phrase is matched with its action in the lesson.

activities.prompt: A speaker repeats a tongue twister. What should change with each repetition?
options: The speaking speed
The riverbank
The ocean
The number of flies
activities.explanation: The speaker should become faster with each repetition.

activities.prompt: Which plan follows the speaking activity?
options: Speak slowly, repeat faster, and count tries.
Speak quickly, repeat slowly, and skip counting.
Speak silently, repeat slowly, and change words.
Speak loudly, repeat faster, and count flies.
activities.explanation: Start slowly, become faster with each repetition, and count correct tries.

activities.prompt: A crocodile waits silently near the riverbank. How might it feel?
options: It feels patient and still.
It feels excited and noisy.
It feels cross and careless.
It feels hurried and nervous.
activities.explanation: This fits the crocodile's silent, steady wait.

activities.prompt: A turtle swims slowly in the ocean. How does its movement seem?
options: It seems calm and steady.
It seems rushed and hurried.
It seems sudden and jumpy.
It seems fast and frantic.

It mistakes swimming for hurried movement.
It mistakes slow swimming for sudden movement.
It mistakes the turtle for a fast animal.

activities.explanation: The slow swimming shows a calm, steady pace.

activities.prompt: The activity has three tongue twisters. Which practice plan follows the rules?
options: Say slowly, speed up, then count correct tries.
Say quickly first, then slow down each time.
Say slowly, stay slow, then count each mistake.
Say fast first, change words, then count speakers.

why.Say quickly first, then slow down each t: Starting fast misses the slow first step.
why.Say slowly, stay slow, then count each m: Staying slow misses rising speed, and mistakes are not counted.
why.Say fast first, change words, then count: Changing words spoils practice, and speakers are not counted.

activities.explanation: This plan uses slow speech, rising speed, and counting.

activities.prompt: Four fierce frogs fight for flies. What does this suggest?
options: They all want the same flies.
They are calmly resting together nearby.
They do not care about flies.
They are working together in peace.

Resting together does not fit fierce fighting.
Carelessness would not explain fighting for flies.
Peaceful work does not fit fierce fighting.

activities.explanation: Fighting for flies shows that they want them.

activities.prompt: This tongue twister says fast frogs flip-flop. Why is it hard?
options: The repeated f sounds may confuse words.
The frogs seem to move very slowly.
The fields seem totally empty right now.
The sentence has only one hard sound.

It mistakes the word 'fast' for slow movement.
It focuses on the fields instead of the sounds.
It misses the repeated f sounds in several words.

activities.explanation: Many f words can make a tongue twister tricky.

activities.prompt: Funny frogs flap their floppy feet. How does the scene seem?
options: Playful and quite light.
Quiet and completely still.
Calm and very careful.
Sharp and quite frightening.

It mistakes flapping feet for being still.
It misses the playful word choices.
It misses the funny word choices.

activities.explanation: 'Funny' and 'floppy' make the scene playful.

lessons.sceneCaption: A green sea turtle swims in the ocean at Jetty Park, Cape Canaveral, Florida.

lessons.title: My Frog's World and Writing

activities.prompt: What would your frog’s world look and sound like?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Build Hopper's World
activities.body: Choose a pond, forest or rainy area for your frog's world. Draw Hopper in the setting. Place poem words around the frog's drawing. Use colours to make the world look lively. Hopper writes his message from a big lily leaf pad. Hopper likes splashing in water when it rains. Hopper likes eating mosquitoes. Frogs have smooth, moist skin and long legs for hopping. Moist means slightly wet.
keyPoints: Choose a pond, forest or rainy area.
Draw Hopper and place poem words around the drawing.
Use colours and show what Hopper likes.
activities.explanation: Your picture can include Hopper, poem words, colours and favourite activities.

activities.prompt: It is raining. You are drawing Hopper's world. What should you choose?
steps: Choose a pond because Hopper likes splashing in water when it rains.
Draw Hopper because a frog can be drawn in the chosen setting.
Put poem words around him because words can surround a frog drawing.
Add colours because they can make Hopper's world look lively.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Show What Hopper Likes
activities.body: Your picture can show what Hopper likes. Show him splashing when it rains, sitting in a puddle, or croaking. You can also show him eating insects. If you include a toad, give it rough, bumpy skin and shorter legs. Give the frog smooth, moist skin and long legs for hopping.
keyPoints: Show Hopper's rain, puddle, croaking and insect activities.
Give frogs smooth, moist skin and long legs.
Give toads rough, bumpy skin and shorter legs.
activities.explanation: These details show Hopper's activities and the differences between frogs and toads.

activities.prompt: What does Hopper like doing when it rains?
options: Sleeping in a cave
Walking on clouds
Splashing in water
Flying in the sky
activities.explanation: Hopper likes splashing in water when it rains.

activities.prompt: Hopper writes his message from a big lily leaf pad.
activities.explanation: Yes. Hopper writes his message from a big lily leaf pad.

activities.prompt: Hopper likes eating ______ and other insects.
activities.hint: This is one of the insects Hopper eats.
activities.explanation: Hopper likes eating mosquitoes and other insects.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes a frog?
options: Frogs have rough, bumpy skin.
Frogs have smooth, moist skin.
Frogs have short legs for walking.
Frogs have long legs for running.
activities.explanation: Frogs have smooth, moist skin. Their long legs help them hop.

activities.prompt: Match each animal part with its description.
pairs: shorter legs for walking or hopping
activities.explanation: Frogs have smooth skin and long legs. Toads have bumpy skin and shorter legs.

activities.prompt: Which sentence uses the correct details for both animals?
options: A toad has smooth, moist skin and long legs.
A frog has rough, bumpy skin and shorter legs.
A toad has rough, bumpy skin and longer legs.
A frog has smooth, moist skin and long legs.
activities.explanation: Frogs have smooth, moist skin and long legs. Toads have rough, bumpy skin and shorter legs.

activities.prompt: Rain begins outside. Hopper likes splashing, sitting in puddles, and croaking. Mosquitoes and other insects are nearby. How does Hopper most likely feel?
options: pleased and ready to enjoy the rain
afraid and ready to hide away
bored and ready to leave at once
worried and ready to run away

why.afraid and ready to hide away: This assumes the insects frighten Hopper, but he likes eating them.
why.bored and ready to leave at once: This ignores the activities and insects that make him likely to enjoy rain.
why.worried and ready to run away: This treats croaking as fear, but Hopper enjoys croaking.

activities.explanation: His favourite rain activities and nearby insects make enjoyment likely.

activities.prompt: A poem says, “Raindrops fall on a pond. Hopper splashes. Croaks echo nearby.” What kind of setting does the poem suggest?
options: a dry forest-floor setting
a rainy pond setting
a windy rooftop setting
a quiet cupboard setting

why.a dry forest-floor setting: This chooses a forest, but the poem gives rain, water, and splashing.
why.a windy rooftop setting: This ignores the rain, pond, and splashing in the poem.
why.a quiet cupboard setting: This ignores the rain, pond, and splashing in the poem.

activities.explanation: Rain, splashing, and croaks all point to the rainy pond setting.

activities.prompt: You see one animal. Its skin is smooth and moist. Its long legs help it hop. Which animal is it?
options: a frog, with moist skin and long legs
a toad, with moist skin and long legs
a frog, with bumpy skin and short legs
a toad, with bumpy skin and short legs

why.a toad, with moist skin and long legs: This uses a toad, which has rough skin and shorter legs.
why.a frog, with bumpy skin and short legs: This mixes the features; a frog has smooth, moist skin.
why.a toad, with bumpy skin and short legs: This describes a toad, while the clues show smooth skin and long legs.

activities.explanation: A frog has smooth, moist skin and long legs for hopping.

activities.prompt: A poem says, “Raindrops fall below my broad leaf. I croak above the pond.” Where does Hopper write from?
options: on a small leaf in a forest
on a big lily leaf pad
on the rough back of a toad
on the smooth body of a frog

why.on a small leaf in a forest: This mistakes any leaf for the lily leaf pad above the pond.
why.on the rough back of a toad: This chooses an animal instead of the leaf where Hopper writes.
why.on the smooth body of a frog: This chooses Hopper's body instead of the leaf where he writes.

activities.explanation: The broad leaf above the pond points to Hopper's lily leaf pad.

lessons.title: Let Us Do and the Water Animal

activities.prompt: Can you find the hidden animals and discover how the dolphin finds its way?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Drawing, Moving and Finding the Way
activities.body: First, you will look for five hidden things and follow drawing steps carefully. You will draw a duck in the given space. Then you will move three crayons to change a fish’s direction. Finally, you will meet the Ganges river dolphin. It is the national aquatic animal. It cannot see well, so it uses sounds to find its way in water.
keyPoints: Five things are hiding in the picture.
Read the drawing steps carefully before drawing the duck.
Move three crayons to change the fish’s direction.
The Ganges river dolphin uses sounds to find its way.
activities.explanation: This lesson combines drawing, moving crayons and learning about the Ganges river dolphin.

activities.prompt: How does a dolphin find its way when it cannot see well?
steps: The dolphin cannot see well, so its eyes cannot guide it well.
It uses sounds in the water, so sounds help it find its way.
Therefore, the dolphin finds its way by listening.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Many Are Hiding?
activities.prompt: How many of them are hiding in the picture?
options: Three
Five
More than five
Less than three
activities.explanation: Five of them are hiding in the picture. Good spotting!

activities.title: Read the Steps
activities.prompt: The steps for the drawing should be read carefully.
activities.explanation: Reading the steps carefully helps you follow the drawing instructions.

activities.title: Match Each Clue
activities.prompt: Match each clue with its correct answer.
pairs: Uses sounds to find its way
activities.explanation: Moving crayons changes the fish’s direction. The dolphin finds its way using sounds.

activities.title: Can the Dolphin See Well?
activities.prompt: The Ganges river dolphin can see well.
activities.explanation: The Ganges river dolphin cannot see well. It uses sounds to find its way.

activities.title: Order the Changes
activities.prompt: Put these changes in order.
items: The fish swims in the changed direction
activities.explanation: Moving the crayons changes the fish’s direction, so the fish swims in that changed direction.

activities.title: How Does the Dolphin Find Its Way?
activities.prompt: How does the Ganges river dolphin find its way in the water?
options: By using sounds
By using bright colours
By making the water move
By hiding near rocks
activities.explanation: It cannot see well, so it uses sounds to find its way in the water.

activities.prompt: Four animals are seen among the five hidden ones. What is missing?
options: One more animal is still hiding.
One hiding animal left the picture.
The picture must have six animals.
The child saw one animal two times.

This mistakes movement out of the picture for staying hidden.
This adds an animal, but the picture has five.
This explains seeing four, but not the missing fifth animal.

activities.explanation: Five animals hide, and four are seen, so one remains.

activities.prompt: A child draws a duck outside the given space. Which rule did the child miss?
options: The duck should stay in the given space.
The fish should change its swimming direction.
The five hidden animals should stay hidden.
The dolphin should listen for nearby sounds.

why.The fish should change its swimming dire: This rule concerns moving crayons, not placing the duck.
why.The five hidden animals should stay hidd: This rule concerns hiding animals, not drawing the duck.
why.The dolphin should listen for nearby sou: This rule helps the dolphin find its way underwater.

activities.explanation: The duck must be drawn in the given space.

activities.context: After rain, a child sits beside a pond near a muddy drain. The child sees a frog in the wet grass and a cheerful tadpole in the water. The frog’s colours match the plants and trees around it. Later, it flicks out its tongue to catch food and croaks loudly. The child notices its webbed feet and wonders how it swims so easily. The child also wonders whether a snake is nearby.
activities.prompt: What should the child do after wondering whether a snake is nearby?
options: Move away from the grass and stay clear of the possible snake
Walk closer to the grass to find the frog
Stay beside the pond and wait
Move towards the muddy drain

why.Walk closer to the grass to find the fro: Going closer could bring the child closer to a possible snake.
why.Stay beside the pond and wait: Waiting beside the pond does not remove the possible danger.
why.Move towards the muddy drain: The muddy drain is not necessarily safer than the grass.

activities.explanation: A frog must beware of snakes, so the child should keep clear.

activities.context: After rain, a child sits beside a pond near a muddy drain. The child sees a frog in the wet grass and a cheerful tadpole in the water. The frog’s colours match the plants and trees around it. Later, it flicks out its tongue to catch food and croaks loudly. The child notices its webbed feet and wonders how it swims so easily. The child also wonders whether a snake is nearby.
activities.prompt: Why can the frog swim so easily in the pond?
options: Because its tongue catches food in the water
Because it can live both on land and in water
Because its webbed feet help it swim
Because it looks like a tiny fish

why.Because its tongue catches food in the w: The tongue is used for catching food, not swimming.
why.Because it can live both on land and in: Being able to live in water does not explain easy swimming.
why.Because it looks like a tiny fish: Looking like a tiny fish describes a tadpole, not a frog.

activities.explanation: Webbed feet help a frog swim easily.

activities.prompt: Explain how a frog can hide well among plants and trees.
activities.answer: A frog can hide well because its colours may match the plants and trees around it. Grass and leaves give it extra cover. When its colouring and the nearby cover match, it is harder for others to notice the frog.
points: Colours can match plants and trees
Grass and leaves help it hide
Matching colours and cover help it stay unnoticed
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After rain, a student sat beside a pond and watched a frog. The frog hopped about in a muddy drain and caught food with its tongue. When the student moved closer, the frog moved among grass and leaves, where its colours helped it hide. Later, the student noticed a fish-like tadpole in the pond. At night, the student saw a tiger hunting silently, while elephants lived in large groups in forests.
activities.prompt: Why did the frog become difficult to see after moving among the grass and leaves?
options: Its colours can match the plants and trees, making it harder to see.
Its webbed feet make it harder to see among the plants.
Its tongue makes it harder to see among the plants.
Its tadpole form makes it harder to see among the plants.

why.Its webbed feet make it harder to see am: Webbed feet help with swimming, not hiding.
why.Its tongue makes it harder to see among: The tongue is used for catching food.
why.Its tadpole form makes it harder to see: A tadpole is a young frog, not the hiding adult in the case.

activities.explanation: Matching colours help the frog hide from danger.

activities.context: After rain, a student sat beside a pond and watched a frog. The frog hopped about in a muddy drain and caught food with its tongue. When the student moved closer, the frog moved among grass and leaves, where its colours helped it hide. Later, the student noticed a fish-like tadpole in the pond. At night, the student saw a tiger hunting silently, while elephants lived in large groups in forests.
activities.prompt: A snake is near the frog. Which action best uses what the student knows about the frog?
options: Move into the greenery so that its colours can make it harder to see.
Stay in the open water so that its webbed feet can help it swim away.
Hop through the muddy drain and rely on its tongue to keep the snake away.
Sit among the plants and rely on its webbed feet to hide it.

why.Stay in the open water so that its webbe: Open water does not use the frog’s hiding features.
why.Hop through the muddy drain and rely on: The tongue catches food and cannot keep the snake away.
why.Sit among the plants and rely on its web: Webbed feet help with swimming, not concealment.

activities.explanation: Grass, leaves and matching colours help the frog hide from danger.

activities.prompt: Explain how a frog uses its webbed feet and tongue for different purposes.
activities.answer: A frog’s webbed feet help it swim with ease. Its tongue is for catching food, not for swimming. The frog can also hop about in a muddy drain. Therefore, webbed feet are useful in water, while hopping helps it move around a muddy drain.
points: Webbed feet help the frog swim.
The tongue catches food.
Hopping helps it move around a muddy drain.
The two features have different uses.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At the riverbank, a crocodile waits silently while a turtle swims slowly in the ocean. The speaking activity includes three tongue twisters. First, each tongue twister should be spoken slowly. With every repetition, the speaker becomes faster and can count each correct try. The three lines are: “Four fierce frogs fight for flies.” “Fast frogs flip-flop across fluffy fields.” “Funny frogs flap their floppy feet.”
activities.prompt: After the first slow attempt, what should the speaker do next?
options: Speak the next repetition at a faster pace.
Speak the next repetition at the same slow pace.
Stop after the first attempt and skip the repetitions.
Begin a different tongue twister without changing pace.

why.Speak the next repetition at the same sl: Keeping the same pace would not follow the planned speed change.
why.Stop after the first attempt and skip th: Stopping early would leave the repetitions incomplete.
why.Begin a different tongue twister without: Changing twisters at this point would not follow the planned sequence.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that speed increases with every repetition.

activities.context: At the riverbank, a crocodile waits silently while a turtle swims slowly in the ocean. The speaking activity includes three tongue twisters. First, each tongue twister should be spoken slowly. With every repetition, the speaker becomes faster and can count each correct try. The three lines are: “Four fierce frogs fight for flies.” “Fast frogs flip-flop across fluffy fields.” “Funny frogs flap their floppy feet.”
activities.prompt: If the speaker becomes fast on the first tongue twister, how should the speaker begin the second one?
options: The speaker should speak it slowly at first.
The speaker should begin it at the same fast pace.
The speaker should skip the second tongue twister.
The speaker should count it as a correct try before saying it.

why.The speaker should begin it at the same: The faster pace applies to later repetitions, not the first attempt at a new tongue twister.
why.The speaker should skip the second tongu: All three tongue twisters are included in the speaking activity.
why.The speaker should count it as a correct: A try must be spoken before it can be counted as correct.

activities.explanation: Each tongue twister, including the second one, should begin slowly.

activities.prompt: How should the speaker practise the three tongue twisters in the speaking activity?
activities.answer: The speaker should begin each of the three tongue twisters slowly. After the first attempt, the speaker should become faster with every repetition. The speaker can count each correct try, so the activity starts with slow speaking and continues with quicker repetitions while keeping a record of successful attempts.
points: Each tongue twister begins slowly.
Speed increases with every repetition.
The speaker can count correct tries.
The activity moves from slow attempts to quicker repetitions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How can the student use poem words and colours to show Hopper’s world in the drawing?
activities.answer: The student can place poem words around Hopper’s drawing and add colours to the rainy-area scene. The poem words connect the poem with the picture, while the colours make Hopper’s world look lively. Keeping Hopper visible also shows the frog in the chosen setting.
points: Poem words are placed around the frog’s drawing.
Colours make Hopper’s world look lively.
Hopper is shown in the chosen rainy-area setting.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a picture, five water animals are hiding. Before making a drawing, a child reads the steps carefully and draws a duck in the given space. The child then moves three crayons, and the fish changes direction. Meanwhile, a child learns that the Ganges river dolphin is the national aquatic animal. Although it cannot see well, it uses sounds to find its way in the water.
activities.prompt: What should the child do before drawing the duck?
options: Follow the directions closely
Start drawing without checking
Move three crayons first
Look for the hidden animals

why.Start drawing without checking: Drawing without checking may not follow the instructions.
why.Move three crayons first: Moving crayons comes later in the activity.
why.Look for the hidden animals: Looking for hidden animals does not prepare the child to draw.

activities.explanation: The steps should be read carefully.

activities.context: In a picture, five water animals are hiding. Before making a drawing, a child reads the steps carefully and draws a duck in the given space. The child then moves three crayons, and the fish changes direction. Meanwhile, a child learns that the Ganges river dolphin is the national aquatic animal. Although it cannot see well, it uses sounds to find its way in the water.
activities.prompt: How can the Ganges river dolphin find its way when it cannot see well?
options: By using sounds
By hiding in a picture
By moving crayons
By drawing a duck

why.By hiding in a picture: The picture is part of the child's drawing activity.
why.By moving crayons: Moving crayons changes the fish's direction.
why.By drawing a duck: Drawing the duck is a separate school task.

activities.explanation: It uses sounds to find its way in water.

chapters.title: What a Tank!
chapters.summary: In this chapter: water conservation and traditional tanks; punjab’s unique water tanks; contractions and exclamatory sentences; animal family words.

lessons.title: Water Conservation and Traditional Tanks

activities.prompt: How did old communities keep their water safe through every season?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Saving Water Together
activities.body: People have practised saving water for hundreds of years. Old water structures stored water and protected cities from floods. They also provided drinking water and brought people together. Some communities in India still use traditional water management methods. In Tamil Nadu, Ooranis store rainwater for drinking and farming.
keyPoints: Old water structures stored water and protected cities from floods.
These structures provided drinking water and brought people together.
Ooranis store rainwater for drinking and farming.
activities.explanation: Traditional water structures have helped people save water for hundreds of years.

activities.prompt: A family in Tamil Nadu wonders about an Ooranis. Why can it help with drinking and farming?
steps: An Ooranis stores rainwater, because it keeps a supply for later.
This stored water serves drinking, because Ooranis provide drinking water.
It also serves farming, because one supply can support both uses.
So an Ooranis saves rain while helping with two needs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Different Kinds of Tanks
activities.body: Tankas are common in Rajasthan’s Thar region. They are underground tanks. These tanks can store water for six to seven months. Home tanks can hold hundreds or thousands of litres of water. Home tanks are usually built or kept on roofs. A tank built on a roof is called an overhead water tank.
keyPoints: Tankas are underground tanks in Rajasthan’s Thar region.
Tankas can store water for six to seven months.
Tanks built on roofs are called overhead water tanks.
activities.explanation: Traditional tanks can be underground or built on roofs.

activities.title: Old Water Structures
activities.prompt: What did old water structures do?
options: They stored water.
They stored grain.
They built roads.
They kept animals.
activities.explanation: Old water structures stored water. They also protected cities from floods.

activities.title: Traditional Methods Today
activities.prompt: Some communities in India still use traditional water management methods.
activities.explanation: Yes! These methods are still used by some communities in India.

activities.title: Match Structures with Details
activities.prompt: Match each water structure with the correct detail.
activities.explanation: Ooranis are in Tamil Nadu, while Panam Keni wells are in Kerala. Tankas are common in Rajasthan’s Thar region.

activities.title: The Thar Region
activities.prompt: Tankas are common in Rajasthan’s ______ region.
activities.hint: This region is part of Rajasthan.
activities.explanation: Tankas are common in Rajasthan’s Thar region. They are underground tanks.

activities.title: Panam Keni Wells
activities.prompt: Panam Keni wells in Kerala are known for drying up.
activities.explanation: Good try! Panam Keni wells are known for not drying up.

activities.title: Choose the Local Tank
activities.prompt: Which traditional tank is common in Rajasthan’s Thar region?
options: Ooranis
Tankas
Panam Keni
Home tanks
activities.explanation: Tankas are common in Rajasthan’s Thar region. They are underground tanks.

activities.prompt: Heavy rain sends water toward an old structure. What does this help the city do?
options: Protect itself from flooding.
Store water for drinking.
Bring more people together.
Keep every street dry.

This option notices only the drinking-water role.
This option notices only the shared community role.
This option wrongly assumes that every street stayed dry.

activities.explanation: The structure protected cities from floods.

activities.prompt: Neighbours meet at an old tank while collecting water. How do they probably feel?
options: Worried about the old tank.
Afraid of drinking the water.
Connected to their neighbours.
Angry with their neighbours.

This mistake treats meeting as a reason to worry.
This mistake treats shared water as a reason to fear.
This mistake treats meeting as a reason to be angry.

activities.explanation: The tank brought people together, so they likely felt connected.

activities.prompt: A guide points to a tank on a roof. What does “overhead” suggest here?
options: It is below the ground.
It is above the ground.
It is behind the house.
It is beside the road.

The facts place home tanks on roofs, not below ground.
Nothing in the facts places the tank behind the house.
Nothing in the facts places the tank beside a road.

activities.explanation: A roof tank is above the ground, so “overhead” fits.

activities.prompt: A poem says rain rests in an Ooranis. It mentions people and fields. What does it imply?
options: Ooranis store rain for drinking and farming.
Ooranis store rain only for farming.
Ooranis keep rain away from people.
Ooranis are used only in Kerala.

The poem mentions people too, so “only farming” is too narrow.
The poem says the Ooranis holds rain for people, not away from them.
This mistake mixes up Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

activities.explanation: The poem links stored rain with people and fields, showing drinking and farming.

activities.prompt: During a dry month, a family chooses a Panam Keni well. What can the family expect?
options: The well will likely keep giving water.
The well will probably become empty soon.
The well will only work during rain.
The well will dry up very quickly.

why.The well will probably become empty soon: This mistake treats a lasting well as one that empties soon.
This mistake assumes the well works only when it rains.
This mistake assumes the well loses its water quickly.

activities.explanation: A Panam Keni well is known for not drying up.

lessons.title: Punjab’s Unique Water Tanks

activities.prompt: Imagine a water tank shaped like a football—what could make that possible?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tanks with Playful Shapes
activities.body: Punjab lies in the northwestern part of India. Rural Punjab is known for its unique water tank designs. Some tanks look like flowers, footballs, roosters, statues or aeroplanes. A farmer’s tank may look like a tractor, bullock cart or rooster. All these tanks are made of cement. Steel rods form the frame. Concrete gives the final shape. The finished tank is installed on the house’s roof.
keyPoints: Rural Punjab has unique water tank designs.
Steel rods form the frame.
The finished tank is installed on the roof.
activities.explanation: These tanks have playful shapes, strong frames and special cement designs.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants a tank shaped like a rooster on the house’s roof. Why can this happen?
steps: A farmer’s tank may look like a rooster, so the farmer’s wanted design is possible.
Steel rods make the frame, because every one of these cement tanks has one.
Concrete gives the final shape, so it completes the rooster design.
The finished tank is installed on the house’s roof, so the farmer’s wish can become real.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How a Tank Is Made
activities.body: These special tanks are made of cement. Steel rods are used to make the frame of each tank. Concrete gives the tank its final shape. The finished tank is installed on the house’s roof. Their unique designs are special to rural Punjab’s communities.
keyPoints: Cement is used to make the tanks.
Steel rods make the frame.
Concrete gives the final shape.
activities.explanation: The frame, shape and roof installation help make each tank.

activities.prompt: All these tanks are made of steel.
activities.explanation: Good try! The tanks are made of cement. Steel rods are used for their frames.

activities.prompt: The finished tank is installed on the house’s ______.
activities.hint: It is the top part of a house.
activities.explanation: Well done! The finished tank is installed on the house’s roof.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct detail.
pairs: Material used for all these tanks
activities.explanation: Great matching! You found the place, feature, shapes and material.

activities.prompt: Why are steel rods used in these tanks?
options: To make each tank’s frame
To give each tank its final shape
To install each tank on the roof
To choose each tank’s playful design
activities.explanation: Exactly! Steel rods are used to make the frame of each tank.

activities.prompt: These unique tanks are special to rural Punjab’s communities.
activities.explanation: Yes! Their unique designs are special to rural Punjab’s communities.

activities.prompt: A farmer’s tank looks like a rooster. How might the farmer feel about it?
options: proud of its special shape
worried about its cement wall
angry at its steel frame
afraid of its final shape

why.worried about its cement wall: This assumes cement causes worry, but no trouble is described.
why.angry at its steel frame: This blames the steel frame for a shape the farmer wanted.
why.afraid of its final shape: This assumes the finished design frightens the farmer without support.

activities.explanation: The unusual rooster shape can give the farmer pride.

activities.prompt: A football fan sees a tank shaped like a football. Why may the fan like it?
options: Its shape reflects the fan’s interest in football.
Steel rods form its hidden frame.
Concrete forms its hidden frame.
It stands on a house’s roof.

This mistakes the frame’s material for the reason for the shape.
This confuses concrete’s shaping work with frame-making.
This mistakes the tank’s position for the fan’s reason for liking it.

activities.explanation: The football shape directly matches the fan’s interest.

lessons.title: Contractions and Exclamatory Sentences

activities.prompt: What do words like "aren't" and "Wow!" have in common?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Short Forms and Strong Feelings
activities.body: Short forms put two words together as one word. Some letters are left out. An apostrophe takes their place. For example, “aren’t” means “are not”, and “wouldn’t” means “would not”. Exclamatory sentences show strong emotions. Words such as “Wow”, “Hurrah” and “Oh” can show strong feelings. An exclamation mark helps us spot an exclamatory sentence.
keyPoints: Short forms combine two words into one word.
An apostrophe takes the place of missing letters.
Exclamatory sentences express strong emotions.
activities.explanation: Great start! You have learned two useful parts of the lesson.

activities.prompt: A girl wants two tasks. She wants “are not” as one word and a strong feeling. How should she write it?
steps: A short form fits because it joins two words into one.
Some letters are left out so the words can become one.
An apostrophe marks those missing letters in “aren’t,” meaning “are not.”
An exclamation mark helps show her strong feeling in “We aren’t ready!”
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meaning of a Short Form
activities.prompt: Which short form means “are not”?
options: aren’t
wouldn’t
Wow
Hurrah
activities.explanation: Well done! “Aren’t” means “are not”.

activities.title: The Missing-Letter Spot
activities.prompt: What takes the place of missing letters?
options: An apostrophe
An exclamation mark
A strong feeling
A short form
activities.explanation: Good choice! An apostrophe takes the place of missing letters.

activities.title: Complete the Short Form
activities.prompt: The short form “______” means “would not”.
activities.hint: Join the two words and leave out some letters.
activities.explanation: Excellent! “Wouldn’t” is the short form of “would not”.

activities.title: Match Words and Meanings
activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct meaning or use.
activities.explanation: Great matching! You connected each word with its meaning or use.

activities.title: A Word with Feeling
activities.prompt: Which word shows strong feelings?
options: Wow
aren’t
wouldn’t
not
activities.explanation: Yes! “Wow” shows a strong feeling.

activities.title: The Purpose of Exclamatory Sentences
activities.prompt: What does an exclamatory sentence do?
options: Show strong emotions
Leave out some letters
Take the place of letters
Combine two words
activities.explanation: Excellent! Exclamatory sentences express strong emotions.

activities.prompt: A child sees a team win and says, “Wow! We won!” How does the child feel?
options: very excited and happy
very bored and quiet
very tired and calm
very unsure and slow

why.very bored and quiet: Being bored and quiet does not fit the child’s strong reaction.
why.very tired and calm: Being tired and calm does not fit the excited words and mark.
why.very unsure and slow: Being unsure and slow does not fit the child’s strong reaction.

activities.explanation: “Wow” and the exclamation mark show strong, happy feeling.

activities.prompt: A child says, “I would help, but I wouldn’t join the game.” What does this contraction mean?
options: the child would join the game now
the child cannot help the other child
the child would not join the game
the child wants to join another game

why.the child cannot help the other child: This changes the meaning from “would not” to “cannot.”
why.the child wants to join another game: This adds another game that the sentence does not mention.

activities.explanation: “Wouldn’t” means “would not,” so the child will not join.

activities.prompt: A note says, “The toys aren’t here.” What does its apostrophe show?
options: that some letters were left out
that some words were left out
that all letters were left out
that two words became one word

why.that some words were left out: This mistake treats missing letters as missing whole words.
why.that all letters were left out: This mistake says every letter was left out, not some.
why.that two words became one word: This describes the whole short form, not the apostrophe’s job.

activities.explanation: The apostrophe marks the letters left out from “are not.”

activities.prompt: A child drops a special cup and says, “Oh! I broke it!” How does the child most likely feel?
options: calm and full of quiet feeling
happy and full of strong feeling
slow and full of sleepy feeling
upset and full of strong feeling

why.calm and full of quiet feeling: The strong reaction does not match being calm and quiet.
why.happy and full of strong feeling: A broken special cup gives no sign of happiness.
why.slow and full of sleepy feeling: This confuses the speed of an action with the child’s feeling.

activities.explanation: The broken cup and “Oh!” suggest strong, upset feeling.

activities.prompt: A shop has its door closed. A sign says, “We aren’t open.” Why is the sign there?
options: to show the shop is now open
to show the shop is not open
to ask the reader to open it
to promise it will open soon

why.to show the shop is now open: This reverses the meaning of “aren’t,” which means “are not.”
why.to ask the reader to open it: The sign states a fact rather than asking someone to open it.
why.to promise it will open soon: This adds a future promise that the sign does not make.

activities.explanation: The closed shop and “aren’t open” mean the shop is not open.

lessons.sceneCaption: Colorful exclamation-mark stands provide a cheerful visual introduction to exclamatory punctuation.

lessons.title: Animal Family Words

activities.prompt: Which special words belong to the lion, tiger, and rooster families?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Learn animal family words
activities.body: Animal families have special words for their members. The lion family words are lion, lioness and lion cub. The tiger family words are tiger, tigress and tiger cub. The rooster family words are rooster, hen and chick. You will look at animal family pictures. The words are printed below each picture. You can use crayons or colour pencils to add to the picture. You can also think of something you would like to add.
keyPoints: Lion: lion, lioness and lion cub
Tiger: tiger, tigress and tiger cub
Rooster: rooster, hen and chick
Words are printed below each animal picture
activities.explanation: These words help you name different animal family members.

activities.prompt: How can a child use family words and add an idea?
steps: Read each printed word, because it names the animal in its picture.
Group words by family, because each set names animal family members.
Think of something to add, because children can choose their own idea.
Use crayons or colour pencils, because children can add to the picture.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word names the female lion?
options: lion
lioness
lion cub
tiger cub
activities.explanation: The lion family words are lion, lioness and lion cub. Lioness names the female lion.

activities.prompt: A young lion is called a lion ______.
activities.hint: This word shows that the lion is young.
activities.explanation: A young lion is called a lion cub. Great job remembering the family word.

activities.prompt: Match each animal with its female family word.
activities.explanation: These matches show the female words in the lion, tiger and rooster families.

activities.prompt: Which set has all three rooster family words?
options: rooster, cub, tigress
lion, lioness, chick
rooster, hen, chick
tiger, hen, lioness
activities.explanation: The rooster family words are rooster, hen and chick. You found the whole family set.

activities.prompt: The words are printed ______ each animal picture.
activities.hint: The words are not above the picture.
activities.explanation: The words are printed below each animal picture. This helps you match each word with its picture.

activities.prompt: What can you do with crayons and colour pencils in this activity?
options: add to the picture
erase the picture
hide the words
change the family words
activities.explanation: You can use crayons and colour pencils to add to the picture. You can also think of something you would like to add.

activities.prompt: A child smiles and reaches for crayons at the picture activity. Why?
options: The child has an idea to add to the picture.
The child has found a different animal picture.
The child wants to change the printed words.
The child has finished colouring every picture.

why.The child has found a different animal p: This child thinks crayons are used to find other pictures.
why.The child wants to change the printed wo: This child thinks crayons are used to change printed words.
why.The child has finished colouring every p: This child thinks the activity is already complete.

activities.explanation: The child wants to add an idea, using crayons or colour pencils.

activities.prompt: Lion cub and tiger cub share the same last word. What does “cub” show?
options: They both name a young animal.
They both name a grown animal.
They both name a colour pencil.
They both name an animal picture.

The shared word is also used for grown animals.
The shared word is a material, not an animal name.
The shared word names the picture rather than its animal.

activities.explanation: Both lion cub and tiger cub use cub for a young animal.

activities.prompt: A tiger family picture shows tiger and tigress. Which set completes its labels?
options: tiger cub
lion cub
rooster chick
tigress cub

why.lion cub: A lion cub belongs to a different animal family.
why.rooster chick: A rooster chick belongs to a different animal family.
why.tigress cub: This option wrongly joins tigress and cub.

activities.explanation: The tiger family words are tiger, tigress, and tiger cub.

activities.prompt: Three labels read tiger, tigress, and tiger cub. Why do they belong together?
options: They are all tiger family words.
They are all lion family words.
They are all rooster family words.
They are all words for colour pencils.

Only one of these words belongs to the lion family.
Only one of these words belongs to the rooster family.
These are animal words, not names for colour pencils.

activities.explanation: These are exactly the three tiger family words.

activities.prompt: A child thinks of something, then takes a colour pencil. What happens next?
options: The child adds the idea to the picture.
The child chooses another animal family.
The child matches labels to new pictures.
The child puts the pencil away.

This child confuses adding with choosing another family.
why.The child matches labels to new pictures: This child confuses adding with matching labels.
This child thinks taking a pencil ends the task.

activities.explanation: The child is adding the chosen idea to the picture.
