lessons.title: Saving Water and Listening to Suma

activities.prompt: What could Suma learn from a morning without water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water Is Precious
activities.body: Water can be saved in many ways. The simplest way is to stop wasting it. Running water while brushing teeth wastes a lot. Suma found no water when she turned on the tap. Life was difficult without water for brushing, washing and bathing. She promised not to waste water again. Her school planned a Water Conservation Week. Children made posters, and her parents agreed to harvest rainwater at home.
keyPoints: Stop wasting water to save it.
Running water wastes water while brushing teeth.
Posters and rainwater harvesting can help save water.
activities.explanation: Suma's story shows why every drop of water matters.

activities.prompt: How can a child save water while brushing their teeth?
steps: Stop the tap because running water while brushing wastes much water.
Turn it on only when needed because unused water should not be wasted.
Keep this habit because stopping waste is the simplest water-saving way.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Simplest Way
activities.prompt: What is the simplest way to save water?
options: Stop wasting water
Make many posters
Harvest rainwater
Keep the tap running
activities.explanation: Stopping water waste is the simplest way to save water.

activities.title: Nothing Came Out
activities.prompt: Suma turned on the tap, but no ______ came out.
activities.hint: You use this to brush your teeth.
activities.explanation: No water came from the tap, so Suma could not brush her teeth.

activities.title: Events and Details
activities.prompt: Match each event with its related detail.
pairs: Suma could not brush her teeth
Suma's parents agreed to set it up at home
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an event and the detail connected with it.

activities.title: Life Without Water
activities.prompt: What was difficult without water at Suma's home?
options: Brushing, washing and bathing
Poster-making and slogans
Rainwater harvesting
Toilets and drinking water
activities.explanation: Suma needed water for brushing, washing and bathing at home.

activities.title: Suma's Morning
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Suma went to brush her teeth
No water came from the tap
Suma promised not to waste water
activities.explanation: Suma first woke up and found no water when she tried to brush.

activities.title: A Water-Saving Slogan
activities.prompt: Which slogan did the children use on their posters?
options: Save Every Drop
Waste Every Drop
Keep Water Running
Close Every Tap
activities.explanation: The children used the slogan “Save Every Drop” on their posters.

activities.prompt: At Suma’s home, the tap gives no water. How might Suma feel?
options: She feels worried because the water has stopped.
She feels excited because the water has stopped.
She feels bored because the water has stopped.
She feels happy because the water has stopped.

why.She feels excited because the water has: She thinks missing water is something to look forward to.
why.She feels bored because the water has st: She pays no attention to the missing water.
why.She feels happy because the water has st: She believes missing water is good news.

activities.explanation: She knows that water is needed for daily tasks.

activities.prompt: Suma’s school has closed toilets and little drinking water. What does this show?
options: People must use the available water carefully.
People can use all the available water quickly.
People do not need water for daily life.
People should waste more water at school.

why.People can use all the available water q: The child misses the link between water and daily needs.
The child thinks the shortage means water is not useful.
why.People should waste more water at school: The child thinks less drinking means the shortage is good.

activities.explanation: Water is needed for washing, drinking, and using the toilets.

activities.prompt: Children make a poster with the slogan “Save Every Drop.” What does it ask them to do?
options: Use every drop of water carefully.
Throw every drop of water away.
Leave every tap running all day.
Pour every drop onto the ground.

The child thinks saving means throwing water away.
The child thinks saving means keeping water running.
The child thinks saving means pouring water away.

activities.explanation: The slogan asks people not to waste water.

activities.prompt: At school, children plan posters for Water Conservation Week. What does “conservation” mean here?
options: Saving water and not wasting it.
Using much more water than needed.
Keeping every school tap running.
Making many more posters at school.

The child thinks conservation means using extra water.
The child thinks conservation means wasting running water.
The child thinks conservation only means making posters.

activities.explanation: Conservation means protecting water by not wasting it.

lessons.title: Writing Posters and Exploring Tanks

activities.prompt: How can we make people care about the water tanks around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Plan Your Awareness Poster
activities.body: Create a poster that encourages people to preserve and clean old water tanks. Use the topic “Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign”. Add a catchy slogan, such as “Save Tanks, Save Lives!”. Include a few points about why tanks are important. Invite people to join a cleaning drive or awareness programme. You can also find out how water tanks are cleaned, bring relevant pictures or photographs, and prepare a chart for the class.
keyPoints: Encourage people to preserve and clean old water tanks.
Use the campaign topic and a catchy slogan.
Invite people to join a cleaning drive or awareness programme.
activities.explanation: A clear topic, slogan, important points and invitation will make your poster useful.

activities.prompt: The class is making a tank poster. How should it guide people?
steps: It should encourage preserving and cleaning because these are the campaign’s goals.
The topic should be “Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign” to show its purpose.
It should give a few points so people understand why tanks matter.
It should invite people to join a cleaning drive or awareness programme, so action is clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Add Important Points
activities.prompt: What should your poster include?
options: A few points about why tanks are important
A list of school visiting guests
A story about a photograph album
A description of the class chart paper
activities.explanation: The poster should explain why tanks are important so people understand the message.

activities.title: Complete the Slogan
activities.prompt: Complete the slogan: “Save Tanks, Save ______!”
activities.hint: Use the final word in the given slogan.
activities.explanation: The complete slogan is “Save Tanks, Save Lives!”.

activities.title: Match the Lesson Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct detail.
pairs: Join a cleaning drive or awareness programme
Prepare a chart and put it up in class
Find out how water tanks are cleaned
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea from the lesson with its correct detail.

activities.title: Choose a Learning Task
activities.prompt: What are learners asked to find out?
options: How water tanks are cleaned
Why the crow came to school
Which pictures belong in a poster
Where the awareness programme meets
activities.explanation: Finding out how water tanks are cleaned helps you write an informative poster.

activities.title: Put the School Event in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: The crow interacts with the students.
Learners enact the event with the teacher’s help.
activities.explanation: The crow is invited first, then interacts with students. Learners later enact the event with the teacher’s help.

activities.prompt: The poster topic is “Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign”. Its slogan says, “Save Tanks, Save Lives!”. What should it encourage people to do?
options: They should replace all old water tanks.
They should keep old water tanks dirty.
They should preserve and clean old water tanks.
They should only display pictures of old tanks.

This mistakes replacing old tanks for caring for them.
This goes against the goal of preserving and cleaning tanks.
why.They should only display pictures of old: This treats pictures as the main action instead of support.

activities.explanation: This matches the poster’s goal of preserving and cleaning old tanks.

activities.prompt: The poster topic is “Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign”. It gives a few points about why tanks matter. Why should these points stay?
options: They help people understand why tanks are important.
They explain exactly how every tank should be cleaned.
They provide ten words ending in “er”.
They replace the invitation to join an awareness programme.

why.They explain exactly how every tank shou: This mistakes reasons for importance with cleaning instructions.
This mixes the word exercise with the poster content.
why.They replace the invitation to join an a: This mistakes one poster part for another.

activities.explanation: These points help people understand why tanks are important.

activities.prompt: The campaign invites people to join a cleaning drive or programme. A child says, “I can help.” What is the child thinking?
options: The child can help by making the class word list.
The child can help by hiding the class chart.
The child can help by keeping old tanks dirty.
The child can help by joining the community campaign.

why.The child can help by making the class w: This mistakes a school task for the community invitation.
why.The child can help by hiding the class c: This mistakes hiding work for helping the campaign.
why.The child can help by keeping old tanks: This goes against the goal of preserving and cleaning tanks.

activities.explanation: The invitation gives the child a clear way to help.

activities.prompt: The list needs 10 words ending in “er”. The learner wants a poster word. Which word fits?
options: tank
poster
clean
drive

why.tank: “Tank” ends in “k”, so it does not fit.
why.clean: “Clean” does not end in “er”, so it does not fit.
why.drive: “Drive” ends in “ve”, so it does not fit.

activities.explanation: “Poster” ends in “er” and matches the poster word.

activities.prompt: Learners find out how water tanks are cleaned. They may bring related pictures. They put up a chart in class. Why?
options: The chart can keep the class from learning about tanks.
The chart can make pictures and cleaning less clear.
The chart can show what the class learned about tanks.
The chart can stop the poster from encouraging cleaning.

why.The chart can keep the class from learni: This wrongly treats sharing learning as a barrier.
why.The chart can make pictures and cleaning: This reverses the purpose of showing pictures and findings.
why.The chart can stop the poster from encou: This wrongly treats a class chart as harmful to the campaign.

activities.explanation: Putting it up lets the class share what it learned.

activities.prompt: The school invited the crow to interact with students. Learners will enact the event with the teacher’s help. Why is the teacher’s help useful?
options: The teacher can help learners show their understanding.
The teacher can stop learners from acting.
The teacher can keep the class chart hidden.
The teacher can make the event harder to understand.

why.The teacher can stop learners from actin: This wrongly treats the teacher as stopping the activity.
why.The teacher can keep the class chart hid: This confuses classroom display with the crow’s visit.
why.The teacher can make the event harder to: This misses the teacher’s helping role during the event.

activities.explanation: Acting with help lets learners show what they understand.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A traditional rainwater harvesting tank in Rajasthan stores seasonal rain for later use.
lessons.sceneCaption: A traditional rainwater harvesting tank in Rajasthan demonstrates an old water-saving method.

sceneCredit.text: Rainwater harvesting tank, India by Spiritualfade ( talk ) 09:37, 23 July 2009 (UTC), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Spiritualfade ( talk ) 09:37, 23 July 2009 (UTC)

activities.context: A family in Tamil Nadu uses a traditional rainwater structure for drinking and farming. The family also keeps a home tank on the roof to store water. People in the area gather at the traditional structure. Its old design stores rainwater and guards the town against flood damage, showing how water conservation can support homes and communities.
activities.prompt: The family needs a traditional rainwater store for drinking and farming in Tamil Nadu. Which structure should it choose?
options: An Oorani
A Panam Keni
A tanka
An overhead water tank

why.A Panam Keni: Panam Keni wells are associated with Kerala, not Tamil Nadu.
why.A tanka: Tankas are common in Rajasthan’s Thar region.
why.An overhead water tank: An overhead water tank is a roof tank, not the regional structure needed here.

activities.explanation: Ooranis in Tamil Nadu store rainwater for drinking and farming.

activities.context: A family in Tamil Nadu uses a traditional rainwater structure for drinking and farming. The family also keeps a home tank on the roof to store water. People in the area gather at the traditional structure. Its old design stores rainwater and guards the town against flood damage, showing how water conservation can support homes and communities.
activities.prompt: During heavy rain, the town worries about flooding. Why is the traditional structure useful in this situation?
options: It could reduce the danger of flooding in the town.
It could give the town more rainwater for farming.
It could provide a meeting place after the rain.
It could keep a well in the town from drying up.

why.It could give the town more rainwater fo: Farming uses stored rainwater but does not explain flood protection.
why.It could provide a meeting place after t: Bringing people together is a benefit, but it does not explain flood protection.
why.It could keep a well in the town from dr: Not drying up is a fact about Panam Keni wells, not a general flood-protection benefit.

activities.explanation: Old water structures protected cities from floods.

activities.prompt: Explain how an Oorani, a Panam Keni, a tanka, and an overhead water tank are different.
activities.answer: An Oorani in Tamil Nadu stores rainwater for drinking and farming. A Panam Keni is a well in Kerala known for not drying up. A tanka is common in Rajasthan’s Thar region and stores water underground for six to seven months. An overhead water tank is kept on a roof.
points: An Oorani is connected with Tamil Nadu.
A Panam Keni is a Kerala well.
A tanka is common in Rajasthan’s Thar region.
An overhead water tank is kept on a roof.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In rural Punjab, a farmer has chosen a unique water tank for his house. Steel rods will be used to make the tank’s frame, and concrete will give it its final shape. He wants the tank to resemble a tractor, one possible design for a farmer. After the tank is completed, it will be installed on the house’s roof.
activities.prompt: If the farmer changes the design from a tractor to an aeroplane, what would happen?
options: Only the intended outline would change; the frame, concrete shaping and roof placement would remain.
The steel rods would become unnecessary because an aeroplane shape has no frame.
The concrete would be used to make the frame instead of giving the tank its final shape.
The tank would be installed on the roof before the concrete gives it its final shape.

why.The steel rods would become unnecessary: Every tank still needs a steel-rod frame.
why.The concrete would be used to make the f: Concrete gives the tank its final shape.
why.The tank would be installed on the roof: Installation happens after the tank is completed.

activities.explanation: Changing the design changes the shape, not the materials or installation.

activities.context: In rural Punjab, a farmer has chosen a unique water tank for his house. Steel rods will be used to make the tank’s frame, and concrete will give it its final shape. He wants the tank to resemble a tractor, one possible design for a farmer. After the tank is completed, it will be installed on the house’s roof.
activities.prompt: If the farmer also wants a tank for a football fan, what should he do?
options: Choose a football-shaped design while keeping the steel rods, concrete and roof installation.
Choose a tractor-shaped design because football fans cannot have shaped tanks.
Use steel rods alone, without concrete, for the football-shaped tank.
Place the steel frame on the roof before giving the tank its final shape with concrete.

why.Choose a tractor-shaped design because f: The case does not limit shaped tanks to farmers.
why.Use steel rods alone, without concrete,: Every tank is made of cement and uses steel rods for its frame.
why.Place the steel frame on the roof before: The completed tank is installed after its final shape has been given.

activities.explanation: A football-shaped tank is possible for a football fan.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the steel rods and the concrete in making a tank.
activities.answer: The steel rods are used to make the frame of each tank. Concrete then gives the tank its final shape. The rods therefore form the supporting frame first, while concrete forms the finished shape afterwards. Both are part of making the cement water tanks used in rural Punjab.
points: Steel rods make the frame.
Each tank has a steel-rod frame.
Concrete gives the tank its final shape.
The rods are used before the final shaping with concrete.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a writing activity, a student shortened some expressions by joining words and leaving out some letters. The student used an apostrophe where letters were missing. One short form meant “are not,” and another meant “would not.” The student also wrote “Wow!” to show a strong feeling. The student checked that the apostrophe stood in for the missing letters and that the exclamation mark was present.
activities.prompt: The student decides to write “are not” instead of its short form. What should happen to the spelling?
options: The combined word and the missing-letter mark are no longer needed.
The combined word stays, but an exclamation mark replaces the apostrophe.
The apostrophe stays even though no letters are left out.
The separate words must be joined without any mark.

why.The combined word stays, but an exclamat: An exclamation mark cannot replace the apostrophe because it identifies exclamatory sentences.
why.The apostrophe stays even though no lett: If no letters are left out, there is no need for an apostrophe.
why.The separate words must be joined withou: Joining the words without a mark would hide the letters that were left out.

activities.explanation: Writing the words separately removes the shortened form and the missing letters.

activities.context: During a writing activity, a student shortened some expressions by joining words and leaving out some letters. The student used an apostrophe where letters were missing. One short form meant “are not,” and another meant “would not.” The student also wrote “Wow!” to show a strong feeling. The student checked that the apostrophe stood in for the missing letters and that the exclamation mark was present.
activities.prompt: Why does the student’s use of “Wow!” help show that the sentence is exclamatory?
options: The word signals intense emotion, and the punctuation signals the sentence type.
The word combines two words and removes some letters.
The punctuation shows that the words mean “are not.”
The word turns the sentence into a question and removes the emotion.

why.The word combines two words and removes: Combining words and removing letters describes how short forms are made.
why.The punctuation shows that the words mea: The meaning “are not” belongs to “aren’t,” not to an exclamation mark.
why.The word turns the sentence into a quest: An exclamation mark helps identify strong emotion rather than turning the sentence into a question.

activities.explanation: “Wow” shows a strong feeling, and the exclamation mark helps identify an exclamatory sentence.

activities.prompt: Explain why an apostrophe appears in short forms such as “aren’t” and “wouldn’t.”
activities.answer: An apostrophe takes the place of letters left out when two words are shortened into one word. It does not simply decorate the word. For example, “aren’t” means “are not,” and “wouldn’t” means “would not.”
points: Short forms combine two words into one word.
Some letters are left out when the short form is made.
The apostrophe takes the place of the missing letters.
“Aren’t” means “are not,” and “wouldn’t” means “would not.”
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the Animal Family Words activity, the children looked at animal family pictures. The words were printed below each picture. One child was unsure which label belonged with the young animal in the lion picture. Another checked the tiger picture because its family also included a word for a young animal. The children could use crayons and colour pencils to add to the pictures. One thought of something to add and began working on the lion picture.
activities.prompt: Suppose the label for the young animal in the lion picture has been removed. What should the child do?
options: Restore it as lion cub because the picture belongs to the lion family.
Restore it as lioness because the picture belongs to the lion family.
Restore it as tigress because the picture belongs to the tiger family.
Restore it as chick because the picture belongs to the rooster family.

why.Restore it as lioness because the pictur: Lioness is in the lion family, but it is not the young-animal word.
why.Restore it as tigress because the pictur: Tigress belongs to the tiger family, not the lion family.
why.Restore it as chick because the picture: Chick belongs to the rooster family, not the lion family.

activities.explanation: Lion cub is the young-animal word in the lion family.

activities.context: During the Animal Family Words activity, the children looked at animal family pictures. The words were printed below each picture. One child was unsure which label belonged with the young animal in the lion picture. Another checked the tiger picture because its family also included a word for a young animal. The children could use crayons and colour pencils to add to the pictures. One thought of something to add and began working on the lion picture.
activities.prompt: The child has thought of something to add to the lion picture. What should the child do next?
options: Use crayons or colour pencils to add the idea to the lion picture.
Use crayons to add a large patch of colour that hides the printed lion-family words.
Use colour pencils to add a different animal family over the lion family picture.
Use crayons to add no animal or idea because the picture is already complete.

why.Use crayons to add a large patch of colo: Hiding the words would not add the child's idea properly.
why.Use colour pencils to add a different an: The addition should help the lion family picture rather than cover it.
why.Use crayons to add no animal or idea bec: The child is allowed to add something they would like to add.

activities.explanation: This uses the available materials to add the child's idea.

activities.prompt: How does the activity help children learn animal family words?
activities.answer: The activity shows animal family pictures with the words printed below them. Children can match each picture with the correct word, such as lion, lioness, lion cub, tiger, tigress, tiger cub, rooster, hen, or chick. Crayons and colour pencils then let children add their own ideas to the pictures.
points: Animal family pictures are used.
The words are printed below each picture.
Children match pictures with family words.
Crayons and colour pencils can be used to add ideas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: One morning, Suma woke up and went to brush her teeth, but no water came from the tap. Without water, daily life became difficult. At school, the toilets were closed and little drinking water was available. People in her neighbourhood felt upset. Suma decided to change her habits. Her school later announced a Water Conservation Week, and the children made posters. At home, her parents agreed to set up a rainwater harvesting system.
activities.prompt: Suppose water had come out when Suma turned on the tap and she had left it running while brushing. What would have happened?
options: Suma would have wasted a lot of water.
No water would have been wasted.
People in the neighbourhood would have felt less upset.
Suma's parents would not have needed a rainwater harvesting system.

The tap was running, so water was being wasted.
why.People in the neighbourhood would have f: Using extra water does not solve the shortage.
why.Suma's parents would not have needed a r: Rainwater harvesting can help even when taps work.

activities.explanation: Running water while brushing wastes water.

activities.context: One morning, Suma woke up and went to brush her teeth, but no water came from the tap. Without water, daily life became difficult. At school, the toilets were closed and little drinking water was available. People in her neighbourhood felt upset. Suma decided to change her habits. Her school later announced a Water Conservation Week, and the children made posters. At home, her parents agreed to set up a rainwater harvesting system.
activities.prompt: Why were the children making posters during Water Conservation Week?
options: The posters could encourage everyone to save water.
The school had plenty of drinking water.
The posters showed that Suma's parents had already built a rainwater system.
Poster-making could replace the need to stop wasting water.

The school actually had little drinking water.
why.The posters showed that Suma's parents h: Her parents had agreed to set up the system, not built it.
why.Poster-making could replace the need to: Posters support saving but cannot replace action.

activities.explanation: Poster slogans can spread the message of conservation.

activities.context: One morning, Suma woke up and went to brush her teeth, but no water came from the tap. Without water, daily life became difficult. At school, the toilets were closed and little drinking water was available. People in her neighbourhood felt upset. Suma decided to change her habits. Her school later announced a Water Conservation Week, and the children made posters. At home, her parents agreed to set up a rainwater harvesting system.
activities.prompt: If water returned to Suma's home, what should she do while brushing her teeth?
options: She should stop the running water and avoid wasting it.
She should keep the tap running while she brushes.
She should use the water only for brushing and ignore washing and bathing.
She should wait until Water Conservation Week before changing how she uses water.

why.She should use the water only for brushi: Water is also needed for washing and bathing.
why.She should wait until Water Conservation: Saving water should not be delayed until a special week.

activities.explanation: This stops water from being wasted.

activities.prompt: Explain why the lack of water made life difficult for Suma and her community.
activities.answer: Without water, Suma could not brush, wash or bathe as usual. At school, the toilets had to be closed and only little drinking water was available. This shortage upset people in the neighbourhood because their daily needs could not be met.
points: No water for brushing, washing or bathing
Toilets closed at school
Little drinking water available
Neighbourhood people were upset
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Campaign poster: “Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign.” It should encourage preserving and cleaning old water tanks and use “Save Tanks, Save Lives!” It will include a few points on why tanks matter and invite participation in a cleaning drive or awareness programme. Learners may bring relevant pictures, find out how tanks are cleaned, and prepare a chart for class. The school invited the crow to interact with them; they will enact it with the teacher’s help.
activities.prompt: The poster explains why tanks matter, but it does not ask readers to act. Which addition best completes it?
options: Invite readers to join a tank-cleaning or awareness activity.
Place another image on the poster without adding a message.
Repeat the campaign slogan and ask for no action.
Put up the class chart in place of an invitation on the poster.

why.Place another image on the poster withou: More images do not ask people to participate.
why.Repeat the campaign slogan and ask for n: Repeating the slogan does not create an invitation.
why.Put up the class chart in place of an in: Displaying the chart is preparation, not poster content.

activities.explanation: This directly gives people an action to take.

activities.context: Campaign poster: “Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign.” It should encourage preserving and cleaning old water tanks and use “Save Tanks, Save Lives!” It will include a few points on why tanks matter and invite participation in a cleaning drive or awareness programme. Learners may bring relevant pictures, find out how tanks are cleaned, and prepare a chart for class. The school invited the crow to interact with them; they will enact it with the teacher’s help.
activities.prompt: While preparing the poster, learners realise that they do not yet know how water tanks are cleaned. What should they do next?
options: Find out how water tanks are cleaned.
Guess a cleaning method because the poster is due.
Skip the cleaning information because the slogan is catchy.
Use pictures only and do not find out how cleaning works.

why.Guess a cleaning method because the post: Guessing could give incorrect cleaning information.
why.Skip the cleaning information because th: The slogan does not explain how cleaning is done.
why.Use pictures only and do not find out ho: Pictures cannot replace learning the process.

activities.explanation: Finding out is the stated preparation task for learners.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: What a Tank!

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct detail.
activities.explanation: India’s communities use different kinds of water tanks. Each one has its own special place or feature.

activities.prompt: Old water structures provided drinking water and brought people together.
activities.explanation: Old water structures did much more than store water. They also served communities.

activities.prompt: Match each learning task with its detail.
pairs: a chart and put it up in class
activities.explanation: These tasks help you learn about water tanks. You can show your learning through words, pictures and charts.

activities.prompt: An apostrophe takes the place of the ______ letters.
activities.hint: These letters are left out when short forms are made.
activities.explanation: An apostrophe shows where letters have been left out. This helps us recognise short forms.

activities.prompt: Which sentence shows a strong feeling?
options: Wow, what a tank!
The tank is on the roof.
I made a poster.
The water tank is cement.
activities.explanation: “Wow” shows a strong feeling. The exclamation mark also helps identify this sentence.

activities.prompt: “aren’t” means “is not”.
activities.explanation: “aren’t” means “are not”. Its missing letters are shown by an apostrophe.

activities.prompt: Match each animal with another word from its family.
activities.explanation: Animal pictures help us learn family words. Each pair belongs to the same animal family.

activities.prompt: Put the tank-making steps in order.
items: Concrete gives the tank its final shape.
The finished tank is installed on the roof.
activities.explanation: The steel frame comes first. Concrete then shapes the tank before it is installed.

activities.prompt: Suma promised herself that she would never waste water ______.
activities.hint: She made this promise after facing life without water.
activities.explanation: Suma decided never to waste water again. Her difficult experience changed the way she cared for water.

chapters.title: Unit 4: Ups and Downs
chapters.summary: In this chapter: gilli danda poem; prefixes and abstract nouns; ownership and how to play; words, questions and double letters.

lessons.title: Gilli Danda Poem

activities.prompt: What do the children discover when their small gilli soars into the sky?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Playing Gilli Danda
activities.body: Children gather in the playground to play Gilli Danda with a stick and a small gilli. Before swinging and hitting it, they count to three. The gilli flies high beneath the bright blue sky. The children laugh, play happily together, and keep playing with their friends. They also play in the sun's golden rays and feel free when they swing the stick. The poem calls Gilli Danda a fine game.
keyPoints: Children play with a stick and a small gilli.
They count to three before swinging.
The gilli flies high beneath the bright blue sky.
activities.explanation: The children enjoy a fine game in the playground.

activities.prompt: Why does the gilli suddenly fly high when a child swings the stick?
steps: The game uses a stick and a small gilli, so the stick can hit the gilli.
The children count to three so they swing at the right time.
When the stick hits the gilli, the gilli rises into the air.
It flies high beneath the blue sky, so the swing sends it upward.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where Do They Play?
activities.prompt: Where do the children gather to play Gilli Danda?
options: In the playground
In the classroom
In the library
In the market
activities.explanation: The children gather in the playground before playing.

activities.title: Count Before Swinging
activities.prompt: Before swinging and hitting the gilli, the children count to ______.
activities.hint: This number tells them when to swing.
activities.explanation: The children count to three before they swing and hit the gilli.

activities.title: Match the Poem's Details
activities.prompt: Match each part of the poem with its detail.
pairs: flies beneath the bright blue sky
activities.explanation: The gilli flies, the stick brings freedom, and the sun has golden rays.

activities.title: The Gilli in the Sky
activities.prompt: Which description of the gilli matches the poem?
options: The gilli rests beneath the bright blue sky.
The gilli flies beneath the bright blue sky.
The gilli hides beneath the bright blue sky.
The gilli rolls beneath the bright blue sky.
activities.explanation: The poem says the gilli flies high beneath the bright blue sky.

activities.title: Order the Game
activities.prompt: Put these parts of the game in the correct order.
items: Swing the stick and hit the gilli
The gilli flies high into the air
activities.explanation: Counting comes first, then the swing and hit, and then the gilli flies.

activities.title: A Happy Game
activities.prompt: Which detail best shows that the children enjoy the game?
options: They count to three before swinging.
They play in the golden rays of the sun.
They laugh and play happily together.
The gilli flies beneath the bright blue sky.
activities.explanation: Their laughter and happy play show that they enjoy Gilli Danda.

activities.prompt: A child hits a small gilli with the stick. What will likely happen next?
options: It will fly high into the sky.
It will stay close to the ground.
It will return straight to the hand.
It will remain beside the stick.

This assumes the gilli cannot rise after the hit.
This assumes the gilli returns to the hand by itself.
This assumes the gilli stays fixed beside the stick.

activities.explanation: The hit sends the gilli high into the bright blue sky.

activities.prompt: The children count to three before the swing. Why might this help their game?
options: It tells them when to swing the stick.
It makes the gilli become smaller.
It tells them the game is ending.
It makes them lose the gilli.

This confuses the count with a change in size.
This mistakes the count for a sign that the game ends.
This confuses the count with losing the gilli.

activities.explanation: Counting to three gives them a clear time to swing.

activities.prompt: The poem shows a bright blue sky and golden sun rays. What does this suggest?
options: They are playing outside in sunshine.
They are playing inside a dark room.
They are playing while heavy rain falls.
They are playing after the sun is gone.

This mistakes bright sunlight for a dark room.
This mistakes the golden sun rays for heavy rain.
This mistakes sunlight for a time after sunset.

activities.explanation: The blue sky and golden sun rays show sunshine outdoors.

activities.prompt: The poem calls Gilli Danda a fine game. How does the poet feel?
options: The poet likes and praises the game.
The poet thinks the game is boring.
The poet wants to stop the game.
The poet is afraid to play it.

This mistakes praise for thinking the game is boring.
This mistakes praise for wanting the game to end.
This mistakes praise for fear of playing.

activities.explanation: Calling the game fine shows that the poet praises it.

activities.prompt: The children keep playing and laugh happily with their friends. What does this show?
options: They enjoy playing with their friends.
They are angry with their friends.
They want to play the game alone.
They feel bored with each other.

This mistakes happy laughter for anger.
This mistakes playing together for wanting to be alone.
This mistakes happy play for boredom.

activities.explanation: Happy laughter and continued play show that they enjoy it together.

lessons.title: Prefixes and Abstract Nouns

activities.prompt: How can a few letters change what words mean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Learn about prefixes and abstract nouns
activities.body: A prefix is added at the beginning of a word. The two prefixes in this lesson are un- and re-. The prefix un- means not, and re- means again. Sameer could not find his drawing book, so he decided to draw his work again. An abstract noun names something without a physical shape. Sadness is one example. Feelings, thoughts and ideas are abstract nouns too.
keyPoints: The prefix un- means not.
The prefix re- means again.
Feelings, thoughts and ideas are abstract nouns.
activities.explanation: You have learned two prefixes and one kind of noun.

activities.prompt: A child cannot find a drawing book. What do un- and re- show, and what kind of noun is sadness?
steps: Because un- means not, unhappy means not happy.
The child felt sadness because the drawing book was missing.
Because re- means again, the child drew the work again.
Therefore, the prefixes explain the feeling and action, while sadness is abstract.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the meaning
activities.prompt: What does the prefix un- mean?
options: not
again
found
touched
activities.explanation: The prefix un- means not.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: Sameer decided to draw his work ______.
activities.hint: Use the prefix re-.
activities.explanation: The prefix re- means again.

activities.title: Find the meaning
activities.prompt: Which meaning fits uncommon?
options: not easily found
easy to find
easy to touch
easy to draw
activities.explanation: Uncommon means something that is not easily found.

activities.title: Make the matches
activities.prompt: Match each prefix or word to its lesson meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a meaning from this lesson.

activities.title: Choose the abstract nouns
activities.prompt: Which group contains only abstract nouns?
options: feelings, thoughts, ideas
sadness, rose, un-
happiness, un-, re-
rose, drawing, book
activities.explanation: Feelings, thoughts and ideas are all abstract nouns.

activities.title: Order Sameer's events
activities.prompt: Put Sameer's events in the order they happened.
items: Sameer could not find his drawing book
Sameer decided to draw his work again
activities.explanation: Sameer first could not find his drawing book. He became unhappy and then decided to draw his work again.

activities.prompt: A child cannot find a drawing book. How does that child feel?
options: He felt very unhappy.
He felt very happy.
He felt very excited.
He felt very peaceful.

He may think a missing book can make him happy.
He may mix up missing a book with feeling excited.
He may mix up a calm feeling with unhappiness.

activities.explanation: This is right because a missing book made him unhappy.

activities.prompt: A box is uncommon. What does uncommon suggest about finding it?
options: It was easy to find.
It was easy to carry.
It was hard to find.
It was easy to open.

This mistake reverses the meaning of not.
He may think uncommon describes carrying, not finding.
He may think uncommon describes opening, not finding.

activities.explanation: This is right because uncommon means not easily found.

activities.prompt: A child feels happiness, but cannot touch it. What does this show about happiness?
options: It has a physical shape.
It begins with the prefix re-.
It has no physical shape.
It begins with the prefix un-.

He may think a feeling can have a physical shape.
He may think happiness begins with the prefix re-.
He may think happiness begins with the prefix un-.

activities.explanation: This is right because happiness cannot be touched.

lessons.title: Ownership and How to Play

activities.prompt: How can we show who owns something and play a fun new game?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Who owns it?
activities.body: Possessive pronouns show ownership or a relationship between people and things. The book on the table belongs to the speaker. The red handbag belongs to the girl. The cycle near the gate belongs to the person being asked. Gilli Danda is played with one short gilli and one long danda. One player hits the gilli with the danda. The other players try to catch the flying gilli.
keyPoints: Possessive pronouns show ownership or relationships.
Different things belong to different people.
Gilli Danda uses a gilli and a danda.
activities.explanation: These examples show who owns things and how Gilli Danda is played.

activities.prompt: A child points to a book on a table and asks whose book it is.
steps: The child points to the book and asks who owns it.
The book belongs to the speaker, so it is the speaker's book.
A possessive word such as 'my' shows this ownership.
The child should therefore say that the book is mine.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Gilli Danda and Ownership
activities.body: One short gilli and one long danda are needed to play Gilli Danda. One player hits the gilli with the danda. The other players try to catch the flying gilli. The cycle near the gate belongs to the person being asked. These crayons belong to the person being addressed.
keyPoints: Gilli Danda uses one short gilli and one long danda.
One player hits the gilli.
The other players try to catch it.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects ownership with the roles in Gilli Danda.

activities.title: Find the owner
activities.prompt: Who owns the red handbag?
options: the girl
Mudit
the speaker
the speaker's cousins
activities.explanation: The red handbag belongs to the girl, so she is its owner.

activities.title: Match each owner
activities.prompt: Match each thing to its owner.
activities.explanation: Each thing is paired with the person or group it belongs to.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: The ______ on the table belongs to the speaker.
activities.hint: Think of the item placed on the table.
activities.explanation: The book on the table belongs to the speaker.

activities.title: Choose the correct object
activities.prompt: What does the player use to hit the gilli?
options: the danda
the gilli
the bowls
the handbag
activities.explanation: One player hits the gilli with the danda.

activities.title: Play in order
activities.prompt: Put the Gilli Danda actions in order.
items: One player hits the gilli with the danda.
The other players try to catch the flying gilli.
activities.explanation: The player hits first, and the others then try to catch the flying gilli.

activities.title: Know possessive pronouns
activities.prompt: What do possessive pronouns show?
options: ownership or a relationship
the colour of an object
the size of a toy
the age of a person
activities.explanation: Possessive pronouns show ownership or a relationship between people and things.

activities.prompt: The book on the table belongs to the speaker. Another child takes it. What might the speaker do?
options: Ask for the speaker's book back.
Ask for the girl's handbag back.
Ask for Mudit's toy train back.
Ask for the cousin's crayons back.

The red handbag belongs to the girl, not the speaker.
The toy train belongs to Mudit, not the speaker.
The crayons belong to the speaker, not the speaker's cousins.

activities.explanation: The taken book belongs to the speaker.

activities.prompt: The red handbag belongs to the girl. Another child takes it. What might the girl do?
options: Ask for her red handbag back.
Ask for the speaker's book back.
Ask for Mudit's toy train back.
Ask for the little girl's bowls back.

The book belongs to the speaker, not the girl.
The toy train belongs to Mudit, not the girl.
The bowls were not taken in this situation.

activities.explanation: The taken handbag belongs to the girl.

activities.prompt: The cycle near the gate belongs to the person being asked. That person says, 'These things are mine.' Who owns the things?
options: The things belong to the speaker.
The things belong to the listener.
The things belong to the girl.
The things belong to Mudit.

This confuses the speaker with the person being asked.
The girl owns the red handbag, not these things.
Mudit owns the toy train, not these things.

activities.explanation: The person being asked owns the things and calls them 'mine'.

activities.prompt: These crayons belong to the speaker. The house with the red roof belongs to the speaker's cousins. How can the speaker name both owners?
options: My crayons and my cousins' house.
My crayons and my cousin's house.
Our crayons and my cousins' house.
Their crayons and my cousins' house.

This wrongly treats the speaker's cousins as one cousin.
This wrongly includes the speaker in the crayons' owners.
This wrongly gives the crayons to other people.

activities.explanation: This gives the crayons to the speaker and the house to the cousins.

activities.prompt: The toy train belongs to Mudit. The bowls belong to the little girl. Another child takes Mudit's train. What might Mudit do?
options: Ask for his toy train back.
Ask for the little girl's bowls back.
Ask for the speaker's crayons back.
Ask for the red handbag back.

The bowls belong to the little girl and were not taken.
The crayons belong to the speaker and were not taken.
The handbag belongs to the girl and was not taken.

activities.explanation: The taken toy train belongs to Mudit.

lessons.title: Words, Questions and Double Letters

activities.prompt: How can we use a dictionary to discover meanings, questions, and double letters?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Explore Words and Questions
activities.body: Use a dictionary to find word meanings. Then use each word in your own sentence. You can rearrange words to make questions. Every question begins with a capital letter and ends with a question mark. Some words have double letters, such as gilli, millet and bullock. You can also circle words with different meanings.
keyPoints: Find meanings with a dictionary.
Make questions with capital letters and question marks.
Some words have double l.
activities.explanation: This card shows the main word skills.

activities.prompt: A child has a dictionary, mixed words, and a double-letter task. What should the child do?
steps: They look up each word because dictionaries show word meanings.
They use it in their own sentence because dictionary words need one.
They rearrange words so a question has a capital and question mark.
They write gilli, millet, and bullock because these give three double-l words.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Double Letters and Meanings
activities.body: Double letters appear together in a word. The words gilli, millet and bullock each have two l letters. For each double letter, write three words. These words may be nouns, adjectives, verbs or adverbs. Different words can have different meanings. The children circle such words, like precious and expensive, or often and always.
keyPoints: Gilli, millet and bullock have double l.
Write three words for each double letter.
Words can have different meanings.
activities.explanation: You can use several kinds of words.

activities.title: Use a Dictionary
activities.prompt: What do the children use a dictionary to find?
options: word meanings
new sentences
double letters
capital letters
activities.explanation: A dictionary helps you find the meaning of a word.

activities.title: Finish a Question
activities.prompt: A question must end with a question mark.
activities.explanation: A question mark shows that the sentence is a question.

activities.title: Find the Double Letter
activities.prompt: The word gilli has ______ letters l.
activities.hint: Look carefully at the spelling of gilli.
activities.explanation: Both l letters sit together in gilli.

activities.title: Choose Double-Letter Words
activities.prompt: Every word chosen for a double letter must be a noun.
activities.explanation: Chosen words may also be adjectives, verbs or adverbs.

activities.title: Match Words with Clues
activities.prompt: Match each word with its clue.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives clues for each word.

activities.title: Order the Parts
activities.prompt: Put these parts of a question in order from start to end.
activities.explanation: A capital letter comes first, and a question mark comes last.

activities.prompt: A child finds a hard word. What should the child do first?
options: Look up its meaning in a dictionary.
Copy the word into a sentence.
Guess the meaning and move on.
Skip the word and keep reading.

This mistakes copying for finding the meaning.
This misses using a dictionary to find the meaning.
This misses checking the meaning in a dictionary.

activities.explanation: This is right because dictionaries show word meanings.

activities.prompt: Words are mixed on a card. How can a child make a question?
options: Rearrange the words into a question.
Copy the words in the same order.
Change the words into longer words.
Replace the words with new words.

This misses rearranging the mixed words.
This misses rearranging the mixed words.
This misses rearranging the mixed words.

activities.explanation: This is right because children rearrange words to make questions.

lessons.title: Making Gilli Danda

activities.prompt: Could we turn waste materials into a fun game for our friends?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making a Gilli Danda
activities.body: Making Gilli Danda starts with waste materials. The danda is a thick twig, wooden stick, or discarded wooden stick. The gilli is made from a thick small twig. Use a rough stone to smoothen the sticks and sharpen both ends of the gilli. Rub the gilli until it is smooth. Then add colour or coloured paper. Both parts should be sturdy and easy to handle.
keyPoints: The gilli is made from a thick small twig.
A rough stone smoothens the sticks and sharpens the gilli.
Both parts should be sturdy and easy to handle.
activities.explanation: Simple materials can become a sturdy and attractive Gilli Danda.

activities.prompt: A child has a discarded wooden stick and wants to make a danda.
steps: A discarded stick can be used because it can become the danda.
A rough stone is used because it smoothens the stick for holding.
Colours can be added because painting makes the stick more attractive.
The danda is ready when it is sturdy and easy to handle.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A discarded wooden stick can also be used as the danda.
activities.explanation: Yes. A discarded wooden stick is another useful material for the danda.

activities.prompt: The rough ______ smoothens the surface of the stick.
activities.hint: It is used for rubbing and smoothing.
activities.explanation: A rough stone smoothens the surface of the stick.

activities.prompt: Match each material with its use.
activities.explanation: Each material has a useful part in making the Gilli Danda.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for making the gilli in order.
items: Make the gilli from a thick small twig.
Sharpen both ends with a rough stone.
Rub the gilli with a stone until it is smooth.
Check that it is sturdy and easy to handle.
activities.explanation: The gilli is shaped, sharpened, smoothed and checked before use.

activities.prompt: The gilli should be about ______ inches long.
activities.hint: Use the length given for the gilli.
activities.explanation: Your book says that the gilli should be about 3–4 inches long.

activities.prompt: Which description fits both the gilli and danda?
options: rough and hard to handle
plain and hard to grip
sturdy and easy to handle
colourful and hard to hold
activities.explanation: Both the gilli and danda must be sturdy and easy to handle.

activities.prompt: The gilli feels rough. A child rubs it with a stone. How does the child feel after it becomes smooth?
options: Happy, because the smooth gilli is easier to hold.
Angry, because the rough stone broke the gilli.
Sad, because smoothing made the gilli lose its colour.
Afraid, because the gilli became much shorter.

why.Angry, because the rough stone broke the: This wrongly assumes smoothing breaks the gilli.
why.Sad, because smoothing made the gilli lo: This wrongly assumes smoothing removes the gilli's colour.
why.Afraid, because the gilli became much sh: This wrongly assumes rubbing makes the gilli much shorter.

activities.explanation: A happy feeling fits because the smooth gilli is easier to hold.

activities.prompt: A story says, “The stone worked until the gilli felt smooth.” What does this line imply?
options: It shows why the gilli will be easier to hold.
It shows that the stone painted the gilli with colour.
It shows that the stone made both parts much shorter.
It shows that the gilli became a discarded wooden stick.

why.It shows that the stone painted the gill: This wrongly thinks smoothing means adding colour.
why.It shows that the stone made both parts: This wrongly thinks rubbing makes the gilli shorter.
why.It shows that the gilli became a discard: This wrongly mixes up the gilli and the discarded danda.

activities.explanation: Smoothing makes the gilli easier to hold, which is the line's purpose.

activities.prompt: The gilli must be sturdy and easy to handle. Which gilli best fits the lesson?
options: A 3–4 inch gilli with smooth sides and both ends sharpened.
A 3–4 inch gilli with rough sides and both ends sharpened.
A gilli under three inches with smooth sides and both ends sharpened.
A 3–4 inch gilli with smooth sides and both ends blunt.

why.A 3–4 inch gilli with rough sides and bo: A rough surface is not smoothened as the lesson requires.
why.A gilli under three inches with smooth s: The gilli should be about 3–4 inches long, not under three inches.
why.A 3–4 inch gilli with smooth sides and b: Both ends should be sharpened, not left blunt.

activities.explanation: It has the right length, a smooth surface, and sharpened ends.

activities.prompt: A child wants a gilli that looks good and is easy to handle. Which plan is best?
options: Smoothen the gilli, then decorate it with colours.
Decorate the gilli, but leave its surface rough.
Paint the gilli, but leave both ends blunt.
Cover the gilli, but do not smoothen it.

why.Decorate the gilli, but leave its surfac: It decorates the gilli but forgets to smoothen the surface.
why.Paint the gilli, but leave both ends blu: It decorates the gilli but does not prepare both ends properly.
It decorates the gilli but forgets to smoothen it.

activities.explanation: Smoothing makes it easier to handle, and colours make it attractive.

lessons.title: Just for Fun

activities.prompt: What is the special something your friends use more often than you do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Play with Words
activities.body: A riddle describes something that belongs to you. Your friends use its answer more often than you do. You must guess it. Next comes a spellathon. Make words with three or more letters. Use only letters shown in the wheel. A letter can be used many times. It cannot be used more often than it appears. Tea and Reach are examples. Then, make a wheel like the example.
keyPoints: The riddle's answer belongs to you.
Your friends use the answer more often than you do.
Spellathon words use shown letters within their counts.
activities.explanation: Learn the riddle clue, spellathon rules, and wheel-making step.

activities.prompt: A child is unsure which words the spellathon accepts.
steps: Start with length, because the spellathon needs three or more letters.
Next check the wheel, because every letter must come from it.
Then check repeats, because no letter can outnumber its wheel count.
So TEA and REACH count; the child can make a wheel.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Riddle Clue
activities.prompt: What does the riddle describe?
options: Something you own
A letter wheel
A spellathon word
A guessed answer
activities.explanation: The riddle describes something that belongs to you. This is its main clue.

activities.title: Solve the Riddle
activities.prompt: The riddle asks the reader to ______ the answer.
activities.hint: Use the action asked for in the riddle.
activities.explanation: The riddle asks the reader to guess the answer. Guessing helps you solve it.

activities.title: Repeated Letters
activities.prompt: Why can a letter appear several times in your words?
options: It appears several times in the wheel.
Every word needs many letters.
The wheel changes after each word.
Words must use every letter.
activities.explanation: A letter can be used many times when it appears several times in the wheel.

activities.title: Match the Words
activities.prompt: Match each clue or word with its matching fact.
pairs: Words with three or more letters
activities.explanation: The riddle answer belongs to you, and friends use it more often. The spellathon counts words with three or more letters. Tea and Reach are examples.

activities.title: Challenge Order
activities.prompt: Put the lesson's word challenges in the order they happen.
items: Make words from the letter wheel
Make a wheel like the example
activities.explanation: First, you guess the riddle's answer. Next, you make words with the wheel. Then, you make a wheel like the example.

activities.title: Follow Every Rule
activities.prompt: Which choice follows every spellathon rule?
options: Make three-letter words within shown letter counts.
Make short words without checking letter counts.
Make long words using letters outside the wheel.
Make words with any allowed letter count.
activities.explanation: This choice uses three or more letters and only shown letters. It also keeps each letter within its shown count.

activities.prompt: The answer belongs to the reader, and friends use it more often. What could it be?
options: The reader's own name
The friend's school bag
The shelf's story book
The classroom's spare pen

why.The friend's school bag: This mistake thinks the belonging clue points to a friend's thing.
why.The shelf's story book: This mistake treats a book on a shelf as belonging to the reader.
why.The classroom's spare pen: This mistake treats a classroom pen as the reader's own thing.

activities.explanation: This fits because friends use a reader's name, which belongs to that reader.

activities.prompt: A child joins the spellathon but writes only two-letter words. What should the child change?
options: Choose words with three or more letters
Use only one letter from the wheel
Stop making words from the wheel
Choose words with just a single letter

why.Use only one letter from the wheel: This mistake thinks only one wheel letter should be used.
why.Stop making words from the wheel: This mistake stops the activity instead of correcting word length.
why.Choose words with just a single letter: This mistake uses the opposite of the three-letter rule.

activities.explanation: The spellathon needs words with three or more letters.

activities.prompt: The wheel shows E many times. How often can a child use E?
options: Many times, but never beyond the wheel count
Only once during the whole wheel activity
Only when the word must end with E
Never again, because E is already shown

why.Only once during the whole wheel activit: This mistake treats many allowed uses as only one use.
why.Only when the word must end with E: This mistake adds an ending rule that is not in the facts.
why.Never again, because E is already shown: This mistake thinks a shown letter cannot be used again.

activities.explanation: A letter can be used many times, but not beyond its wheel count.

activities.prompt: REACH uses wheel letters. Why does the word count?
options: It has three letters and uses wheel letters
It has fewer than three wheel letters
It has three letters but uses other letters
It uses letters that the wheel does not show

why.It has fewer than three wheel letters: This mistake confuses the number of letters with different letters.
why.It has three letters but uses other lett: This mistake thinks being long enough lets a word use any letters.
why.It uses letters that the wheel does not: This mistake thinks the example may need letters outside the wheel.

activities.explanation: The word has three or more letters and uses the shown wheel letters.

activities.context: On a sunny afternoon, the children gather around in the playground to play Gilli Danda. Each one holds a stick and a small gilli. They count to three, and then they swing and hit the gilli. The gilli flies high into the air, beneath the bright blue sky, while the children laugh and play happily together in the golden rays of the sun.
activities.prompt: The children count to three before they swing the stick. Why is this counting helpful for the game?
options: So that every child swings at the right moment and the small gilli is not missed
So that the gilli can fly higher into the air than it normally does
So that the game can finish sooner than it usually does
So that the children can start using a bigger stick

why.So that the gilli can fly higher into th: The height of the gilli's flight comes from the swing itself, not from the counting.
why.So that the game can finish sooner than: Counting to three does not shorten the game; it is part of how it is played.
why.So that the children can start using a b: The stick used in the game stays the same; the count is about timing, not size.

activities.explanation: Counting makes the swings happen together, so a small gilli is hit at the right time.

activities.context: On a sunny afternoon, the children gather around in the playground to play Gilli Danda. Each one holds a stick and a small gilli. They count to three, and then they swing and hit the gilli. The gilli flies high into the air, beneath the bright blue sky, while the children laugh and play happily together in the golden rays of the sun.
activities.prompt: A friend stands just outside the circle of children in the playground, watching the game. What should the friend do to join in?
options: Walk over and play Gilli Danda together with the children who have gathered
Keep watching from outside, because only the first child is allowed to swing the stick
Wait for the whole game to end, because visitors are not allowed to play
Ask for a different game, because Gilli Danda is not worth playing with friends

why.Keep watching from outside, because only: All the children take turns; watching is not what the poem describes them doing.
why.Wait for the whole game to end, because: Nothing in the poem says visitors must wait until the game is over.
why.Ask for a different game, because Gilli: The poem calls Gilli Danda a fine game, so there is no reason to ask for another one.

activities.explanation: The game is played by children gathered together in the playground, so joining the circle is the right move.

activities.prompt: How does the poem show that Gilli Danda is a fine game, and how do the sky and sunlight pictures add to the mood?
activities.answer: The poem calls Gilli Danda a fine game. It shows the children laughing and playing happily together, the gilli flying high into the air beneath the bright blue sky, and the children playing in the golden rays of the sun. These pictures make the game feel joyful and free.
points: The poem directly calls the game a fine one
The children are described as laughing and playing happily
The gilli's flight high beneath the blue sky is used as a happy picture
The golden sunlight adds to the cheerful, carefree mood
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Sameer was unhappy because he could not find his drawing book. He decided to draw his work again. The prefix un- means not, as in unhappy. The prefix re- means again, matching his decision to draw his work again. A prefix is added at the beginning of a word. Uncommon means something that is not easily found. Happiness and rose are both nouns, but happiness is a feeling that cannot be touched, so it is abstract.
activities.prompt: In the case, what does adding re- before draw tell Sameer to do?
options: Repeat the drawing
Draw different work
Do not draw at all
Find the drawing book

why.Draw different work: Again does not mean doing different work.
why.Do not draw at all: Not drawing would use the meaning of un-.
why.Find the drawing book: Finding the book is not the meaning of re-.

activities.explanation: Re- means again, so it matches repeating the drawing.

activities.context: Sameer was unhappy because he could not find his drawing book. He decided to draw his work again. The prefix un- means not, as in unhappy. The prefix re- means again, matching his decision to draw his work again. A prefix is added at the beginning of a word. Uncommon means something that is not easily found. Happiness and rose are both nouns, but happiness is a feeling that cannot be touched, so it is abstract.
activities.prompt: Which word could name Sameer's emotional state in the case?
options: sadness
happiness
book
rose

why.happiness: Happiness is a feeling, but it does not describe his state in the case.
why.book: Book names what he could not find, not his feeling.
why.rose: Rose is a noun, but it is not identified as abstract in the given facts.

activities.explanation: Sadness is an abstract noun and can describe his unhappy feeling.

activities.prompt: Explain how the prefixes un- and re- help explain what happens in the case.
activities.answer: In “unhappy,” un- means not, so it helps show that Sameer is not happy. The prefix re- means again, so it matches his decision to draw his work again. Both prefixes are added at the beginning of a word.
points: Un- means not.
Un- shows that Sameer is not happy.
Re- means again.
Both prefixes are added at the beginning.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A speaker shows a book on a table and says the crayons are theirs. The red handbag belongs to the girl, and the bowls belong to the little girl. A cycle near the gate belongs to the person being asked. A toy train belongs to Mudit. The speaker's cousins own a house with a red roof. Later, players choose Gilli Danda. One player hits the short gilli with the long danda, while the others try to catch the flying gilli.
activities.prompt: The speaker asks the person near the gate about the cycle. Who should be treated as its owner?
options: The person receiving the speaker's question
The girl with the red handbag
The little girl with the bowls
One of the speaker's cousins

why.The girl with the red handbag: The girl owns the red handbag.
why.The little girl with the bowls: The little girl owns the bowls.
why.One of the speaker's cousins: The cousins own the house with the red roof.

activities.explanation: The cycle belongs to the person being asked.

activities.context: A speaker shows a book on a table and says the crayons are theirs. The red handbag belongs to the girl, and the bowls belong to the little girl. A cycle near the gate belongs to the person being asked. A toy train belongs to Mudit. The speaker's cousins own a house with a red roof. Later, players choose Gilli Danda. One player hits the short gilli with the long danda, while the others try to catch the flying gilli.
activities.prompt: After the danda hits the gilli, what should the other players do next?
options: Try to catch the gilli while it is flying
Hit the gilli again with the danda
Wait for the gilli to land without touching it
Keep the danda and watch the others play

why.Hit the gilli again with the danda: One player is stated to hit the gilli.
why.Wait for the gilli to land without touch: The other players should try to catch it.
why.Keep the danda and watch the others play: The danda is used by the player who hits the gilli.

activities.explanation: This matches what the other players are supposed to do.

activities.prompt: How do possessive pronouns help in a situation like the one in the case?
activities.answer: Possessive pronouns show ownership or a relationship between people and things. They make it clear who owns each item, such as the book, crayons, handbag, cycle, toy train, house, or bowls.
points: Show who owns something
Show a relationship between people and things
Make ownership clear
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How should children turn a group of rearranged words into a complete question?
activities.answer: The children should order the rearranged words so that they form a question. The question must start with a capital letter, and the final punctuation must be a question mark. They should check both the opening capital and the ending mark before they finish the question.
points: The words are arranged to form a question.
The question begins with a capital letter.
The question ends with a question mark.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Two children are making Gilli Danda from waste materials. For the gilli, they choose a thick small twig that is about 3–4 inches long. They use a rough stone to sharpen both ends and then rub the gilli until it is smooth. For the danda, they use a discarded wooden stick. They check that both pieces are sturdy and easy to handle. They also add coloured paper for decoration.
activities.prompt: Why do the children rub the gilli with the rough stone after sharpening it?
options: This helps remove rough parts and leave the gilli with a smoother surface.
This is mainly to colour the gilli before decoration.
This makes the gilli longer so it can reach the danda.
This is only for sharpening one end of the gilli.

why.This is mainly to colour the gilli befor: Colouring is a separate decorative step.
why.This makes the gilli longer so it can re: The rubbing step does not make the gilli longer.
why.This is only for sharpening one end of t: The children sharpen both ends, not just one.

activities.explanation: Rubbing helps smooth the gilli’s surface.

activities.context: Two children are making Gilli Danda from waste materials. For the gilli, they choose a thick small twig that is about 3–4 inches long. They use a rough stone to sharpen both ends and then rub the gilli until it is smooth. For the danda, they use a discarded wooden stick. They check that both pieces are sturdy and easy to handle. They also add coloured paper for decoration.
activities.prompt: After the children paint the danda, what change should they expect?
options: The stick will have a more pleasing appearance.
The stick will become sturdy enough for use.
The stick will become sharper at both ends.
The stick will become smooth enough to use.

why.The stick will become sturdy enough for: Painting does not make the stick sturdy.
why.The stick will become sharper at both en: Sharpening is done with a rough stone, not paint.
why.The stick will become smooth enough to u: Smoothing is also done by rubbing with a rough stone.

activities.explanation: Painting makes the stick more attractive.

activities.prompt: How are the gilli and danda prepared for use?
activities.answer: The gilli is made from a thick small twig that is about 3–4 inches long. A rough stone sharpens both ends, and the gilli is rubbed until smooth. The danda is made from a thick twig, wooden stick, or discarded wooden stick. Both pieces should be sturdy and easy to handle.
points: The gilli is about 3–4 inches long.
Both ends of the gilli are sharpened.
The gilli is rubbed until it is smooth.
The danda can be made from a discarded wooden stick.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the spellathon, a child sees the words Tea and Reach made with the letter wheel. The child then builds a new wheel like the example. A classmate says, “The wheel shows a letter twice, so I can use that letter three times in my words.” The child checks the example and explains how often each letter may really be used.
activities.prompt: The classmate wants to use a letter three times, although it appears twice on the wheel. What should the child explain?
options: Each letter must be used no more often than it appears.
Three uses are allowed because a letter may be reused.
The number of letters on the wheel does not matter.
New words do not have to follow the wheel's rules.

why.Three uses are allowed because a letter: Reusing a letter does not remove the limit.
why.The number of letters on the wheel does: The number of times shown does matter.
why.New words do not have to follow the whee: Words must still use the letters shown.

activities.explanation: The wheel limits how often a letter may be used.

activities.context: During the spellathon, a child sees the words Tea and Reach made with the letter wheel. The child then builds a new wheel like the example. A classmate says, “The wheel shows a letter twice, so I can use that letter three times in my words.” The child checks the example and explains how often each letter may really be used.
activities.prompt: The child wants to test the words Tea and Reach on the new wheel. What should the child check first?
options: Each needed letter appears often enough.
Every letter may be used any number of times.
Only one of the words can be tested.
The example does not need to be checked.

why.Every letter may be used any number of t: Unlimited use would break the rule.
A wheel can be used to make several words.
The example shows how the letter limits work.

activities.explanation: Each letter in a word must have enough uses on the wheel.

activities.prompt: What does the riddle ask the reader to do, and how do its clues describe the answer?
activities.answer: The riddle asks the reader to guess the answer. Its clues say that the answer belongs to the reader and that friends use it more often. The answer must therefore fit both clues: it belongs to the reader, while other people use it more often than the reader does.
points: The reader must guess the answer.
The answer belongs to the reader.
Friends use the answer more often.
Both clues help identify the answer.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.title: Playing Gilli Danda
activities.prompt: In Gilli Danda, what does one player do?
options: One player catches it.
One player hits the gilli.
Two players hit together.

activities.explanation: One player hits the gilli. The other players try to catch it.

activities.title: The Prefix re-
activities.prompt: The prefix re- means again.
activities.explanation: Yes! The prefix re- means again.

activities.title: An Abstract Noun
activities.prompt: Sadness is an example of an ______ noun.
activities.hint: This noun is for something without a physical shape.
activities.explanation: Sadness is a feeling. You cannot touch its physical shape.

activities.title: Find the Double Letters
activities.prompt: Which pair has double l in both words?
options: rose and sadness
book and table
gilli and millet
cycle and gate
activities.explanation: Well done! Both gilli and millet have two letters l.

activities.title: Using a Dictionary
activities.prompt: Children use each dictionary word in their own sentence.
activities.explanation: Yes! They find the meaning and use the word in their own sentence.

activities.title: Making a Gilli
activities.prompt: Both ends of the gilli are sharpened with a rough ______.
activities.hint: This smoothens the surface of the sticks.

activities.title: The Riddle
activities.prompt: What does the riddle describe?
options: A game played by children
A tool used for drawing
Something belonging to a friend
Something belonging to you
activities.explanation: The riddle describes something that belongs to you. Your friends use it more often.

activities.title: Spellathon Rules
activities.prompt: A letter can be used more times than it appears in the wheel.
activities.explanation: A letter can be used many times only if the wheel shows it that often.
