lessons.title: Let Us Do and Explore

activities.prompt: Can you spot what does not belong in each picture?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Spot and Write
activities.body: Job Mix-Up pictures each show something unusual. Your job is to spot the strange things carefully. One example has already been completed, so you can see how the activity works. For every picture, write two sentences. Then turn to the Explore pictures, where you can choose a vocation for yourself.
keyPoints: Each Job Mix-Up picture has something unusual.
Notice the strange things and write two sentences.
Explore pictures show vocations you can choose.
activities.explanation: Look carefully, then use your own words to describe what you notice.

activities.prompt: A picture shows a chef with a fire engine. Why is this a Job Mix-Up?
steps: Look for the strange part because each picture has something unusual.
The chef cooks meals, so driving a fire engine is not the chef's job.
Firefighters drive the fire engine, so the picture mixes two jobs.
Notice and explain this mix-up in two sentences for that picture.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose Your Vocation
activities.body: The Explore pictures show many kinds of work. You may choose one of the vocations shown. You may also choose another vocation that is not shown. You can explore beekeeper, photographer, teacher, dancer, chef, pilot, farmer and florist. Every kind of work is equal in value. No job is better or worse than another.
keyPoints: You can choose a shown or unshown vocation.
Explore pictures show many kinds of work.
No kind of work is better or worse.
activities.explanation: Your choice can be special to you, and every vocation has equal value.

activities.prompt: Something unusual appears in every Job Mix-Up picture.
activities.explanation: Yes. Each Job Mix-Up picture contains something unusual for you to notice.

activities.prompt: Who drives the fire engine?
options: A chef
Firefighters
A photographer
A beekeeper
activities.explanation: Firefighters drive the fire engine. A chef cooks delicious meals instead.

activities.prompt: A chef cooks ______ meals.
activities.hint: Choose the word that describes the meals.
activities.explanation: A chef’s job is to cook delicious meals.

activities.prompt: Match each part to what it shows or does.
activities.explanation: Job Mix-Up pictures show unusual things. Chefs cook meals, and Explore pictures show vocations.

activities.prompt: Put the Job Mix-Up tasks in order.
items: Write two sentences for each picture
activities.explanation: The example is ready first. Notice the strange things before writing two sentences.

activities.prompt: A learner chooses a vocation that is not shown. What does the lesson allow?
options: The choice is allowed.
The choice is not allowed because it is not shown.
Only the shown vocations are allowed.
Shown vocations are better than other work.
activities.explanation: You may choose an unshown vocation. No kind of work is superior or inferior.

activities.prompt: A picture shows a chef beside a fire engine. What is the mix-up?
options: The chef is taking the firefighter's job.
The firefighter is taking the chef's job.
Both people are taking the same job.
Neither person is doing a shown job.

why.The firefighter is taking the chef's job: This reverses the two jobs because firefighters drive fire engines.
This mistakes two different jobs for one shared job.
This misses that a chef is one of the shown vocations.

activities.explanation: This is right because a chef cooks meals, not fire engines.

activities.prompt: Two children choose different shown vocations. What should the class understand?
options: Only the first choice deserves respect, because it comes first.
The second choice is less important, because it comes second.
Both choices deserve equal respect, because no work is better.
Shown vocations matter more than unshown ones.

why.Only the first choice deserves respect,: This wrongly makes the first choice better because of its order.
why.The second choice is less important, bec: This wrongly makes the second choice less important because of its order.
why.Shown vocations matter more than unshown: This wrongly treats shown work as better than unshown work.

activities.explanation: This is right because no kind of work is superior or inferior.

activities.context: When the gong sounds ten in the morning, the speaker walks to school. Every day, the speaker meets a hawker who cries out about bangles, and nobody hurries the hawker along. Returning from school at four in the afternoon, the speaker sees the gardener digging. The gardener uses his spade as he likes and gets dusty. Nobody takes him to task when he is baked in the sun. The speaker wishes to be the gardener digging in a garden.
activities.prompt: The gong sounds ten in the morning. What will the speaker do next?
options: They will head to school on foot.
They will remain on the road until four in the afternoon.
They will begin digging in a garden.
They will stay beside the gardener for the whole day.

why.They will remain on the road until four: Four in the afternoon is when the speaker returns from school.
Digging is the gardener's work, not the speaker's.
why.They will stay beside the gardener for t: The speaker sees the gardener after returning from school.

activities.explanation: The speaker walks to school when the gong sounds ten.

activities.context: When the gong sounds ten in the morning, the speaker walks to school. Every day, the speaker meets a hawker who cries out about bangles, and nobody hurries the hawker along. Returning from school at four in the afternoon, the speaker sees the gardener digging. The gardener uses his spade as he likes and gets dusty. Nobody takes him to task when he is baked in the sun. The speaker wishes to be the gardener digging in a garden.
activities.prompt: If the gardener were made to use his spade in only one way, what would change?
options: He would lose some freedom in how he digs.
He would have to cry out about bangles instead.
He would have to return to school before the gong.
He would stop getting dust on his clothes.

why.He would have to cry out about bangles i: Crying out about bangles is the hawker's work.
why.He would have to return to school before: The speaker, not the gardener, walks to school when the gong sounds.
why.He would stop getting dust on his clothe: Allowing only one method would not remove the dust from the gardener's work.

activities.explanation: The gardener normally uses his spade as he likes.

activities.prompt: Explain how the speaker's school day connects with the hawker and the gardener.
activities.answer: The speaker walks to school when the gong sounds ten in the morning and meets the hawker. After school at four in the afternoon, the speaker sees the gardener digging. The hawker has no fixed place or return time, while the gardener may use his spade as he likes.
points: The speaker walks to school when the gong sounds ten.
The speaker meets the hawker every day.
The speaker sees the gardener after school at four.
The hawker has no fixed routine, while the gardener can use his spade freely.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Every evening, when his mother sends him to bed, the boy looks through his open window. The lane is dark and lonely. A street-lamp looks like a giant with one red eye. The watchman swings his lantern and walks with his shadow at his side. Although the watchman never goes to bed, the boy wishes that he were a watchman walking the streets all night. He even imagines the watchman chasing shadows with his lantern.
activities.prompt: If the boy stayed at the open window after his mother sent him to bed, what would he be able to do?
options: Remain at the window and observe the watchman.
Help the watchman catch the shadows in the lane.
Take the watchman’s place on the night walk.
Ask the watchman to lie down and sleep.

why.Help the watchman catch the shadows in t: Chasing shadows is only his imagination, so the watchman does not need his help.
why.Take the watchman’s place on the night w: He wishes to be the watchman, but he does not actually replace him.
The watchman never goes to bed, so asking him to sleep contradicts the lesson.

activities.explanation: He can keep looking through the open window and see the watchman.

activities.context: Every evening, when his mother sends him to bed, the boy looks through his open window. The lane is dark and lonely. A street-lamp looks like a giant with one red eye. The watchman swings his lantern and walks with his shadow at his side. Although the watchman never goes to bed, the boy wishes that he were a watchman walking the streets all night. He even imagines the watchman chasing shadows with his lantern.
activities.prompt: How does the shadow at the watchman’s side change the way his walk appears?
options: It makes him seem accompanied while he walks.
It shows that a second lantern is moving nearby.
It suggests that another watchman is following him.
It makes the lane seem bright and crowded.

why.It shows that a second lantern is moving: A shadow is not another lantern.
why.It suggests that another watchman is fol: He walks with his shadow, not with another watchman.
why.It makes the lane seem bright and crowde: The lane remains dark, and one shadow does not make it bright or crowded.

activities.explanation: The shadow beside him makes him appear not to walk alone.

activities.prompt: Explain why the boy imagines the watchman chasing shadows with his lantern.
activities.answer: The boy is fascinated by the watchman, who stays awake and walks through a dark, lonely lane. The swinging lantern and the shadow beside the watchman give him ideas, so he imagines the watchman turning the night walk into a game of chasing shadows.
points: Explains that the watchman never goes to bed.
Mentions the dark, lonely lane and the watchman’s shadow.
Shows how the lantern and shadow lead to the imagined chase.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The speaker walks to school along a lane while checking sentences: “I have recently read a new book,” “The speaker goes for school,” and “The fox ran fast than the others.” The picture-word list includes a hammer, camera, screwdriver and sickle. A spade is paired with a tool used for gardening, a gong is a metal disc that makes a loud sound, and a lantern is a case that holds a candle or light.
activities.prompt: The speaker wants to use the school practice sentence in writing. What change should be made first?
options: Replace “for” with “to”.
Replace “for” with “at”.
Replace “for” with “from”.
Replace “for” with “by”.

“At school” describes a place rather than the destination in this sentence.
“From school” would describe leaving school instead of going to it.
“By school” would suggest being beside school rather than going there.

activities.explanation: “To school” matches the fact that the speaker walks to school.

activities.context: The speaker walks to school along a lane while checking sentences: “I have recently read a new book,” “The speaker goes for school,” and “The fox ran fast than the others.” The picture-word list includes a hammer, camera, screwdriver and sickle. A spade is paired with a tool used for gardening, a gong is a metal disc that makes a loud sound, and a lantern is a case that holds a candle or light.
activities.prompt: The speaker wants the fox sentence to compare one fox with the others correctly. Which correction should be made?
options: Replace “fast” with “faster”.
Replace “fast” with “fastest”.
Replace “fast” with “more fast”.
Replace “fast” with “most fast”.

“Fastest” is normally used when comparing more than two things.
“More fast” is not the standard comparative form.
“Most fast” is not the standard superlative form.

activities.explanation: “Faster than” is the correct comparative form.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a gong and a lantern?
activities.answer: A gong is a metal disc that makes a loud sound. A lantern is a case that holds a candle or light. The gong is connected with making a loud noise, while the lantern is connected with holding the source of light.
points: Describes a gong as a metal disc.
Explains that a gong makes a loud sound.
Describes a lantern as a case.
Explains that a lantern holds a candle or light.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Learners sit in groups of five and discuss the poem. The poem's speaker wants to do many things. Each group makes two questions with WH-family question words and writes them down. Learners put their textbooks back in their bags. One group shares its questions with the class, and the remaining groups answer them. This continues until every group has shared its questions. The practice word groups are cushion, ration, fashion, tension; mention, attention, nation, vocation.
activities.prompt: After the group discusses the poem, what should it do before sharing with the class?
options: Create two questions with WH-family question words and record them.
Create two questions with WH-family question words but keep them only in their heads.
Create one question with a WH-family question word and record it.
Create two questions without question words and record them.

why.Create two questions with WH-family ques: Keeping the questions only in their heads breaks the written step.
why.Create one question with a WH-family que: The activity requires two questions, not one.
why.Create two questions without question wo: The questions must use question words from the WH-family.

activities.explanation: This follows the required number, word family, and written step.

activities.context: Learners sit in groups of five and discuss the poem. The poem's speaker wants to do many things. Each group makes two questions with WH-family question words and writes them down. Learners put their textbooks back in their bags. One group shares its questions with the class, and the remaining groups answer them. This continues until every group has shared its questions. The practice word groups are cushion, ration, fashion, tension; mention, attention, nation, vocation.
activities.prompt: Why can the remaining groups answer after a group shares, even though the textbooks have been put away?
options: The shared questions tell the remaining groups what to answer.
The sharing group gives the answers instead of the questions.
Every remaining group has independently created the same two questions.
The first group has already answered each question for the class.

why.The sharing group gives the answers inst: The group shares questions, not answers instead of questions.
why.Every remaining group has independently: The remaining groups need not have created identical questions.
why.The first group has already answered eac: The remaining groups answer the presented questions themselves.

activities.explanation: Sharing presents the questions that the remaining groups answer.

activities.prompt: Explain how a group's questions move from discussion to an answer from the remaining groups.
activities.answer: After discussing the poem, each group creates two questions using question words from the WH-family and writes them down. The learners put their textbooks back in their bags. The group then shares its questions with the class, and the remaining groups answer them. This happens until every group has shared.
points: Each group discusses the poem and creates two questions.
The questions use question words from the WH-family.
The questions are written down, and the textbooks are returned to the bags.
One group shares, the remaining groups answer, and every group eventually shares.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a “Let Us Write” lesson, a Class 5 learner plans three family-member descriptions, each of 50 to 60 words. The task asks about the difficult or boring part of each vocation, although the child sees only the fun part. The learner will also consider the vocations of A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, M. Visvesvaraya, M.S. Subbulakshmi and Salim Ali. The class will discuss “vocation,” “work,” paid household work and gender roles before sharing write-ups.
activities.prompt: What is likely to happen if the learner writes only about the fun part of each family member’s job?
options: The writing may be lively, but it may not answer the central question.
It will clearly answer the question about the difficult or boring part of each job.
It will explain why every kind of work should be paid.
It will show that household work does not count as work.

why.It will clearly answer the question abou: Fun details alone do not provide the information requested.
why.It will explain why every kind of work s: The choice of topic does not prove that all work must be paid.
why.It will show that household work does no: Writing about fun parts does not decide whether household work counts as work.

activities.explanation: This is correct because the task specifically asks for difficult or boring parts.

activities.context: During a “Let Us Write” lesson, a Class 5 learner plans three family-member descriptions, each of 50 to 60 words. The task asks about the difficult or boring part of each vocation, although the child sees only the fun part. The learner will also consider the vocations of A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, M. Visvesvaraya, M.S. Subbulakshmi and Salim Ali. The class will discuss “vocation,” “work,” paid household work and gender roles before sharing write-ups.
activities.prompt: After the write-ups are finished, what should the class do next?
options: Listen to classmates’ paragraphs and discuss what each writer learned about work.
Keep the paragraphs unread and avoid a class discussion.
Discuss only the family members whose jobs seem easiest.
Replace each paragraph with a list of the fun parts.

why.Keep the paragraphs unread and avoid a c: Keeping them private would prevent the planned sharing.
why.Discuss only the family members whose jo: Choosing only easier jobs would leave out important learners and ideas.
why.Replace each paragraph with a list of th: A list of fun parts would not include the required thoughts in paragraph form.

activities.explanation: This is correct because learners are expected to share their write-ups with the class.

activities.prompt: How does the lesson use the ideas of “vocation,” “work,” household payment and gender roles?
activities.answer: The teacher should help learners understand “vocation” and “work” by discussing the family members’ jobs and the named people’s vocations. The class should ask whether household work is paid, what activities count as work, and how gender roles affect people’s views about it.
points: Explains the meanings of “vocation” and “work.”
Links the discussion to family members and the named people.
Raises the question of whether household work is paid.
Considers how gender roles affect ideas about work.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a class activity, a learner examined a set of Job Mix-Up pictures. Something unusual appeared in every picture, and the learner had to notice the strange things. One example had already been completed. The learner wrote two sentences for each picture. Later, the learner looked at the Explore pictures and chose a vocation not shown among them.
activities.prompt: After noticing the strange things, what should the learner do next in the Job Mix-Up activity?
options: Write two sentences for each Job Mix-Up picture.
Choose a vocation that is not shown in the pictures.
Write one sentence for each Job Mix-Up picture.
Look only at the completed example and stop.

why.Choose a vocation that is not shown in t: Choosing a vocation belongs to the Explore part of the lesson.
why.Write one sentence for each Job Mix-Up p: One sentence would not meet the task requirement.
why.Look only at the completed example and s: The other Job Mix-Up pictures still need to be completed.

activities.explanation: Correct: the task requires two sentences for each picture.

activities.context: During a class activity, a learner examined a set of Job Mix-Up pictures. Something unusual appeared in every picture, and the learner had to notice the strange things. One example had already been completed. The learner wrote two sentences for each picture. Later, the learner looked at the Explore pictures and chose a vocation not shown among them.
activities.prompt: If a Job Mix-Up picture showed a chef driving a fire engine, what would the learner notice?
options: The chef is doing the firefighter's job instead of cooking.
The firefighter is doing the chef's job instead of driving the fire engine.
Nothing is unusual because jobs can be mixed freely.
The chef and firefighter are both doing their usual jobs.

why.The firefighter is doing the chef's job: The chef, not the firefighter, would be driving the fire engine.
why.Nothing is unusual because jobs can be m: Jobs cannot be mixed freely when the result is strange.
why.The chef and firefighter are both doing: The chef would not be doing the usual job of cooking.

activities.explanation: Correct: a chef cooks delicious meals and does not drive a fire engine.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the hawker's daily work is correct?
options: No fixed place or homecoming time
A fixed place for every afternoon
A fixed homecoming time each night
No morning meeting with the gong
activities.explanation: This freedom lets the hawker work without fixed times or places.

A case holding a candle or light

activities.prompt: Put the speaker's events in the correct order.
items: The gong sounds in the morning
The speaker walks to school along the lane
His mother sends him to bed in the evening

Driving a fire engine
Using a spade in the garden

chapters.title: Glass Bangles
chapters.summary: In this chapter: let us read – firozabad and ravi’s craft; let us read – making the bangles; let us read – ananya’s new designs; let us think and let us learn.

lessons.title: Let us Read – Firozabad and Ravi’s Craft

activities.prompt: What makes Firozabad’s glass bangles so special to Ravi’s family?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ravi’s Glass-Bangle Workshop
activities.body: Firozabad is a busy district in Uttar Pradesh. The town has a rich tradition of glassware. Ravi was a skilled glass artisan, someone who works with glass. His family had made beautiful bangles for a very long time. Each bangle was art. Bangles showed the town's culture and the skill of its artisans. His workshop was always active, with clinking glass and gentle conversation.
keyPoints: Firozabad is in Uttar Pradesh and is known for glassware.
Ravi's family had made beautiful bangles for a very long time.
His workshop was lively with clinking glass and gentle conversation.
activities.explanation: These details connect Firozabad, Ravi, beautiful bangles, and his lively workshop.

activities.prompt: Why does Ravi’s workshop always feel lively?
steps: Ravi’s family has made beautiful bangles for a very long time.
The workshop is busy because artisans are working there.
Clinking glass and a gentle hum show work and talk continue.
Therefore, the workshop feels alive because skilled people are making art together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Firozabad’s Famous Craft
activities.prompt: Which beautiful things make Firozabad famous?
options: Beautiful glass bangles
Busy district life
A long family tradition
A gentle workshop hum
activities.explanation: Firozabad is famous for its beautiful glass bangles.

activities.title: Ravi’s Job
activities.prompt: Ravi was a skilled glass ______.
activities.hint: This person makes things carefully with skill.
activities.explanation: Ravi was a skilled glass artisan.

activities.title: Match the Details
activities.prompt: Match each word with its correct detail.
pairs: Each was a piece of art
Filled with the sound of glass clinking
Made a gentle hum in the workshop
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a person, place, object, or sound with the correct detail.

activities.title: A Sound in the Workshop
activities.prompt: Which sound filled the air in Ravi's workshop?
options: Glass clinking together
Cart wheels passing
Rain on the roof
People singing loudly
activities.explanation: The air was filled with the sound of glass clinking together.

activities.title: What the Bangles Show
activities.prompt: What did Ravi's beautiful bangles show?
options: Firozabad's culture and artisan skill
The town's weather and seasons
The workers' meal times
The town's train routes
activities.explanation: The bangles showed the town's culture and the skill of its artisans.

activities.prompt: Ravi’s family has kept its bangle tradition alive for years. How does Ravi likely feel?
options: He feels proud of his family’s long tradition.
He feels worried about starting a different job.
He feels bored by the work his family does.
He feels ashamed of his family’s long tradition.

why.He feels worried about starting a differ: This imagines Ravi wanting another job, which the facts do not show.
why.He feels bored by the work his family do: This treats the family tradition as something that bores Ravi.
why.He feels ashamed of his family’s long tr: The facts suggest respect for the family tradition, not shame.

activities.explanation: He values the long family tradition shown in the lesson.

activities.prompt: A child sees Ravi’s family bangles and learns about the town. What can the child learn?
options: The town’s culture includes skilled bangle-making.
The town’s culture has no link with bangle-making.
The town’s culture values only speed and not beauty.
The town’s culture is hidden from every town visitor.

why.The town’s culture has no link with bang: This mistakes separate things for connected culture and craft.
why.The town’s culture values only speed and: This wrongly ignores the beauty shown by the town’s bangles.
why.The town’s culture is hidden from every: This assumes culture cannot be shown by objects, but the bangles do show it.

activities.explanation: The bangles show both the town’s culture and artisan skill.

activities.prompt: Glass clinks while artisans talk inside Ravi’s workshop. What does this tell you?
options: The workshop is busy with people working together.
The workshop is quiet because the artisans have stopped.
The workshop is empty because all the work is finished.
The workshop is loud because everyone is shouting angrily.

why.The workshop is quiet because the artisa: This confuses a gentle hum with silence and stopped work.
why.The workshop is empty because all the wo: This assumes the sounds stop, but the workshop is always busy.
why.The workshop is loud because everyone is: This mistakes ordinary workshop sounds for angry shouting.

activities.explanation: The sounds show active work and artisans talking together.

activities.prompt: An artisan hears glass clinking and a gentle hum nearby. How might the artisan feel?
options: Happy, because the lively workshop surrounds them.
Scared, because the sounds seem sudden and strange.
Angry, because the artisans cannot hear each other.
Lonely, because the busy workshop has no one else.

why.Scared, because the sounds seem sudden a: This invents danger, but no danger appears in the scene.
why.Angry, because the artisans cannot hear: This invents anger and ignores the gentle hum.
why.Lonely, because the busy workshop has no: This ignores the activity and conversation around the artisan.

activities.explanation: The sounds suggest a lively place filled with working artisans.

activities.prompt: A skilled artisan makes each glass bangle as a piece of art. What does “craft” mean here?
options: Skilled work that shows care and ability.
Any object that is old and has been kept.
A busy place where many people talk.
A town tradition with no link to working hands.

why.Any object that is old and has been kept: This confuses craft with age, rather than skilled making.
This describes a workshop, not the skill shown in making.
why.A town tradition with no link to working: This mistakes a town tradition for work without skilled hands.

activities.explanation: Craft means skilled work made with care and ability.

lessons.title: Let us Read – Making the Bangles

activities.prompt: How does soft, glowing glass become a beautiful bangle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Bangles Were Made
activities.body: Making glass bangles needed great skill. Ravi and his team heated glass in a furnace. They carefully shaped the hot glass into bangles. Next, they added beautiful colours and designs. Then they cooled the decorated bangles. Ravi gave each bangle his full attention, so every bangle was beautiful and long-lasting.
keyPoints: Glass was heated in a furnace.
Hot glass was shaped into bangles.
Ravi gave each bangle his full attention.
activities.explanation: Great care made the bangles beautiful and long-lasting.

activities.prompt: How can Ravi make every glass bangle beautiful and long-lasting?
steps: They heat glass in a furnace, because hot glass must be shaped.
They shape each bangle with full attention, because great skill is needed.
They add colours and designs, because every bangle should be beautiful.
They cool the decorated bangles to perfection, so every bangle will last.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Heating the Glass
activities.prompt: Where did Ravi and his team heat the glass?
options: In a furnace
In a pot
On a stove
In a mould
activities.explanation: Ravi and his team heated the glass in a furnace.

activities.prompt: They carefully shaped the hot ______ into bangles.
activities.hint: What did they heat and shape?
activities.explanation: They carefully shaped the hot glass into bangles.

activities.title: Match the Steps
activities.prompt: Match each part with what happened to it.
activities.explanation: The glass was heated, shaped, decorated and then cooled.

activities.title: A Busy Festival
activities.prompt: When did demand for glass bangles increase?
options: During Diwali
During winter
On birthdays
At weekends
activities.explanation: Demand increased during Diwali, the festival of lights, celebration and joy.

activities.title: Order of Making
activities.prompt: Put the stages of making the bangles in order.
activities.explanation: The glass was heated, shaped, decorated and cooled.

activities.title: Working Hard
activities.prompt: Why did the artisans work around the clock?
options: To meet the demand
To repair tools
To count colours
To decorate walls
activities.explanation: The artisans worked around the clock because demand had increased.

activities.prompt: Ravi checks one bangle again before moving on. What does this show?
options: He is bored by the bangle work.
He is angry with the hot glass.
He is careful about each bangle.
He wants to leave the bangle unfinished.

The child mistakes careful checking for boredom.
The child mistakes concentration for anger.
The child thinks checking means he will stop working.

activities.explanation: Ravi gives each bangle his full attention.

activities.prompt: The team lets the decorated bangles cool. Why is this important?
options: It helps finish the bangles carefully and well.
It puts new colours onto the soft glass.
It heats the glass so it can be shaped.
It changes the bangles back into plain glass.

Cooling comes after the colours and designs are added.
The glass is heated before it is shaped and cooled.
why.It changes the bangles back into plain g: Cooling does not change the bangles back into glass.

activities.explanation: Cooling the decorated bangles to perfection gives them a careful finish.

activities.prompt: Diwali brings celebration and joy. Why are glass bangles popular among women at Diwali?
options: They need bangles to make the festival lights.
They enjoy colourful bangles for the happy festival.
They want fewer bangles during this happy time.
They think colourful bangles are unpopular then.

why.They need bangles to make the festival l: The child mixes up bangles with the festival’s lights.
why.They want fewer bangles during this happ: The child reverses the increase in demand.
why.They think colourful bangles are unpopul: The child denies that bangles were popular then.

activities.explanation: Popular colourful bangles suit the joy of Diwali.

activities.prompt: Hot glass comes from the furnace. What will the team do next?
options: They will add designs before shaping it.
They will leave it to become a bangle.
They will cool it before it becomes soft.
They will shape it into a bangle.

The facts place shaping before adding colours and designs.
The team must shape the glass; it does not change by itself.
why.They will cool it before it becomes soft: Hot glass is shaped before it is cooled.

activities.explanation: The team carefully shapes the hot glass into a bangle.

lessons.title: Let us Read – Ananya’s New Designs

activities.prompt: How did Ananya make traditional bangles feel new and beautiful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ananya’s Brilliant New Designs
activities.body: Ananya was Ravi’s daughter and had finished school. She wanted to help her father at work. She had a good eye for design. She combined traditional and modern bangle designs. She added floral patterns and geometric shapes. Ravi soon saw the beauty in her designs. The collection became a big success. Women and girls wore the bangles. It helped the whole community. It created more work for local artisans.
keyPoints: Ananya helped her father after finishing school.
She mixed traditional and modern designs.
The successful collection helped the community and artisans.
activities.explanation: Ananya’s careful ideas turned into a successful bangle collection.

activities.prompt: How did Ananya’s design choices lead to a successful bangle collection?
steps: Ananya had a good eye, so she could improve traditional bangles.
She added modern elements to bring old and new designs together.
Ravi first hesitated, but her design beauty soon changed his mind.
Together, her choices won approval and made the collection a big success.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Ananya want to add to traditional bangle designs?
options: modern elements
traditional elements
floral patterns
geometric shapes
activities.explanation: Ananya wanted to add modern elements to traditional bangle designs.

activities.prompt: Ananya added ______ floral patterns and geometric shapes.
activities.hint: Think of the describing word.
activities.explanation: The patterns were delicate, and the shapes were geometric.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its detail.
pairs: saw the beauty in her designs
activities.explanation: These details show Ananya’s work and the collection’s success.

activities.prompt: Why did Ravi change his mind about Ananya’s designs?
options: He saw the beauty
He finished school
Women wore bangles
Demand increased
activities.explanation: Ravi was first hesitant, but soon saw the beauty in Ananya’s designs.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Ravi saw the beauty in the designs
The collection became a big success
activities.explanation: Ravi first hesitated, then saw the beauty. The successful collection later created more work.

activities.prompt: How did increased demand help local artisans?
options: It created more work
It showed both styles
Women wore the bangles
Ananya finished school
activities.explanation: Increased demand created more work for local artisans.

activities.prompt: Ravi first hesitated, but soon saw the beauty in Ananya’s designs. How did he likely feel at first?
options: He was unsure about the new designs.
He was certain the designs would fail.
He was angry with Ananya’s ideas.
He was pleased with the designs already.

This mistake treats hesitation as certainty about failure.
This mistake reads hesitation as anger, which is not shown.
This mistake assumes Ravi was pleased before he hesitated.

activities.explanation: Hesitation means he felt unsure before seeing their beauty.

activities.prompt: Ananya added modern elements to traditional bangles. She used floral patterns and geometric shapes. What does this show about her design goal?
options: She wanted old and new design ideas together.
She wanted to remove old ideas from bangles.
She wanted to use only new ideas in bangles.
She wanted designs with no changes at all.

why.She wanted to remove old ideas from bang: This mistake ignores that she wanted to keep traditional ideas.
why.She wanted to use only new ideas in bang: This mistake misses that she also wanted traditional ideas.
why.She wanted designs with no changes at al: This mistake assumes she avoided changing traditional bangles.

activities.explanation: This matches her wish to combine both kinds of designs.

activities.prompt: The bangle design kept traditional patterns but added modern geometric shapes. In this sentence, what does “traditional” most likely mean?
options: Connected with older, established design ideas.
Used only for the newest and latest ideas.
Free of every shape and design pattern.
Unrelated to any older design ideas.

why.Used only for the newest and latest idea: This mistake treats traditional as the opposite of new.
This mistake thinks traditional means having no patterns.
This mistake treats traditional as having no connection with older designs.

activities.explanation: Older designs are traditional, and the sentence contrasts them with modern shapes.

activities.prompt: The new collection was a big success. Women and girls wore its bangles. What can we infer about the designs?
options: The designs had earned real popular interest.
The designs had earned very little interest.
Only one person had tried the new bangles.
The bangles were popular with men alone.

why.The designs had earned very little inter: The success and wearers show the opposite of little interest.
why.Only one person had tried the new bangle: A big success cannot involve only one new wearer.
The facts mention women and girls wearing the bangles, not men.

activities.explanation: Success and many wearers together show strong popular interest.

lessons.title: Let us Think and Let us Learn

activities.prompt: Shall we discover how to show what happened first in a story?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Think, Learn and Write
activities.body: Let us think about work, learning and writing. Ravi's team heated glass in a furnace to make the bangles. The new collection created more work for local artisans. Writers should use capital letters, full stops and commas where needed. Past perfect shows an action completed before another action in the past. Past simple shows the later action in the past.
keyPoints: Capital letters, full stops and commas help clear writing.
Past perfect describes the earlier action.
Past simple describes the later action.
activities.explanation: These ideas help us describe earlier work, clearer writing and actions in order.

activities.prompt: Ananya began working at the factory after finishing school. How can we show that school ended first?
steps: Ananya finished school before she joined the factory.
The first action needs past perfect because it happened earlier.
Past perfect follows subject plus has or have, then verb and object.
We write: Ananya had completed her schooling before she joined the factory.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Ravi's team heat in the furnace?
options: glass
portrait
factory
cinema
activities.explanation: The lesson says they heated glass in a furnace to make bangles.

activities.prompt: Writers should use ______ letters, full stops and commas where needed.
activities.hint: The lesson names a kind of letter.
activities.explanation: The lesson says writers should use capital letters, full stops and commas.

activities.prompt: The new collection created more work for local artisans.
activities.explanation: The new collection created more work for local artisans.

activities.prompt: Who had completed school before joining the factory?
options: Ravi
Shivangi
Ananya
Artisans
activities.explanation: Ananya had completed her schooling before she joined the factory.

activities.prompt: Match each earlier action with the later action.
activities.explanation: In each pair, the left action happened before the right action.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of the past perfect rule in order.
activities.explanation: The rule is Subject + has/have + Verb + Object.

activities.prompt: A child had brushed their teeth before the lights went out. What came first?
options: The teeth were brushed before the lights went out.
The teeth were brushed after the lights went out.
The teeth and lights were brushed together.
The lights were brushed before the teeth were brushed.

why.The teeth were brushed after the lights: This wrongly places brushing after the lights went out.
why.The teeth and lights were brushed togeth: This wrongly treats both actions as happening together.
why.The lights were brushed before the teeth: This wrongly changes brushing into an action on the lights.

activities.explanation: This shows brushing happened before the lights went out.

activities.prompt: Ravi’s team had heated the glass before it made the bangles. What happened first?
options: The glass was heated before the bangles were made.
The bangles were made before the glass was heated.
The glass and bangles were heated together.
The bangles were heated before the glass was made.

why.The bangles were made before the glass w: This reverses the order of heating and making.
why.The glass and bangles were heated togeth: This wrongly makes both actions happen at once.
why.The bangles were heated before the glass: This confuses the glass with the finished bangles.

activities.explanation: Past perfect marks heating as the earlier action.

activities.prompt: The new collection gave local artisans more work. How might they have felt?
options: Happy that they had more work to do.
Angry that nobody wanted their work.
Sad that their work had ended.
Worried that no more work would come.

Anger does not follow from receiving more work.
Sadness would fit if their work had ended.
More work alone does not show worry about the future.

activities.explanation: More work can make people feel happy and useful.

activities.prompt: The movie had ended before we reached the cinema hall. Why use “had ended”?
options: It shows the ending happened first.
It shows the ending happened second.
It shows both events happened today.
It shows the ending happened last.

This wrongly places the ending after our arrival.
This wrongly treats both past actions as present actions.
Past perfect marks the earlier action, not the later one.

activities.explanation: Past perfect shows the ending happened before our arrival.

lessons.title: Let us Speak and Let us Listen

activities.prompt: What words can we say, and how can we listen carefully together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speaking and listening carefully
activities.body: Say each practice line and notice repeated sounds and key words. Listen for what happens in the bangles story and the cooking story. Children can share crafts or traditions from their region when they are linked to festivals. Glass bangles are important in Indian culture, especially during festivals. In the cooking story, the family roasts flour and adds ghee and sugar. The mixture cools, becomes round laddus, and is decorated.
keyPoints: Notice repeated sounds and key words in practice lines.
Glass bangles are important during festivals.
Follow the steps from roasting flour to decorated laddus.
activities.explanation: Listen carefully and keep every word clear.

activities.prompt: How do the children make decorated laddus from the roasted mixture?
steps: The mother roasts the flour, so it turns golden brown.
The father adds ghee and sugar to prepare the mixture for shaping.
The mixture goes into a bowl so that it can cool.
Once cool, they shape small laddus and decorate them with chopped nuts.

activities.prompt: In “Ravi read a red book,” what does “red” describe?

It describes the book's owner.

It describes the reading speed.

This mistake treats “red” as naming the owner.
This mistake treats “red” as describing the length.
This mistake treats “red” as describing reading speed.

activities.prompt: Babli buys beautiful bangles, but they break. How might she feel?

She may feel excited about the broken bangles.
She may feel calm about the broken bangles.
She may feel proud of the broken bangles.

why.She may feel excited about the broken ba: This mistake thinks breaking is an exciting event.
why.She may feel calm about the broken bangl: This mistake thinks breaking causes no unhappy feeling.
why.She may feel proud of the broken bangles: This mistake thinks broken bangles are a reason for pride.

activities.explanation: Beautiful bangles breaking can make Babli feel upset.

activities.prompt: A child repeats “Red lorry blue lorry” many times. What is the child doing?
options: Practising how to say the line.
Counting how many lorries there are.
Drawing the red and blue lorries.
Choosing which lorry looks better.

This mistake treats repeating words as counting objects.
This mistake assumes the words describe a drawing task.
This mistake assumes the child is choosing between lorries.

activities.prompt: “Ten tiny turtles take turns talking.” What does “take turns” suggest?

They all talk at the same time.
They talk without taking turns.
They never talk to one another.

This mistake ignores the idea of each turtle waiting.
This mistake notices “talking” but ignores “take turns.”
This mistake changes talking into complete silence.

Roasting makes the flour wet.
Roasting makes the flour blue.
Roasting makes the flour smaller.

This mistake wrongly links roasting with adding water.
This mistake gives the flour a colour that was not stated.
This mistake confuses a colour change with a size change.

lessons.title: Let us Write, Let us Do and Let us Explore

activities.prompt: Ready to write, create, explore, and discover how your money can grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Write, explore and save
activities.body: You will write about a festival you recently celebrated and a picture you saw with your teacher. You will find Indian places known for crafts. You will also learn what the place named by your State or Union Territory is famous for, then speak about it. Next, you will follow steps to create a rangoli. Finally, you will learn how a savings account keeps money safe and gives interest as a reward.
keyPoints: Write two paragraphs with the required word lengths.
Research craft places and what your area is famous for.
Create a rangoli and learn about saving money.
activities.explanation: This lesson brings together writing, craft research, rangoli and saving.

activities.prompt: A child received birthday money and wants to keep it safely.
steps: The child should use a bank account because it is safe for keeping money.
Birthday money can be put there because a Savings Account can hold it.
After one year, the bank adds five rupees because saving earns interest.
So the child should save it while knowing it can be withdrawn anytime.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which task matches an 80–100-word paragraph?
options: Writing about a recently celebrated festival
Writing about a picture with your teacher
Finding Indian places known for crafts
Learning what your area is famous for
activities.explanation: You write an 80–100-word paragraph about a festival you recently celebrated.

activities.prompt: A bank account is a safe place for keeping money.
activities.explanation: Yes, a bank account keeps your money safe.

activities.prompt: Match each task with its description.
pairs: Find Indian places known for crafts
Speak about what your State or Union Territory is famous for
activities.explanation: Each task has a clear purpose in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the lesson tasks in the order you will do them.
items: Find Indian places known for crafts
Find what your State or Union Territory is famous for
Speak about what your State or Union Territory is famous for
activities.explanation: You first complete both writing tasks, then research and speak about local fame.

activities.prompt: What can you do with money in a savings account at any time?
options: Add it but never withdraw it
Withdraw it but never add it
Add or withdraw it
Neither add nor withdraw it
activities.explanation: Money can be added or withdrawn from a savings account at any time.

activities.prompt: Match each banking word with the correct description.
pairs: A safe place for keeping money
Where birthday money can be put
Five rupees added by the bank
activities.explanation: A savings account keeps money safe, and saving earns interest.

activities.prompt: A bank account is safe for keeping money. Birthday money can go into a Savings Account. Why is saving it there a good choice?
options: The money stays safe and saving earns interest.
The money stays safe, but saving earns no reward.
The money earns interest, but it is not safe.
The money stays safe, but it must stay there forever.

why.The money stays safe, but saving earns n: This misunderstands interest as no reward for saving.
why.The money earns interest, but it is not: This misunderstands a bank account as an unsafe place for money.
why.The money stays safe, but it must stay t: This confuses saving with being unable to withdraw money anytime.

activities.explanation: This is right because saving keeps money safe and earns interest.

activities.prompt: The bank adds five rupees after a year. The child saved money. What does this extra money show?
options: Saving money earns a reward called interest.
Interest means the child must pay the bank.
Interest means the saved money is no longer the child's.
Interest means savings cannot earn a reward.

why.Interest means the child must pay the ba: This confuses interest with a payment made to the bank.
why.Interest means the saved money is no lon: This misunderstands interest as taking away the child's savings.
why.Interest means savings cannot earn a rew: This confuses interest, which is a reward, with no reward.

activities.explanation: This is right because the extra five rupees is interest for saving.

activities.prompt: Money can be added or withdrawn from a savings account at any time. A child needs birthday money now. What can the child do?
options: Withdraw some money from the savings account.
Wait one year before taking money out.
Ask the bank to add five rupees now.
Keep the money outside the savings account.

This confuses interest waiting time with withdrawal waiting time.
This confuses interest, which comes after a year, with money added now.
why.Keep the money outside the savings accou: This avoids the account because the child thinks saved money cannot be withdrawn.

activities.explanation: This is right because money can be withdrawn from a savings account anytime.

activities.prompt: Children follow steps to create a beautiful rangoli. Why do the steps help?
options: They guide the child through making the rangoli.
They show where the child should open a bank account.
They find places known for different Indian crafts.
They tell the child what their State is famous for.

why.They show where the child should open a: This mistakes rangoli steps for instructions about a bank account.
why.They find places known for different Ind: This mistakes rangoli steps for the craft-place activity.
why.They tell the child what their State is: This mistakes rangoli steps for the State or Union Territory activity.

activities.explanation: This is right because the steps guide the child while making the rangoli.

activities.context: In the busy district of Firozabad, Ravi continues his family’s long-standing craft of making beautiful glass bangles. Each bangle is a piece of art, showing the town’s culture and the skill of its artisans. Ravi’s workshop is always a centre of activity. The air is filled with the sound of glass clinking together, while the artisans’ conversation makes a gentle hum.
activities.prompt: If the artisans stopped talking while Ravi worked, what would probably happen next?
options: The workshop would remain lively, but its gentle background hum would disappear.
The workshop would become completely silent because the glass would stop clinking.
The sound of the clinking glass would suddenly become much louder.
The bangles would stop showing the town’s culture and the artisans’ skill.

why.The workshop would become completely sil: Incorrect: the glass could still clink even without conversation.
why.The sound of the clinking glass would su: Incorrect: stopping conversation would not make the clinking sound louder.
why.The bangles would stop showing the town’: Incorrect: the bangles’ cultural meaning comes from their design and craftsmanship, not conversation.

activities.explanation: Correct: quiet conversation would remove the hum, but the workshop would remain active.

activities.context: In the busy district of Firozabad, Ravi continues his family’s long-standing craft of making beautiful glass bangles. Each bangle is a piece of art, showing the town’s culture and the skill of its artisans. Ravi’s workshop is always a centre of activity. The air is filled with the sound of glass clinking together, while the artisans’ conversation makes a gentle hum.
activities.prompt: Which detail best explains why Ravi’s workshop is a centre of activity?
options: The clinking glass and the hum of artisans talking fill the workshop with sound.
Firozabad is a busy district in Uttar Pradesh.
Ravi’s family has made beautiful bangles for a very long time.
Firozabad is famous for its beautiful glass bangles.

why.Firozabad is a busy district in Uttar Pr: Incorrect: the district may be busy, but this does not directly describe the workshop.
why.Ravi’s family has made beautiful bangles: Incorrect: the family’s long history does not show what happens in the workshop now.
why.Firozabad is famous for its beautiful gl: Incorrect: the town’s fame does not explain the activity inside Ravi’s workshop.

activities.explanation: Correct: the two sounds directly show that the workshop is active.

activities.context: During Diwali, demand for glass bangles rose. Ravi and his team heated glass in a furnace and carefully shaped the hot glass into bangles. They added beautiful colours and designs, then cooled the decorated bangles to perfection. Ravi gave each bangle his full attention and checked that every one was beautiful and long-lasting. The bangles came in many colours and were popular among women. To meet the high demand, the artisans worked around the clock.
activities.prompt: Diwali demand is high and the team is tired after working around the clock. What should they do to keep the quality of their bangles?
options: Keep following the careful steps and give every piece the same close attention.
Skip the cooling stage so more pieces can be sent out sooner.
Shape the glass less carefully because speed matters more.
Stop decorating the pieces so the team can work faster.

why.Skip the cooling stage so more pieces ca: Cooling is necessary to complete the process properly.
why.Shape the glass less carefully because s: Careless shaping could spoil the hot glass.
why.Stop decorating the pieces so the team c: The bangles need colours and designs.

activities.explanation: Careful work and full attention protect beauty and long-lasting quality.

activities.context: During Diwali, demand for glass bangles rose. Ravi and his team heated glass in a furnace and carefully shaped the hot glass into bangles. They added beautiful colours and designs, then cooled the decorated bangles to perfection. Ravi gave each bangle his full attention and checked that every one was beautiful and long-lasting. The bangles came in many colours and were popular among women. To meet the high demand, the artisans worked around the clock.
activities.prompt: If the artisans could no longer work around the clock, what would be the most likely result?
options: Fewer bangles would be available, so some of the increased demand could go unmet.
More bangles would be available, so all the increased demand would be met.
The number of colours would increase without any extra work.
The same number of bangles would be available because working hours do not affect production.

why.More bangles would be available, so all: Fewer working hours do not guarantee greater production.
why.The number of colours would increase wit: New colours require decoration and careful work.
why.The same number of bangles would be avai: Working hours affect how many bangles can be made.

activities.explanation: Less working time could reduce production and leave some demand unmet.

activities.prompt: Explain why making glass bangles required great skill.
activities.answer: Making glass bangles required great skill because the glass had to be heated in a furnace, shaped while hot, decorated, and cooled properly. The worker also had to give every bangle full attention so that it looked beautiful and lasted for a long time.
points: The glass was heated in a furnace.
The hot glass was carefully shaped.
Colours and designs were added.
Every bangle received full attention.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ananya had completed her schooling and was eager to help Ravi with his work. With a good eye for design, she combined traditional bangle designs with modern elements, adding delicate floral patterns and geometric shapes. Ravi was first hesitant, but soon saw the beauty in her designs. The collection showed both kinds of elements and became a big success. Women and girls wore the bangles, increased demand created more work for local artisans, and the whole community benefited.
activities.prompt: After the success of Ananya’s designs, what should Ravi do next?
options: Encourage Ananya to keep developing designs that respect the old style while adding fresh ideas.
Limit all future designs to traditional patterns and ignore Ananya’s new ideas.
Ask Ananya to stop contributing because she has already completed her schooling.
Reject Ananya’s future ideas without considering how well her previous ideas were received.

why.Limit all future designs to traditional: Option 2 ignores the value of the modern elements.
why.Ask Ananya to stop contributing because: Option 3 wrongly treats completed schooling as the end of Ananya’s contributions.
why.Reject Ananya’s future ideas without con: Option 4 ignores the success of Ananya’s previous designs.

activities.explanation: Option 1 supports creativity while keeping traditional designs.

activities.context: Ananya had completed her schooling and was eager to help Ravi with his work. With a good eye for design, she combined traditional bangle designs with modern elements, adding delicate floral patterns and geometric shapes. Ravi was first hesitant, but soon saw the beauty in her designs. The collection showed both kinds of elements and became a big success. Women and girls wore the bangles, increased demand created more work for local artisans, and the whole community benefited.
activities.prompt: If Ravi had continued to refuse Ananya’s ideas, what would likely have happened?
options: Her ideas might have received less support, so the successful designs and wider community benefits might not have followed.
The collection would have included only old patterns, because fresh ideas were less important.
Local artisans would have received much less work, even though the community would have remained unaffected.
Women and girls would have rejected the bangles because Ravi had not approved the designs.

why.The collection would have included only: Option 2 wrongly suggests that traditional designs alone were more important.
why.Local artisans would have received much: Option 3 contradicts the positive effect that greater demand had on the community.
why.Women and girls would have rejected the: Option 4 focuses on Ravi’s approval rather than the beauty and appeal of Ananya’s work.

activities.explanation: Option 1 connects Ravi’s support with the later success and community benefits.

activities.prompt: How did the success of Ananya’s collection affect the community?
activities.answer: The collection’s success meant that women and girls wore the new bangles. It also had a positive impact on the whole community. In particular, demand increased, so local artisans had more work. Ananya’s design ideas therefore affected customers, the community, and the people making the bangles.
points: Women and girls wore the new bangles.
The collection was a big success.
Demand increased.
Local artisans received more work.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi’s team heated glass in a furnace to make bangles. Ananya was Ravi’s daughter, and she had completed her schooling before she joined the factory. The new collection created more work for local artisans. Shivangi had finished the portrait before I called her, just as a movie had ended before we reached the cinema hall.
activities.prompt: If Ananya had joined the factory before completing her schooling, which choice should she make?
options: She should not enter the factory until her education is complete.
She should enter the factory first and finish her schooling later.
She should treat both actions as past simple because they happened in the past.
She should treat both actions as past perfect because the first action came first.

why.She should enter the factory first and f: This reverses the required order of the actions.
why.She should treat both actions as past si: The earlier completed action needs past perfect, not past simple.
why.She should treat both actions as past pe: Only the first action uses past perfect; the second uses past simple.

activities.explanation: The first action must be completed before the second action begins.

activities.context: Ravi’s team heated glass in a furnace to make bangles. Ananya was Ravi’s daughter, and she had completed her schooling before she joined the factory. The new collection created more work for local artisans. Shivangi had finished the portrait before I called her, just as a movie had ended before we reached the cinema hall.
activities.prompt: If the new collection continued, what would happen to local artisans?
options: Their workload would increase.
Their workload would decrease.
Their workload would remain unchanged.
They would have no work.

The given fact does not show that their work decreased.
The collection caused an increase rather than no change.
The case states that the artisans received more work.

activities.explanation: The collection created more work for local artisans.

activities.prompt: Explain why past perfect is used for the first action in Ananya’s sentence and how it differs from past simple.
activities.answer: Ananya had completed her schooling before she joined the factory. Her schooling was completed first, so it uses past perfect. Joining the factory happened later and uses past simple. The pattern for the first action is Subject + has/have + Verb + Object.
points: Identifies schooling as the first completed action.
Explains that it happened before she joined the factory.
Uses past perfect for the first action.
Uses past simple for the second action.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a festival, children share crafts and traditions from their regions that are linked to festivals. Meera says, “Red lorry blue lorry,” and the group practises listening and speaking. The mother roasts chickpea flour in a pan until it turns golden brown. The father adds ghee and sugar, and the mixture goes into a bowl to cool. Meera and Arjun then shape it into small round balls. The children decorate each laddu with chopped nuts.
activities.prompt: The flour is still pale when the father is ready to add ghee and sugar. What should he do first?
options: Wait until the roasted flour has turned golden brown before adding ghee and sugar.
Add ghee and sugar while the flour is still pale, and leave everything in the pan.
Add sugar before roasting the flour, but wait to add ghee until the mixture is in a bowl.
Pour ghee into the pan before roasting begins, and add sugar afterwards.

why.Add ghee and sugar while the flour is st: Adding the ingredients before the flour reaches the right colour changes the correct order.
why.Add sugar before roasting the flour, but: Sugar is added together with the ghee after roasting, not before it.
why.Pour ghee into the pan before roasting b: Ghee is added after the flour has been roasted, not before roasting begins.

activities.explanation: The flour turns golden brown during roasting, and the ghee and sugar are added afterwards.

activities.context: During a festival, children share crafts and traditions from their regions that are linked to festivals. Meera says, “Red lorry blue lorry,” and the group practises listening and speaking. The mother roasts chickpea flour in a pan until it turns golden brown. The father adds ghee and sugar, and the mixture goes into a bowl to cool. Meera and Arjun then shape it into small round balls. The children decorate each laddu with chopped nuts.
activities.prompt: A child shares a craft from the child’s region that is linked to a festival. What should the group do?
options: Invite the child to explain the craft while everyone listens carefully.
Invite the child to explain, but let everyone talk over the speaker at the same time.
Ask the child to show the craft without explaining it because only listening is needed.
Wait until the festival has ended before allowing the child to share the craft.

why.Invite the child to explain, but let eve: Talking over the speaker prevents the group from listening carefully.
why.Ask the child to show the craft without: Listening includes hearing an explanation about the craft that is being shared.
why.Wait until the festival has ended before: Children can share festival-linked crafts and traditions during the festival activity.

activities.explanation: Explaining and listening help the group practise speaking and listening during the sharing activity.

activities.prompt: Explain why the mixture is transferred to a bowl before it is shaped.
activities.answer: The mixture is transferred to a bowl so that it can cool. Meera and Arjun shape it into small round balls after that. The children then decorate each laddu with chopped nuts. Therefore, cooling in the bowl comes before shaping, and decorating comes last.
points: The bowl is used so the mixture can cool.
Shaping into small round balls happens after cooling.
Decorating each laddu with chopped nuts comes after shaping.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child received birthday money and put it into a Savings Account. After a year, the bank added five rupees as interest, so the child had the birthday money and the bank’s reward. The child also planned to follow the steps to create a beautiful rangoli. When the child needed some of the saved money, the child remembered that money can be added or withdrawn from a savings account at any time and chose to withdraw only part of it.
activities.prompt: After one year, which choice best shows what the child should do with the five-rupee interest?
options: Leave the birthday money saved and withdraw only the five-rupee reward if it is needed.
Leave the five-rupee reward saved and withdraw the birthday money instead.
Take out both the birthday money and the five-rupee reward.
Do not withdraw anything, because only the bank can return saved money.

why.Leave the five-rupee reward saved and wi: The original birthday money can remain safely saved.
why.Take out both the birthday money and the: Withdrawing everything would leave no money in the account.
why.Do not withdraw anything, because only t: Savings can be withdrawn whenever they are needed.

activities.explanation: The five rupees is extra money earned as interest.

activities.context: A child received birthday money and put it into a Savings Account. After a year, the bank added five rupees as interest, so the child had the birthday money and the bank’s reward. The child also planned to follow the steps to create a beautiful rangoli. When the child needed some of the saved money, the child remembered that money can be added or withdrawn from a savings account at any time and chose to withdraw only part of it.
activities.prompt: Why did the child’s balance become larger after one year?
options: Keeping the deposit in the account brought the child an extra amount as a reward.
The child’s plan to make a beautiful rangoli caused the balance to grow.
Withdrawing money caused the account to gain another five rupees.
Receiving birthday money caused the bank to add five rupees immediately.

why.The child’s plan to make a beautiful ran: Making a rangoli is not the reason for earning interest.
why.Withdrawing money caused the account to: Withdrawal reduces the money available in the account.
why.Receiving birthday money caused the bank: The five rupees was added after a year as interest.

activities.explanation: Money saved in an account earns interest as a reward.

activities.prompt: How does putting birthday money into a Savings Account help a child who wants to plan for making a rangoli?
activities.answer: The child can put birthday money into a Savings Account, where it is safe. Some can be withdrawn whenever it is needed for making the rangoli. After a year, the bank adds five rupees as interest. This rewards the child for saving, while the rest remains available.
points: Birthday money can be put into a Savings Account.
A Savings Account is a safe place for money.
Money can be withdrawn whenever it is needed.
The bank adds five rupees after a year as interest.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.
